## Suggested Reading Paths {#sec-vol2-about-reading-paths}

The chapters are ordered so that each can draw on everything before it, but not every chapter consumes the one immediately before it. @Fig-vol2-chapter-dependencies draws the direct dependencies, derived from the chapters' own cross-references: an arrow means the later chapter uses a model, mechanism, or constraint that the earlier one establishes. Two features of the map guide the choice of path. First, every chapter lies on a route to @sec-conclusion, whose six principles cite every chapter of Parts I through IV, so no chapter is a dead end. Second, several dependencies cross part boundaries: fleet orchestration builds on both @sec-collective-communication and @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability, and serving builds on orchestration. Consecutive chapters without an arrow mark a change of thread rather than a gap. @Sec-performance-engineering, for example, returns to the cost of a single distributed job and builds on the communication model, while @sec-fleet-orchestration feeds the serving chapter that follows it.

```

Epoch AI's database of notable models records, for each training run it can document, the compute the run consumed together with how many accelerators it used and for how long [@epochai2026notable]. Plotted run by run, training compute climbs steadily on a logarithmic scale, and it separates early single-node vision models from multi-node transformer training (@fig-training-compute-trend, panel a). Because training compute is the product of the accelerator count, the training duration, and the rate each accelerator delivers, the same records also show where the growth came from. Across the `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.run_count_str` runs from 2012 through 2024 that report all three, compute grew about `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.compute_mult_str` per year. The accelerator count grew `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.count_mult_str` per year, the duration `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.duration_mult_str`, and the delivered rate per accelerator, which folds in both faster hardware and better utilization, `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.rate_mult_str` (@fig-training-compute-trend, panel b). A higher delivered rate per accelerator supplied roughly half of the exponential. More accelerators running for longer supplied the other `{python} TrainingComputeGrowth.fleet_share_pct_str`, and that half is the fleet's to deliver.

title: The scale discontinuity
caption: **The scale discontinuity**: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C$^3$ roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.
alt: Two panels. Left, labeled single machine: one node frame holding four dark accelerator squares above four stacks of HBM layers, each accelerator joined to its stack by a link that crosses a red dashed band labeled memory wall; text below reads no peers to wait for. Right, labeled fleet: a scheduler and recovery box above a dashed enclosure holding eight small node frames in two rows, each a miniature of the left node with four accelerators; all connect to a central network fabric bar that sits inside a red dashed band labeled network wall. One node is marked failed, one is marked slow with a dashed red border, and the other six are labeled waiting. A legend maps dark blue to compute C1, amber to communication C2, and violet to coordination C3.
section: Span bracket: AlexNet to Llama 3, the climb the prose names.
context:
:::

Moving from one machine to many changes the governing physics of the system, not merely its device count. A single node is bound locally by the memory wall between its accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and it has no peers to wait for. A fleet executes across a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places and recovers the job, which exposes the workload to the network wall, to stragglers, and to routine node failures (@fig-scale-moment-discontinuity).

title: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps
caption: **Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps**: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker's gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.
alt: Two timelines with time running left to right. Left, MapReduce: map tasks 1 and 2 run, emit a green output square, and are labeled done; map task 3 runs briefly, is marked failed with a red cross, and then a re-run alone bar on the same lane emits its output, which feeds a reduce bar on the lane below. Right, synchronous training: workers 0 and 1 finish their compute bars early and then show gray wait segments, while worker 2 runs a long red dashed bar labeled slow; all three bars end at an amber AllReduce band, after which an update bar runs on the lane below.
section: Independent tasks vs. synchronous fleet dynamics {#sec-introduction-traditional-vs-ml-fleet-dynamics-c43e}
context:
:::

The two execution pathways differ at the point of failure (@fig-traditional-vs-ml-fleet). In MapReduce, a failed map task is retried on its own while its peers complete. In synchronous data-parallel training, where every worker holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of each batch, every worker must contribute its gradient to an AllReduce, a collective operation that combines the gradients of all workers and returns the result to each of them, before the shared parameter update can occur. A slow map task can delay downstream reduction and job completion, but other map tasks finish without waiting; in synchronous training, by contrast, healthy workers sit idle whenever a straggler delays the collective.

title: Model training compute trends
caption: **Model training compute trends**: Training compute has grown exponentially, accelerating dramatically in the deep learning era. The fitted trends shift from roughly 1.4$\times$ per year before 2010, close to Moore's Law (a doubling about every 2 years), to roughly 4$\times$ per year inside the deep learning era, far steeper than Moore's Law. The fastest stretch was steeper still. Within the 2012--2019 frontier subset measured by an earlier study [@amodei2018ai], compute doubled approximately every 3.4 months. This trajectory explains why efficiency has become a strategic imperative rather than an optional optimization.
alt: Scatter plot of training compute from 1950 to 2025 on log scale. Points show exponential growth accelerating after 2012, with a fitted trend of about 1.4x per year before 2010, close to Moore's Law at about 2 years per doubling, and about 4x per year in the deep learning era, far steeper than Moore's Law.
context:
```

The growth trajectory establishes demand for larger fleets; empirical scaling laws guide how that demand should be allocated. At the budgets traced at the scale moment, estimating the return on additional resources is an engineering necessity rather than a research curiosity. Over the longer history of AI, the fitted growth rate of training compute itself changed around 2010, from about 1.4$\times$ per year, close to Moore's Law, to about 4$\times$ per year in the deep learning era [@sevilla2022] (@fig-compute-trends). A fourfold annual rise is two doublings a year, while accelerators per run doubled about once a year over the period traced at the scale moment. Training compute is the product of accelerator count, per-accelerator throughput, and run duration, so faster accelerators and longer runs supply the other doubling. A demand curve that steep makes misallocation expensive, which is why the model-loss measurements that follow matter.

title: Optimal compute allocation
caption: **Optimal compute allocation**: For fixed computational budgets, language model performance depends on balancing model size and training data size; the left panel maps training loss across parameter counts, identifying an efficiency sweet spot for each FLOP level. The center and right panels quantify how optimal parameter counts and token requirements scale predictably as compute increases, demonstrating the need to scale model size and data together to use large training budgets efficiently.
alt: Three-panel figure. Left: IsoFLOP curves with U-shaped valleys identifying optimal model sizes. Center: optimal parameters scaling with compute. Right: optimal tokens scaling with compute. Both follow power-law relationships.
context:
@Fig-compute-optimal decomposes this compute-optimal allocation across three empirical views. In the left panel, U-shaped IsoFLOP contours\index{IsoFLOP curve!optimal model size} plot training loss against parameter counts for fixed compute budgets, with each curve's valley minimum identifying the optimal model capacity for that FLOP ceiling. The center and right panels track how optimal parameters and training tokens scale along coordinated power-law trajectories as compute expands, confirming that compute-optimal training\index{Compute-optimal training!resource allocation} requires advancing model size and token volume in tandem. The highlighted projection markers extrapolate these fits to larger budgets, for example 63B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens for a total of a little over $5 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs,[^fn-flops-work-rate] illustrating how compute-optimal frontiers guide resource allocation before cluster execution begins.

[^fn-flops-work-rate]: **FLOPs vs. FLOP/s**\index{FLOP/s vs. FLOPs}: FLOPs denotes total computational work (operations performed), while FLOP/s denotes hardware throughput (operations per second)\index{FLOP/s!work vs. throughput}; confusing the two leads to incorrect cost estimates. GPT-3 required `{python} Gpt3StatsScenario.gpt3_training_ops_str` of work; an A100 delivers `{python} Gpt3StatsScenario.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` of throughput. Dividing work by peak throughput gives ideal wall-clock time, the roughly `{python} Gpt3SingleAccelerator.ideal_years_str` years on one A100 computed at the scale moment. Actual time is approximately $\text{work}/(\EfficiencyHw \PeakRate)$, where the hardware utilization $\EfficiencyHw$ is the achieved fraction of peak throughput, so utilization below one multiplies ideal time by $1/\EfficiencyHw$.

title: Scaling laws and compute optimality
caption: **Scaling laws and compute optimality**: Larger models consistently achieve better performance with increased training data and compute, but diminishing returns necessitate careful resource allocation during training. Optimal model size and training duration depend on the available compute budget, as evidenced by the convergence of loss curves at different parameter scales and training token counts.
alt: Two log-scale plots. Left: test loss vs. tokens processed for models from 10^3 to 10^9 parameters, showing larger models achieve lower loss. Right: loss vs. compute, showing convergence at different parameter scales.
context:
@kaplan2020scaling demonstrated that transformer-based language-model loss follows predictable power-law relationships with model parameters, dataset size (measured in tokens), and total computational budget. The result was not a license to increase every dimension blindly; it showed that model quality depends on coordinated allocation across those resources, a point later sharpened by Chinchilla's compute-optimal scaling analysis [@hoffmann2022chinchilla].

Two further results appear in Kaplan's measurements across parameter scales from $10^3$ to $10^9$ (@fig-kaplan-scaling). Larger models are more sample-efficient, reaching a target loss with substantially fewer training tokens. Compute-efficient training therefore stops far short of full convergence, because an early-stopped larger model attains the target loss with less total compute than a smaller model trained to its plateau.

title: Loss vs. dataset size across model scales
caption: **Loss vs. dataset size across model scales**: Test loss curves show how models of different sizes (393.2K to 708M parameters) benefit from increased training data. Larger models achieve lower loss, but all curves exhibit diminishing returns at high token counts. Points and curves are digitized from Figure 4 (left) of @kaplan2020scaling, so values carry the precision of a reading from the published plot.
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of loss vs. tokens in dataset. Six curves for model sizes from 393.2K to 708M parameters, shaded from light to dark blue by model size and labeled at their right ends; the three largest also use square, diamond, and triangle markers. Italic labels mark small models: capacity plateau between the two flattest curves, shared power-law descent along the line the larger curves follow together, and large models: lower floor, set under the lowest curve where it levels off below all the others.
context:
Applying scaling laws in practice is a scarcity diagnosis, which asks which resource prevents balanced growth first. Compute budget, data availability, and model size create three regimes with different optimal responses.

In a compute-limited regime\index{Compute-limited regime!resource allocation}, compute scarcity restricts scaling potential despite abundant training data; measured learning curves guide the allocation between model size and training tokens within that budget. In a data-limited regime\index{Data!limited regime}, computational resources exceed what the available dataset can support, meaning that increasing model size is useful only if validation measurements show that the available data can support additional capacity. Between these extremes lies the optimal regime\index{Optimal regime!Chinchilla frontier}, where compute and data grow in balance following compute-optimal scaling laws, as DeepMind demonstrated with Chinchilla by outperforming much larger models through proportional scaling of model size and training data [@hoffmann2022chinchilla]. Recognizing which regime governs a given project prevents common inefficiencies: over-parameterized models with insufficient training data, or under-parameterized models that waste available compute. For the fleet, the diagnosis decides where the next investment goes. A compute-limited project needs accelerator-hours, while a data-limited one gains more from the storage and data pipelines of @sec-data-storage than from additional accelerators.

title: The reliability collapse
caption: **The reliability collapse**: The simultaneous availability of every node required by an unreplicated job, shown as a function of job size for two per-node availability levels under an independence assumption. At `{python} ReliabilityGap.node_availability_str` per-node availability (blue), all-node availability is only `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_1k_str` for a `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_small_str`-node job and approaches zero for a `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_large_str`-node job. Even `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_pct_str` per-node availability (green) yields `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_four_nines_10k_str` at `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_large_str`-node scale.
alt: Line chart with log-scale x-axis showing simultaneous all-node availability vs. job size from 1 to 10000 required nodes. Two curves decline from 100 percent, labeled 99.9 percent and 99.99 percent per node. The 99.9 percent curve reaches 36.8 percent at 1000 nodes and 0.0045 percent at 10000, with the region under it beyond 1000 shaded red and labeled collapse zone; the 99.99 percent curve reaches the same 36.8 percent at 10000 nodes, and an arrow between the two equal points is labeled one more nine postpones the collapse.
context:
For a single component, `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_pct_str` availability corresponds to `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_downtime_str` of unavailability per 365-day year. This is a time fraction, not a count of failures.

If each node has an illustrative `{python} ReliabilityGap.node_availability_str` availability and an unreplicated job requires every node, the probability that all `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_small_str` required nodes are available simultaneously is only `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_1k_str`. Scale that job to `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_large_str` required nodes, and this probability drops to `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_10k_str`. Adding a nine to every node only postpones the collapse, because the exponent $\RequiredComponentCount$ eventually overwhelms any per-node availability below one (@fig-reliability-gap-collapse).

title: The C$^3$ Intersection Landscape
caption: **The C$^3$ Intersection Landscape**: Each circle is one operational dimension (Compute, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1$, the node substrate; Communication, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2$, the network backbone; Coordination, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$, the orchestration layer), labeled with the Fleet Law term it contributes to step time. Each pairwise lens names the interaction between two dimensions: hiding network latency behind computation, maximizing fleet goodput against failure, and synchronizing collectives. At the center, where all three meet, is fleet ML systems engineering. @Tbl-c3-intersections lists the techniques and chapters for each region.
alt: Three overlapping circles labeled Compute C1 (node substrate, T compute over N), Communication C2 (network backbone, T comm of N), and Coordination C3 (orchestration layer, T sync of N). The pairwise overlaps are labeled hiding network latency (C1 and C2), maximizing fleet goodput (C1 and C3), and collective synchronization (C2 and C3). A box at the center, where all three overlap, reads fleet ML systems engineering.
context:
At the center ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$), all three constraints converge simultaneously. Partitioning a model determines both which device computes each operation and what information must cross the network; recovering a failed partition requires restoring the corresponding shared state. These dependencies explain why parallelism, state sharding, and serving policies must be designed together.

Each dimension contributes one term to the distributed step time, and each pairwise overlap names an interface where the dimensions trade costs: hiding latency, preserving goodput, and synchronizing collectives (@fig-c3-taxonomy).

title: Anatomy of a Fleet Law step
caption: **Anatomy of a Fleet Law step**: Each row is one training step for the same workload, with local computation on the upper lane and communication and synchronization on the lower lane. Read the step length from the bracket, not from any single bar: overlap (gray band) removes only the transfer time that runs beneath compute, so doubling the devices halves $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount$ yet leaves $\DistributedStepTime(2\DeviceCount)$ well past the ideal half-length step (dashed line), by the hatched span. Bar lengths are illustrative, not measured.
alt: Two timelines. Top, N devices: a long blue compute bar, and on a second lane an amber communication bar that starts under the end of the compute bar, followed by a violet synchronization bar; a gray band marks where the two bars overlap, and a bracket spans the whole step, with a tick at its midpoint. Bottom, 2N devices: a compute bar half as long, a slightly longer communication bar, a longer synchronization bar, and a shorter bracket. A dashed line drops from the midpoint tick, marking half the original step, and the part of the 2N step to the right of it is hatched and labeled beyond ideal.
context:
*   $\OverlappedTime$ is the Co-Design ($\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2$, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$, $\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3$) term, representing communication or coordination hidden behind useful compute via techniques such as interleaving forward and backward work across pipeline stages, running transfers on separate execution streams, and writing checkpoints asynchronously.

Doubling the device count shows why the subtraction matters. The local compute term falls to $\IronLawComputeTime/(2\DeviceCount)$, but communication and barrier synchronization persist, and the shorter compute window leaves less room to hide transfers, so $\OverlappedTime$ shrinks as well. The step on $2\DeviceCount$ devices therefore takes well over half as long as the step on $\DeviceCount$ (@fig-fleet-law-step).

## Foundational Concepts {#sec-vol2-introduction-foundational-concepts}

Three architectural maps organize this book: the fleet stack locates system responsibility, C$^3$ and the Fleet Law diagnose execution cost, and the lighthouse archetypes test those costs across representative production workloads. The fleet stack, traced upward from the hardware of one node in @sec-vol2-introduction-engineering-crux, arranges the fleet into eight rows grouped into four ascending bands (@fig-fleet-stack). Capabilities fixed in the lower rows, from facility cooling and RDMA fabrics up through distributed execution, constrain the serving runtimes and governance mechanisms above them.

## The Structure of This Textbook {#sec-vol2-introduction-structure}

This textbook organizes around the fleet stack\index{Fleet Stack!textbook structure}, progressing from the physical substrate through the logic of distribution to societal governance. The chapter sequence is a dependency map rather than a topic inventory. Silicon, cooling, and network limits constrain training partitioning; partitioned algorithms create fault-tolerance and orchestration obligations; and those mechanisms support production operation. Requirements also flow in the other direction: security, governance, and service targets constrain which lower-layer designs are acceptable. Part I builds the physical cluster substrate, Part II coordinates distributed execution and fault recovery, Part III optimizes deployment and inference at scale, and Part IV enforces governance, security, and sustainability invariants (@fig-vol2-roadmap).

title: The accelerator spectrum
caption: **The accelerator spectrum**: Each die is drawn as a grid of 100 cells divided between arithmetic units (dark) and control, cache, and other logic (light), with the medium cells marking the spread of each approximate, illustrative share. Read left to right, the arithmetic share grows from 5 to 10 percent on a CPU to over 90 percent on a custom ASIC, because hardwired dataflow replaces instruction fetch, decode, and scheduling; each step buys throughput per watt by narrowing the range of model architectures the silicon runs well.
alt: Four square dies side by side, CPU, GPU, TPU, and custom ASIC, above an arrow running from general purpose to more specialized. Each die is a 10 by 10 grid of cells: dark cells for arithmetic units, medium cells for the range of estimates, and light cells for control, cache, and other logic. The dark share grows from left to right, labeled 5 to 10 percent for the CPU, 50 to 60 percent for the GPU, 70 to 80 percent for the TPU, and over 90 percent for the custom ASIC. A legend directly under the dies names the three cell types, and the arrow closes the figure below it.
context:
Specialized accelerators reduce this tax by replacing general-purpose control with a dataflow matched to the workload. In the approximate shares of @fig-accelerator-spectrum, the arithmetic fraction of the die rises from roughly 5--10 percent on a CPU to 50--60 percent on a GPU, 70--80 percent on a Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), and over 90 percent on a custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). The shares mark a direction rather than measured proportions for any product. The selection question is how much of the complete workload can use the specialized hardware.

:::

title: Wafer-scale engine (WSE) architecture
caption: **Wafer-scale engine (WSE) architecture**: A DGX H100 node (left) joins eight separately packaged GPUs through an NVSwitch fabric and must leave the chassis over InfiniBand to reach other nodes, so every exchange crosses a package, board, or network boundary. A WSE (right) instead uses most of a 300 mm wafer as one routed mesh of cores, each with local SRAM; defect-aware routing steers traffic around unusable cores, and the on-wafer mesh replaces off-package transfers for mapped operations. The WSE-3 figures are the vendor's reported totals and are not directly comparable to GPU HBM bandwidth.
alt: Two panels. Left: a DGX H100 node with eight GPU boxes labeled 80 GB, four above and four below a horizontal NVSwitch bar labeled 450 GB/s per GPU each way; an arrow labeled InfiniBand NDR, 50 GB/s per port, leads from the node to a dashed box labeled other nodes. Right: a circular wafer filled with a grid of small core squares joined by mesh links; one core is marked defective with a red X and a highlighted route bends around it. A legend identifies the core, the defective core, and the route, and a note reads WSE-3: 900,000 cores and 44 GB of SRAM, 21 PB/s aggregate SRAM bandwidth.
section: │       configuration, not the CS-3 registry TDP, so it stays a cited literal.
context:
@Fig-wafer-scale-engine contrasts the package and board boundaries of a multi-GPU chassis with wafer-scale integration. The eight GPUs exchange state within the chassis through NVSwitch; transfers to other nodes cross the external network. A wafer-scale engine instead routes between 900,000 on-wafer cores on the 300 mm wafer\index{Wafer-scale integration!physical constraints}. Defect-aware routing\index{Wafer-scale integration!defect tolerance} lets the fabric use working regions despite local manufacturing flaws. In the documented CS-2 configuration, twelve power supplies in a 9+3 redundant arrangement could deliver up to 23 kW to the WSE-2 [@Cerebras2021]. That configuration-specific design illustrates why wafer-scale power delivery and cooling require system-level liquid-cooling hardware rather than a conventional accelerator heatsink.

Wafer-scale engines specialize the *physical* architecture while retaining flexibility in the *computational* model through programmable cores. Their scale-up approach replaces some package- and board-level transfers with on-wafer movement. Capacity and data injection still constrain which parts of a workload can benefit from that locality.

title: Compute, bandwidth, and power scale at three different rates
caption: **Compute, bandwidth, and power scale at three different rates**: Dense FP16 Tensor throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal design power for NVIDIA data center accelerators, normalized to the V100 on a log scale, where the shaded gap between the compute and bandwidth lines is the growth in arithmetic intensity a kernel needs to stay compute-bound. These are peak specifications, not measured application throughput. Specifications come from the MLSysIM hardware registry.

Series are labeled directly at their right ends: dense FP16 Tensor throughput reaching 18 times, memory bandwidth 8.9 times, and dashed thermal design power 3.3 times. context:
For infrastructure planners, the same history shows that high-end accelerator generations can turn over faster than the facility that houses them. The V100 remained the flagship training GPU for approximately three years (2017--2020). The A100 held that position for roughly two years (2020--2022). Hopper and Blackwell continued that short-cadence pattern in the mid-2020s.

The planning implication is that a data center built for accelerators must anticipate refresh cycles before the first rack arrives. @Tbl-gpu-evolution connects those generations to changes in interconnect capacity and power. From V100 to B200, dense FP16 throughput rose 18$\times$, memory bandwidth 8.9$\times$, and TDP 3.3$\times$ (@fig-gpu-scaling-trends). These are growth multiples over the whole span, not annual rates, and their ratios carry the planning lesson. Each byte delivered from memory must now feed about twice as many operations, and each watt of the power allowance supplies more than five times as many peak operations. The first ratio changes which workloads can approach peak throughput; the second, multiplied by device count, sets the proposed rack load. A facility refreshed only for compute density therefore outruns both its memory delivery and its cooling envelope.

title: Accelerator memory tiers
caption: **Accelerator memory tiers**: Peak memory bandwidth and capacity separate local-SRAM designs (solid stars), HBM accelerators (half-tone filled circles), and edge and shared-LPDDR devices (hollow squares); all three are memory, so they share one hue and differ by marker. The dotted arrow marks the design trade-off: moving data closer to compute raises bandwidth but reduces capacity.
alt: Log-log scatter plot of memory capacity vs. peak memory bandwidth. All markers use one blue memory hue, and a shaded region encloses each cluster in three clearly stepped tints, darkest for the tier nearest compute: solid stars for local-SRAM designs at low capacity and very high bandwidth, with the outlying WSE-3 wafer in its own small region near 44 GB, half-tone filled circles for HBM accelerators at tens to hundreds of gigabytes and lower bandwidth, and hollow squares for edge and shared-LPDDR devices at the lowest bandwidth. A dotted arrow points from the HBM cluster toward the SRAM cluster, labeled closer to compute: more bandwidth, less capacity.
context:
The implications are concrete in our running example. Our `{python} InfraFrontierMemoryWallRecap.frontier_params_b_str` model's weights occupy `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.weights_fp16_gb_str` in FP16. In dense autoregressive decode at batch size 1, each generated token uses all of those weights, whose footprint far exceeds on-chip storage, so every token must stream them in from memory. Suppose, hypothetically, that one H100 could hold them. Streaming the whole `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.weights_fp16_gb_str` through that device's HBM at about `{python} MemoryBandwidthIntroRecap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` takes over 100 ms per token, long enough to be a perceptible pause between generated words. No real H100 holds the model, so the figure is a floor on bandwidth demand rather than a prediction of deployed latency, but it shows that the memory wall is a delay a user can notice, not an abstract architectural ratio.

Three levers lower that floor. Sharding spreads the weights across more memory paths, so each path streams fewer bytes. Quantization shrinks the bytes themselves. Reuse lets each fetched byte feed more arithmetic, which HBM's bandwidth and on-chip tiling make possible. The roofline model, recapped for one machine in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-roofline, tests whether the resulting data supply can feed the arithmetic units. Its ridge point, peak arithmetic divided by memory bandwidth, is the number of operations a kernel must perform per byte fetched before arithmetic rather than memory becomes the limit. The ridge point recurs throughout the analysis below, and @sec-compute-roofline evaluates it for the H100. Where each architecture places its bytes sets how much bandwidth those levers can draw on (@fig-accelerator-memory-tier-map), because moving the active working set closer to arithmetic increases available bandwidth while reducing the capacity that can reside there.

title: Tensor Core tiling strategy
caption: **Tensor Core tiling strategy**: Read left to right. To compute one tile of the output matrix $\GemmOutputMatrix$, the kernel streams matching slices of $\GemmLeftOperand$ and $\GemmRightOperand$ from HBM (left) into the SM's shared memory (center), where Tensor Core instructions (right) multiply them many times over while the FP32 partial sums for that $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile stay in registers. Only after every slice along the shared $\GemmInnerDimension$ dimension has been accumulated is the finished $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile written back to HBM once, so each byte fetched from HBM feeds many multiply-accumulate operations. The tile shapes shown ($128 \times 32$ slices, a $128 \times 128$ output tile) are one typical choice; kernels tune them to the chip.
alt: Three panels joined by arrows. Left, HBM with full matrices at 3.35 TB/s: matrix A with a row band split into K slices, matrix B with a column band split into K slices, one slice of each dark, and matrix C with one outlined output tile. Center, shared memory with 228 KB per SM: a tall A tile of 128 by 32 and a wide B tile of 32 by 128. Right, Tensor Cores and registers: a grid of small MMA instruction squares above a C tile of 128 by 128 holding FP32 sums. A dashed loop above the panels returns from the Tensor Cores to HBM, labeled repeat per K slice: load the next pair. A solid arrow below returns from the Tensor Cores to C in HBM, labeled after the last slice: write the C tile once.

title: HBM 3D-stacked architecture
caption: **HBM 3D-stacked architecture**: Left: high-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die, links them vertically with through-silicon vias (TSVs), and places the stack on a silicon interposer beside the GPU die, so each stack reaches the GPU over a 1,024-bit interface only millimeters long. Right: DDR5 instead sits on a DIMM across the motherboard, reached over a 64-bit channel through centimeters of board trace. The wider, shorter path raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit, but HBM bandwidth and capacity remain finite, so the memory wall moves rather than disappears.
alt: Two cross-section panels. Left, HBM stacked beside the die: a GPU die and a stack of eight DRAM dies on a base logic die sit side by side on a silicon interposer above the package substrate, with dashed vertical TSVs through the stack and a thick short link through the interposer labeled 1,024 bits wide, millimeters long. Right, DDR5 across the board: a CPU with its memory controller and a DIMM holding several DRAM chips stand on a motherboard, joined by a thin trace through the board labeled 64 bits wide, centimeters long.
context:
The physical distance from the DIMM slot to the processor die is measured in centimeters, and every centimeter of copper trace introduces capacitance, signal attenuation, and energy loss. At DDR5 data rates (4,800--6,400 MT/s per pin), the signal conditioning circuits must compensate for significant channel impairment, consuming substantial power per bit transferred. Increasing the data rate on these long traces requires progressively more power for signal conditioning, creating a diminishing-returns curve that DDR5 is already approaching.

HBM sidesteps that board-level degradation through 2.5D integration (@fig-hbm-architecture). Instead of driving signals horizontally across centimeters of motherboard trace over a narrow 64-bit bus, it stacks DRAM dies vertically and places the stack beside the processor on a silicon interposer.

title: The H100 roofline landscape
caption: **The H100 roofline landscape**: Attainable FP16 throughput is the lower of two ceilings, the memory-bandwidth slope (blue) and the compute roof (orange), which meet at the dashed ridge point. Each dot places a representative workload by its arithmetic intensity; workloads left of the ridge stay capped by bandwidth however much compute the chip offers, and only those to its right can approach peak throughput.
alt: Log-log roofline plot for H100 FP16 showing memory-bound and compute-bound regions with five ML workloads from LLM decode at the low-intensity left edge to LLM training on the compute roof.
context:
The Roofline's diagnostic power extends beyond individual kernels to entire training runs. For our `{python} InfraFrontierMemoryRooflineRecap.frontier_params_b_str` model, the computation graph contains thousands of distinct operations with different arithmetic intensities. The dense feed-forward network layers are dominated by large general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) with high arithmetic intensity, placing them firmly in the compute-bound regime where Tensor Core utilization is the bottleneck. Conversely, operations like layer normalization and element-wise activations possess low arithmetic intensity, sitting deep in the memory-bound region where the compute units idle while waiting for data. Attention kernels can land on either side of the ridge, depending on the shapes and reuse examined above, and long decode contexts add key-value traffic without comparable reuse. This diagnostic distinction dictates the optimization strategy: memory-bound layers benefit from kernel fusion (reducing HBM round-trips), while compute-bound layers benefit from precision reduction (moving from FP16 to FP8, which effectively raises the hardware's compute ceiling).

Whole phases spread even wider than individual operators. The idealized intensities of decode and training differ by `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.train_gap_mult_str`, which is why the same hardware shows very different utilization across them. Batch-1 decode sits near `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.decode_intensity_str`, far left of the ridge and deeply bound by memory bandwidth, while large-batch training near `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.train_intensity_str` crosses the ridge and reaches the compute roof (@fig-roofline-landscape). The training point assumes that `{python} RooflineLandscapeMath.training_batch_size_str` tokens on one accelerator share each weight read, the local reuse that a large global batch alone does not guarantee, so it counts tokens rather than sequences and local rather than global batch. It is a contrast case, not a universal intensity for training. Actual placement requires counting bytes at the memory level being modeled and accounting for tensor shapes, fusion, and reuse.

## The Node {#sec-compute-node}

The running model needs more memory than one accelerator provides. A node supplies several accelerators in one chassis, but each retains its own memory; dividing the work creates communication that the local fabric must sustain. Tensor parallelism divides an operation across accelerators, pipeline parallelism assigns successive model stages to different groups, and data parallelism assigns different training examples to model replicas whose updates must be combined. These strategies impose different traffic patterns. The node design determines whether that traffic crosses a slow ring\index{Network topology!ring}, a dense mesh\index{Network topology!full mesh}, or a switch-backed crossbar\index{NVSwitch!crossbar topology}. @Fig-node-topology-comparison diagrams these three intra-node wiring options for an eight-GPU chassis, contrasting the link scaling and network diameter of a two-link ring (up to four hops) and a 28-link full mesh against a single-hop NVSwitch crossbar.

title: Pod-scale network topologies
caption: **Pod-scale network topologies**: Two dominant ways to wire a pod. Left: a switched fat-tree, drawn here as a two-tier leaf and spine fabric in which every leaf switch connects to every spine switch and has as many uplinks as node ports, so any half of the nodes can talk to the other half at full rate (full bisection bandwidth). InfiniBand clusters such as DGX SuperPOD use this design, and larger pods add a third, core tier above the spines. Right: a 2D torus wires each node directly to its four neighbors, and the dashed stubs wrap each row and column around to its opposite edge; bisection bandwidth grows only as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ClusterNodeCount})$, so the torus is cheaper at scale but rewards workloads with strong locality, as in Google TPU pods. The choice shapes which parallelism strategies run efficiently.

Left, Switched fat-tree: four spine switches in a top row, four leaf switches below with a link from every leaf to every spine, and four nodes under each leaf; leaf L1's four uplinks and four node links are highlighted, and the footer reads L1: 4 uplinks = 4 node ports, full bisection bandwidth. Right, 2D torus: a four-by-four grid of nodes joined to their horizontal and vertical neighbors, with dashed stubs at every row and column end marking wrap-around links; a dashed vertical bisection cut runs down the middle, and the four row links it crosses plus the row wrap-around stubs are highlighted. The footer reads bisection grows as the square root of the node count, each node links to 4 neighbors.

## The Pod {#sec-compute-pod}

Training our `{python} InfraFrontierStragglerRecap10.frontier_params_b_str` model on a single DGX H100 node (8 GPUs, `{python} SingleNodeTrainingTime.node_peak_fp8_tflop_per_s_str` of aggregate FP8 peak) would take about `{python} SingleNodeTrainingTime.node_years_str` years at the efficiency assumed below, even if the model state could fit. Roughly `{python} SingleNodeTrainingTime.nodes_for_target_str` nodes bring the compute-only time down to two weeks, and about `{python} SingleNodeTrainingTime.nodes_for_one_day_str` nodes bring it to a single day, before any communication or recovery overhead. A pod is the cluster-scale unit that makes this possible: many racks under one high-speed fabric, power envelope, and cooling design. Pod design is the first point where topology, power, and failure domains become shared infrastructure rather than per-rack concerns. @Fig-pod-network-topology contrasts two dominant pod-scale fabrics: a two-tier leaf-and-spine fat tree providing full bisection bandwidth across all node uplinks, and a 2D torus wiring each node to its immediate neighbors with $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ClusterNodeCount})$ bisection scaling to reduce switch count and exploit traffic locality.

title: The five-level network model for ML training
caption: **The five-level network model for ML training**: Read from the bottom up, each level builds on the one below and becomes more abstract. Level 1 moves bits over wires and optics; Level 2 turns links into reliable, low-overhead transfers between accelerators; Level 3 arranges switches into a topology; Level 4 governs how the fabric behaves under load and congestion; and Level 5 integrates all of them into a production cluster.

L5, cluster design: pod integration, job placement, failure domains. Beside each band a small schematic shows the level's concrete form: L1, a four-level stepped waveform between two transceivers labeled SerDes; L2, a GPU and its NIC, both labeled, sending to a remote NIC and GPU; L3, two switches linked to all four switches below them; L4, three converging inputs feeding a nearly full queue, with a dashed red arrow labeled PAUSE leaving the queue and pointing back over the inputs; L5, a row of six racks joined by a common bar.

that corresponding model replicas apply the same update. This operation, called AllReduce, returns the combined result to every participating worker. The model has `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` of gradient data at two bytes per parameter, the 16-bit gradients of mixed-precision training that this chapter assumes throughout (FP32 gradients would double the figure). That model-wide figure is not what any one GPU sends. When a reduction partitions the gradient across all `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_value_str` ranks, each rank owns a 1/`{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_value_str` share, a few hundred megabytes, which is the gradient-shard size the transport examples below use; the job's tensor, pipeline, and data-parallel split (@sec-distributed-training-systems) sets each GPU's actual payload. Worked examples that switch to another model, precision, or payload state their parameters explicitly. A delayed transfer on the step's critical path can leave the other `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.peer_gpus_str` GPUs waiting at a job-wide synchronization boundary. The fabric's contribution to training time therefore depends on which transfers the next computation needs and how much of their cost remains exposed. In that role the fabric is not auxiliary infrastructure; it is the synchronization backbone that decides whether the cluster trains as one machine.

Within the multi-tier fleet hierarchy framed by @fig-fleet-stack, the fabric turns isolated accelerator nodes into a coherent training system. Accelerators, power delivery, cooling, racks, and pods define what each node can compute in isolation; the fabric determines whether the nodes can act together before communication cost overwhelms computation. This chapter organizes that design space as a **five-level model**\index{Five-level model!definition} of co-dependent tiers (@fig-network-five-level-model), climbing from serializer/deserializer (SerDes) signaling and copper or optical reach at Level 1 to the integration of a production cluster at Level 5. Each level is developed at the point where its physical or protocol limit becomes the binding constraint.

Which traffic must cross that gap depends on how the job is partitioned. The placement that follows from the same hierarchy keeps tensor parallelism, with its per-layer exchanges, inside the NVLink domain and lets pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas span nodes. The fabric adds one lever to that picture. Each data-parallel replica can sum gradients over several microbatches before an exchange (gradient accumulation\index{Gradient accumulation!communication frequency}), reducing how often it must cross the node boundary at the cost of changing the batch and update schedule. Pipeline and data parallelism can therefore cross slower node boundaries when their transfer sizes and computation leave enough time for the required exchanges. Combining these three strategies is called 3D parallelism; their execution schedules are developed in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-hybrid-parallelism-3d-loop, while their traffic requirements already constrain the fabric.

Exposed communication leaves gaps between dependent compute phases. @Fig-bandwidth-cliff-gantt illustrates that cost with two assumed training schedules on a common 230 ms axis, each containing 100 ms forward and backward compute phases. The 8-GPU intra-node case assumes a 1 ms AllReduce and spends 99.5 percent of the step in those compute phases; the 64-GPU inter-node case assumes a 30 ms AllReduce and spends 87 percent in computation. The two AllReduce durations are illustrative inputs chosen to show the effect, not values derived from the link rates above, and the percentages are shares of the schedule rather than measured arithmetic utilization.

title: From NRZ to PAM4 signaling
caption: **From NRZ to PAM4 signaling**: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric's fixed $\MessageStartupLatency$ latency.
alt: Two waveform panels with six equal symbol slots marked by dashed vertical lines. Left, NRZ: a square wave switching between levels 1 and 0, with one tall shaded band between the two levels and an arrow labeled full swing; below, a strip of six cells holds the bits 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, labeled 6 bits. Right, PAM4: a stepped wave among four levels labeled 00, 01, 10, and 11, with three thin shaded bands between adjacent levels and an arrow labeled one-third swing across one band; below, a strip of twelve cells grouped in pairs holds two bits per symbol, labeled 12 bits.
context:
```

The price is noise margin. With four levels packed into the same voltage swing, the gap between adjacent levels in PAM4\index{PAM4 signaling!voltage levels} shrinks to one third of the NRZ gap (@fig-pam4-vs-nrz), making the link highly susceptible to noise. Consequently, high-speed links operate near the physical limits of reliable detection and require **forward error correction (FEC)**\index{Forward Error Correction!definition}\index{FEC!definition} at the physical layer, commonly using Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)-family codes in high-speed Ethernet designs [@anslow2016rsFec; @ethernetAlliance2025roadmap]. FEC processing is an implementation-dependent latency term; IEEE 802.3df operator material treats roughly 100 ns of host-side FEC with the RS(544,514) code (called KP4 in the standard) and hundreds of nanoseconds of end-to-end module latency as meaningful at AI/HPC fabric timescales [@yin2022fecRequirements]. Because each switch on a path decodes and re-encodes the signal, the FEC cost accumulates with the number of switches a packet traverses. This chapter counts a path's length as its **hop count**\index{Hop count!definition}, distinguishing inter-switch links from switch traversals when the two differ. A packet that traverses three switches, the leaf-spine-leaf route of a two-tier fabric, incurs a scenario budget of `{python} FECLatency.three_hop_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.three_hop_high_ns_str` of one-way FEC latency, or `{python} FECLatency.round_trip_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.round_trip_high_ns_str` for a round trip. Against the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient of the 175B job, a few hundred nanoseconds are negligible, because bulk transfers are governed by bandwidth. The cost lands instead on small, latency-bound messages, such as the control handoffs that coordinate pipeline stages, and on collectives whose many sequential steps each pay it. This physical-layer latency sets a floor on the fabric's fixed startup latency, formalized in @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model as the $\MessageStartupLatency$ term, that no software optimization can remove.

title: GPUDirect RDMA data path
caption: **GPUDirect RDMA data path**: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears.
alt: A sending node drawn as its board layout: host memory with a registered buffer and the CPU root complex along the top, a wide PCIe switch in the middle, and GPU memory holding an n-byte payload beside the RDMA NIC along the bottom. A solid green path climbs from GPU memory into the PCIe switch and drops straight down to the NIC, which sends to the fabric. A dashed gray path climbs from GPU memory through the switch to the CPU, then into host memory, labeled 1, write n, and back out, labeled 2, read n, before descending through the switch to the NIC; a note under host memory reads about 2n bytes of bus traffic. A key labels the solid path GPUDirect RDMA and the dashed path staged via host memory.
section: │ Context: Transport — NDR line rate in TCP/RDMA discussion.
context:
RDMA bypasses the kernel data path. Offloading transport logic to the NIC allows applications to read and write registered remote memory without per-message kernel intervention. For ML, GPUDirect RDMA\index{GPUDirect RDMA!accelerator memory},[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass] the path that dense nodes pair with one NIC per GPU (@sec-compute-dense-nodes), extends this principle to accelerator memory [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Within a sending node (@fig-gpudirect-data-path), GPUDirect RDMA routes an $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload (what one participant sends, not the model-wide gradient state) along the solid green peer-to-peer path through the PCIe switch straight to the RDMA NIC, bypassing host memory entirely. Without this direct memory access (DMA) bypass, the dashed gray staging path must first copy $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and subsequently read $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes out to the NIC, generating roughly $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of redundant host-memory bus traffic. The network still transfers the payload, and the PCIe path may comprise multiple DMA transactions; the optimization removes staging copies rather than collapsing the transfer into one transaction.

[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass]: **GPUDirect RDMA**\index{GPUDirect RDMA!zero-copy}: Introduced by NVIDIA for Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0, GPUDirect RDMA enables a direct PCIe path between GPU memory and third-party peer devices such as network interfaces [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Before GPUDirect, every gradient transfer had to stage through host memory, consuming CPU memory bandwidth that competes with data loading. Eliminating this bounce path is one reason overlapping communication with backward-pass computation is feasible at scale.

title: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks
caption: **Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks**: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC's transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy.
alt: Two panels, each divided by dashed lines into user space, kernel, and hardware bands. Left, TCP/IP sockets: training framework in user space, then socket API, TCP/IP stack, and NIC driver in the kernel, then the Ethernet NIC; beside the stack, three payload tiles marked n attach to the framework, the socket API, and the NIC driver and are labeled user buf, socket buf, and TX ring; dashed arrows labeled copy 1 and copy 2 join them, and a thin solid arrow labeled DMA read carries the TX ring into the Ethernet NIC; the footer reads CPU copies data and runs the transport. Right, RDMA verbs: NCCL above the verbs API in user space, then a single amber arrow straight through the empty kernel band, labeled kernel not on the data path, to the RDMA NIC with transport in hardware; a GPU memory box beside the NIC holds a single payload tile and feeds the NIC through a short green arrow; the footer reads NIC reads GPU memory directly (GPUDirect).
context:
[^fn-infiniband-protocol-origin]: [offset=-32mm] **InfiniBand**\index{InfiniBand!origin}: Formed in 1999 from the merger of two competing server I/O standards (Future I/O and NGIO), InfiniBand was originally designed to replace PCI as a general-purpose system interconnect. Its pivot to HPC networking preserved the credit-based, hardware-managed flow control that server I/O demanded, and that heritage is why InfiniBand provides native losslessness without the PFC fragility of Ethernet-based RDMA fabrics.

This architectural choice is visible at the protocol boundary. @Fig-ib-roce-stack partitions the protocol stack across user-space, kernel, and hardware bands, contrasting traditional socket overhead against direct verbs hardware offload. While the conventional copied TCP/IP path illustrated on the left uses two software copies across kernel buffer boundaries and software protocol execution, the RDMA stack (right) traces a single amber bypass arrow straight from the collective communication library (such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, or NCCL) and the user-space **verbs API**\index{Verbs API!definition} to the RDMA NIC, keeping the operating system entirely off the active data path.

Measured crossover points vary with the end-to-end path.

Each series is labeled with its startup latency and bandwidth, the Ethernet label above its plateau and the InfiniBand label below. For the InfiniBand path, two dotted asymptotes, a horizontal startup floor alpha and a diagonal transmission line n over beta, meet directly beneath its crossover point.
section: │ How: RoCE alpha on a 400 Gb/s Ethernet link, same messages as NetworkAlphaBeta.
context:
In the 175B training job, a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str` control message, such as the notification that tells a pipeline stage its next microbatch is ready, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_small_ib_us_str`, with bandwidth contributing only `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_bw_pct_str` of the total. Faster links therefore offer little benefit for this handoff. A `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_grad_mb_str` gradient shard, roughly the share of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient that each of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_str` owns when a reduction partitions it across the whole cluster, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_ib_ms_str`; doubling bandwidth to `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.doubled_beta_gb_per_s_str` would approximately halve its transfer time.

Across the full range of message sizes, each path traces a flat latency-dominated plateau that bends into a linear bandwidth-dominated regime (@fig-alpha-beta-crossover). On the modeled NDR path, the knee at `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_ib_kb_str` marks where transmission time overtakes the `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_alpha_us_str` startup latency; the 100 Gb/s RoCE path sits on a higher floor of `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_alpha_us_str` and bends near `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_eth_kb_str`. The exact positions reflect the assumed $\MessageStartupLatency$ and $\LinkBandwidth$ scenario parameters rather than invariant protocol constants. On both paths, startup latency governs sub-kilobyte control handoffs, whereas multi-megabyte gradient shards sit well inside the bandwidth-bound regime.

context:
```

A measured collective shows both regimes and where the two-parameter model needs care. NVIDIA publishes the full output of the standard NCCL all-reduce benchmark on one node of eight H100 GPUs connected by NVLink, sweeping message sizes from 8 bytes to 16 GB [@nvidia2026exemplarnccl]. @Fig-nccl-allreduce-measured plots the measured time beside the two-parameter model built from two summary values, the median time of the small messages as $\MessageStartupLatency$ and the delivered rate of the largest message as $\LinkBandwidth$. The small messages sit on a floor of about `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.floor_us_str` µs regardless of size, and the largest messages approach `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.bw_str` of algorithm bandwidth (`{python} MeasuredAllReduce.peak_busbw_str` of bus bandwidth, the benchmark's hardware-normalized rate). Between the two, the model places the knee near `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.knee_mb_str` MB, but the measured time runs up to `{python} MeasuredAllReduce.mid_ratio_mult_str` the model's prediction for messages of 8 to 128 MB, where the delivered bandwidth is still ramping toward its peak. The model is therefore close at the two ends and optimistic in the middle, and that middle range is where the gradient buckets of data-parallel training often fall.

title: A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency
caption: **A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency**: Four switch queues form the cycle of @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle. Follow the solid arrows clockwise: each full buffer holds packets that need space in the next. The dashed PAUSE frames run counterclockwise, so each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while awaiting space in its downstream successor, and no queue can drain until a watchdog drops packets.
alt: Four switch boxes arranged as a ring, switch 1 at the top, 2 at the right, 3 at the bottom, and 4 at the left, each containing a full red four-slot queue labeled b1 to b4 and the words queue full. Solid dark arrows curve clockwise around the outside of the ring from switch 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1, labeled b1 to b2, b2 to b3, b3 to b4, and b4 to b1. Dashed red arrows labeled PAUSE curve counterclockwise around the inside of the ring between the same switches, and the center of the ring reads deadlock.
section: The graph mechanics of buffer-dependency deadlocks {#sec-network-deadlock-graph}
context:
$$\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \dots \to \PacketBuffer_k \to \PacketBuffer_1$$ {#eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle}

When each buffer in the cycle fills beyond its configured pause threshold, each port asserts a PFC PAUSE frame to its predecessor. Because no buffer can advance a packet into a paused successor, no buffer can drain, and no port can de-assert its PAUSE signal. The entire cycle freezes permanently. @Fig-pfc-credit-deadlock models this mutual protocol interlock across a four-switch ring whose queues ($\PacketBuffer_1$ through $\PacketBuffer_4$) are completely full. Solid gray arrows trace packet forwarding dependencies advancing clockwise ($\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \PacketBuffer_3 \to \PacketBuffer_4 \to \PacketBuffer_1$), while dashed red PAUSE frames propagate counterclockwise. Each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while waiting for its downstream successor to drain, permanently freezing all four queues until an external watchdog intervenes to drop frames.

title: Parallel file system architecture
caption: **Parallel file system architecture**: A client makes one metadata request (MDS $\to$ MDT) to learn a file's stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS $\to$ OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.
alt: Architecture diagram with compute clients on the left, a metadata server and a column of object storage servers in the middle, and storage targets on the right. A violet line labeled lookup runs from client 1 to the metadata server, whose target holds a stripe map listing OSTs 1 through N. Green lines join every client through a shared vertical bus to every object storage server. Each object storage target holds stripe tiles of one file: OST 1 holds 0, N, 2N; OST 2 holds 1, N+1, 2N+1; and so on to OST N, with the first tile of each target filled dark green.
context:
:::

@Fig-storage-pfs-architecture traces how a Lustre-style parallel file system decouples metadata lookups from bulk data movement, separating two concerns that traditional file systems handle together [@schwan2003lustre]. Metadata servers (MDS)\index{Metadata Server!namespace management}\index{MDS|see{Metadata Server}} manage the namespace (persisting file layouts and attributes on metadata targets, or MDTs): file creation, directory listings, permission checks, and lock management. Object storage servers (OSS)\index{Object Storage Server!data block striping}\index{OSS|see{Object Storage Server}}[^fn-oss-pfs-disambiguation] manage the actual data blocks, each serving a stripe of every large file. When a client opens a 10 GB training shard, the MDS tells the client which OSS nodes hold which stripes, and the client reads from all of them in parallel. A Lustre[^fn-lustre-parallel-origin] deployment with 100 OSS nodes, each providing 10 GB/s, delivers an aggregate 1 TB/s.

Each submission emulates a set of accelerators that consume samples with a fixed per-sample compute time, so the storage system, not a real GPU, sets the pace, and reports the read throughput the system sustained while keeping the emulated accelerators at least 90 percent busy (70 percent for CosmoFlow) [@mlcommons2024storage; @devarajan2021dlio]. Per accelerator, the median demand differs about `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.workload_spread_mult_str` across workloads, and ResNet-50, demanding among image-classification jobs, is the lightest of the three because its samples are small 2D images while 3D U-Net reads whole medical volumes. An emulated H100 needs about `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.unet_h100_str` for 3D U-Net on medical volumes, `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.cosmo_h100_str` for CosmoFlow, and `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.resnet_h100_str` for ResNet-50 (@fig-mlperf-storage-demand, panel b). Emulating H100s instead of A100s raises every workload's demand by `{python} StorageDemandMeasured.gen_ratio_mult_range_str`, because the faster accelerator shortens $\IronLawComputeTime$ while the bytes per batch stay the same. A storage tier sized for one accelerator generation is therefore undersized for the next, even when the dataset and the model do not change.

### Pipelining and prefetching {#sec-storage-pipelining}

Pipelining\index{Pipelining!data loading} is the single-node overlap that turns the sum of input and compute time into their maximum, as recalled in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-dam-coordination-sum-max. Staging and preparing batch $\BatchIndex+1$ on host resources while the GPU trains on batch $\BatchIndex$ hides input work when delivery keeps pace and enough prepared work absorbs latency variation, as the sequential and overlapped storage, CPU, and GPU lanes of @fig-data-pipeline-vol2 show. title: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path
caption: **Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path**: Both panels draw the same node: CPU and host DRAM above a PCIe switch, NVMe and GPU below it. Green routes are DMA transfers of payload bytes. In the buffered path (a), payload climbs into host DRAM and comes back down, and the CPU copies every payload from the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer before the accelerator's DMA can start. In the GDS path (b), NVMe transfers directly into GPU memory, and the dashed CPU link shows the submission and completion work that remains.
alt: Two panels with the same layout: a CPU and a host DRAM box on top, a PCIe switch bar in the middle, and an NVMe SSD and a GPU containing HBM at the bottom. Panel a: a green route labeled DMA 1 runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch up into a kernel buffer in host DRAM; a gray copy arrow joins the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer, with the CPU attached by a link labeled copy; a second green route labeled DMA 2 runs from the pinned buffer down through the switch into HBM. Panel b: one green route labeled DMA runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch into HBM without entering host DRAM, and a dashed gray arrow labeled control runs from the CPU to the NVMe SSD.
section: GPUDirect Storage and the CPU Data-Copy Bypass {#sec-storage-gds}
context:
GDS changes the payload path without eliminating the software control path. The cuFile API\index{GPUDirect Storage!cuFile direct DMA} registers a GPU memory region for direct DMA. Subsequent reads transfer payload data from NVMe to GPU memory without an intermediate system-memory bounce buffer, while cuFile, the virtual file system, kernel storage drivers, and `nvidia-fs` remain involved in submission and coordination. The CPU issues the I/O and checks for completion but avoids the payload-copy work of the traditional path.

The benefit from GDS matters when host payload movement is a limiting stage after other pipeline work is accounted for. In @fig-gds-path, the conventional path takes two DMA hops through intermediate host-DRAM bounce buffers, while GDS takes a single direct DMA transfer. The direct path eliminates the CPU payload-copy stage, but the dashed control link shows that the host CPU still orchestrates transfer submission and completion.

title: The complete data path
caption: **The complete data path**: Columns are storage tiers, ordered from the durable object store (left) to accelerator memory (right). Training data moves right and bypasses the parallel file system in this running example; checkpoints return left through it. Solid arrows mark copies the training loop waits on; dashed arrows mark copies that run once per job or in the background. The dashed outline is one GPU node: every copy the training loop waits on stays inside it.
alt: Five tier columns headed object storage, parallel file system, local NVMe, host DRAM, and GPU HBM; a dashed outline labeled one GPU node encloses the last three, and the first two are labeled shared services. Training data row: a dataset in object storage, a dashed arrow labeled stage once across the empty parallel file system column to a staged copy on local NVMe, then solid arrows to a prefetch box in host DRAM and a batch in GPU HBM, plus a thinner optional GDS bypass arrow from NVMe over host DRAM to HBM. Checkpoints row: a solid arrow from model state in HBM to a local shard on NVMe labeled local save (pause), then dashed arrows to a durable copy on the parallel file system labeled async copy and to a retained copy in object storage labeled retain selected. A key distinguishes solid and dashed arrows.
context:
At the end of the training job, the final model checkpoint is promoted from the parallel file system to object storage for long-term retention. The local NVMe copies are deleted during job cleanup. If the model is deployed for inference, it is loaded from object storage into the serving cluster's HBM, completing the lifecycle of data movement through the hierarchy.

The total number of data copies in this lifecycle is instructive. Each training sample traverses: object storage $\to$ NVMe (staging), NVMe $\to$ host DRAM (read), host DRAM $\to$ GPU HBM (transfer). Each checkpoint traverses: GPU HBM $\to$ NVMe (local save), NVMe $\to$ parallel file system (async copy), parallel file system $\to$ object storage (long-term retention). Every copy consumes bandwidth and contributes latency. The engineering goal is to minimize copies on the critical path (the training loop) and tolerate additional copies on noncritical paths (staging and archival). @Fig-storage-complete-data-path maps both lifecycles across the tiers, with solid arrows for synchronous critical-path copies and dashed arrows for asynchronous background transfers. For training inputs moving rightward, the active loop waits only on local promotion into HBM (or the optional GDS bypass); for checkpoints flowing leftward, the exposed pause is confined to the local NVMe save while parallel-file-system replication and archival retention proceed off the critical path.

title: Two-phase checkpoint staging
caption: **Two-phase checkpoint staging**: Read the lanes left to right. Training pauses only for the local NVMe write ($\TimeInstant_0$ to $\TimeInstant_1$); the copy to the parallel file system overlaps later training steps, and the coordinator publishes the manifest last ($\TimeInstant_3$). Between $\TimeInstant_1$ and $\TimeInstant_3$ the new generation exists only as staged shards, so the previous committed generation remains the restore point.
alt: Timeline with four horizontal lanes labeled training, local NVMe, parallel FS, and coordinator above a time axis marked t0 through t3. A short red paused block in the training lane lines up with a local write block; long blocks show training continuing, an asynchronous copy to the parallel file system, checksum verification, and manifest publication. Brackets below the axis mark the span from t1 to t3 as staged and the span after t3 as restorable.

:::

The exposed pause and the durability boundary therefore fall at different moments. @Fig-storage-checkpoint-staging aligns these milestones across four concurrent execution lanes. Training pauses only during the local NVMe shard write ($\TimeInstant_0$ to $\TimeInstant_1$), resuming on live state while the parallel file system absorbs the asynchronous copy ($\TimeInstant_1$ to $\TimeInstant_2$) and the coordinator validates checksums before publishing the manifest last ($\TimeInstant_3$).

title: Data-movement accounting boundaries
caption: **Data-movement accounting boundaries**: Successively broader paths involve different storage and communication components. The schematic identifies what an energy estimate must include; it assigns no universal distance law or fixed energy multiplier. Compare energy per transferred byte only after specifying endpoints, interfaces, switches, and utilization.
alt: One data path drawn left to right through physical components joined by amber links: a local SRAM cell grid, a stack of HBM dies, an intra-node crossbar, a SerDes chip, an optical transceiver, switches, and a remote node. At the crossbar a short branch rises to a peer GPU die, which ends that branch. Three brackets below all start at the SRAM: Package ends after HBM, Node ends after the crossbar and its peer GPU branch, and Fabric path ends at the remote node; the dark part of each bracket spans the components that boundary adds.
context:
:::

Moving data consumes energy across storage arrays, interfaces, serializers, transceivers, and switches. A transfer that starts in local SRAM can stay on-package in high-bandwidth memory (HBM)\index{HBM}\index{High-Bandwidth Memory|see{HBM}}, cross to an intra-node peer GPU, or traverse intermediate switches to a remote node, and each step widens the physical accounting boundary\index{Energy consumption!data movement hierarchy} that an energy estimate must include (@fig-data-movement-hierarchy). Each boundary activates distinct physical components: on-package links, intra-node crossbars, serializers, optical transceivers, and switch fabrics. Distance alone does not determine energy per bit, and an endpoint-only estimate cannot be compared directly with a complete fabric-path estimate. Locality remains useful because it can avoid transfers and active interfaces; the energy saving must be evaluated under the same workload, utilization, and accounting boundary.
