```
The opening ring budget shows why data movement can become the governing constraint at scale. A single AllReduce on a 70B model's gradients consumes seconds of wall-clock time, which becomes exposed delay when no independent computation overlaps it, and a training campaign repeats it at every step, so a seemingly modest improvement to the collective repays itself many times over. That budget is one instance of the network wall that @sec-introduction-communication-becomes-dominant-e1b6 established, in which exposed communication takes a growing share of each step as a fixed workload spreads across more devices. @Fig-compute-comm-timeline charts that trend for illustrative tiers from 8 to 4,096 GPUs, where compute falls from 75 percent of the step to 20 percent. The fractions are assumed regimes rather than measurements; gradient size, local batch size, partition topology, and asynchronous overlap determine where the critical path actually lies.

title: Interconnect bandwidth conventions
caption: **Interconnect bandwidth conventions**: Selected advertised intra-node and inter-node capacities, expressed per direction. NVLink points sum a GPU's links; PCIe uses one x16 interface, and InfiniBand uses one port. These capacities reveal a hierarchy but are not equal-sized endpoint budgets or achieved collective rates. Algorithm selection additionally requires startup cost, port count, routing, and contention. Points sit at each generation's first commercial product year; rates and first-product years are from IEEE 802.3, InfiniBand Trade Association, PCI-SIG, and NVIDIA specifications and product announcements.
alt: Log-scale line chart of one-way capacity from 2011 to 2025: an orange intra-node curve per GPU rising from PCIe 3.0 through NVLink 1.0 to 5.0, and a lower violet curve for one InfiniBand port from FDR to XDR. The band between the two curves is shaded gray, and a double-headed arrow at 2025 marks a ninefold gap between NVLink 5.0 and InfiniBand XDR.
context:
: **Interconnect Performance Parameters**: Effective per-message launch latency ($\MessageStartupLatency$, including the software stack), per-direction link bandwidth ($\LinkBandwidth$, the one-way deliverable rate that enters $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$; NVLink's datasheet `{python} InterconnectAlphaBeta.nvlink_bidir_str` is the bidirectional total, so its $\LinkBandwidth$ is the `{python} InterconnectAlphaBeta.nvlink_bw_str` one-way rate), and the computed crossover size $\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth$ at each row's $\MessageStartupLatency$ midpoint (for InfiniBand NDR, at the representative `{python} InterconnectAlphaBeta.ndr_alpha_anchor_us_str` used throughout this chapter), where communication transitions from latency-bound to bandwidth-bound. {#tbl-interconnect-parameters}

The same comparison across generations shows that the roughly ninefold per-direction cliff between a GPU's NVLink capacity and its one InfiniBand port, which @sec-compute-bandwidth-hierarchy established for the H100 generation, is not an artifact of one product cycle (@fig-bandwidth-divergence). Every point in the figure is per direction, so NVLink values are half the bidirectional datasheet totals, exactly as for the NVLink 4.0 row of @tbl-interconnect-parameters. A gap of that order has persisted for a decade even as both tiers grew. A GPU's NVLink aggregate and a single network port are different endpoint boundaries, but that persistent gap is why collective design must be hierarchy-aware, because unpartitioned traffic routed across the slower external fabric saturates it long before the local links are busy.

title: Four central collective primitives
caption: **Four central collective primitives**: Standardized patterns for group communication in distributed systems. In each panel the four rows are ranks 0 to 3, read left to right from each rank's input, through the collective, to what each rank holds afterward. (1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. (4) AllToAll: every process sends unique data to every other process. The two foundational primitives Broadcast (rank 0 sends to all) and Reduce (all aggregate to rank 0) compose the patterns shown here and are defined in the surrounding prose.
alt: Four panels, AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, and AllToAll, each with rows for ranks 0 to 3. Each row shows the rank's input buffer as small tiles, an amber collective band, and the output buffer. AllReduce: four chunks a to d per rank become four green sums on every rank. AllGather: one chunk per rank becomes four chunks a to d on every rank. ReduceScatter: four chunks per rank become one green sum per rank, sum a on rank 0 through sum d on rank 3. AllToAll: rank i's chunks a_i to d_i are transposed so rank 0 holds a0 to a3, rank 1 holds b0 to b3, and so on. Chunk a has a bold outline in every panel.
context:
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating a non-blocking collective as complete when its initiation call returns. The returned request or stream event represents work in flight. A dependent consumer must wait for completion, and a late rank can extend that dependency even though the collective is not a barrier.

:::

title: Ring AllReduce data flow
caption: **Ring AllReduce data flow**: Four GPUs in a logical ring, each gradient split into chunks A to D; the wrap-around link closes the ring from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. (a) After the $\DeviceCount-1$ ReduceScatter steps, in which every GPU sends one chunk to its neighbor and adds the chunk it receives, each GPU holds one fully reduced chunk. (b) After $\DeviceCount-1$ AllGather steps that forward those finished chunks around the same ring, every GPU holds the full sum. Every link carries data in every step, so each GPU sends $2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\CollectivePayloadSize$ bytes in total, while the $2(\DeviceCount-1)$ steps each pay one startup latency $\MessageStartupLatency$.
alt: Two rows of four GPU cards linked left to right by amber arrows, with an amber wrap-around link from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. Each GPU holds four chunk tiles A to D. Row a, after ReduceScatter: each GPU holds one green fully reduced chunk, a different one per GPU, and its other tiles are partially filled in gray to show how many ranks' contributions they hold. Three small tiles ride on each link, naming the chunk that link carries at steps 1, 2, and 3, with fill growing step by step. Row b, after AllGather: every GPU holds all four chunks as green full sums, and the tiles on each link are green.
context:
```

Across the $2(\DeviceCount-1)$ send/receive rounds each rank moves $\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount$ bytes per round, for $2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount$ bytes sent and the same received. The bandwidth term therefore reaches the information-theoretic lower bound, while the latency term grows as $2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency$. @Fig-ring-allreduce traces this two-phase state progression across a four-GPU ring with wrap-around links. In row (a), $\DeviceCount-1 = 3$ ReduceScatter steps circulate gradient chunks A through D until each GPU holds exactly one fully reduced partition (green $\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{A}$ through $\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{D}$). In row (b), $\DeviceCount-1 = 3$ subsequent AllGather steps forward those finished shards around the ring until every device holds the complete sum.

The Double Binary Tree curve applies modest latency and bandwidth overhead factors (1.2$\times$ and 1.05$\times$) to its ideal cost.

Ring and Butterfly achieve bandwidth optimality with different latency characteristics, while Double Binary Tree combines logarithmic depth with a near-optimal byte term. The Tree row refers to the simple full-message model, not every tree implementation. {#tbl-allreduce-comparison}

title: Hierarchical AllReduce
caption: **Hierarchical AllReduce**: Three-phase decomposition that exploits the intra-node/inter-node bandwidth gap. Phase 1 performs intra-node aggregation over NVLink (an NVLink ring acting as a ReduceScatter that leaves each GPU holding a node-shard partial sum), leaving a payload of $\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode$ on each of the $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ GPUs per node. Phase 2 runs an AllReduce across corresponding GPUs using InfiniBand. Phase 3 completes intra-node distribution over NVLink (the AllGather that returns each GPU to the full result). The schematic shows two representative ranks per node; the same decomposition applies to $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ ranks.
alt: Three panels for the three phases, each showing Node 0 above Node 1, each node holding GPU 0 and GPU 1 cards with two shard tiles. Thick NVLink bars join the GPUs inside a node and dashed InfiniBand links join corresponding GPUs across nodes; in each panel only the links in use are amber and the others are light gray. Phase 1, ReduceScatter: NVLink lit, each GPU holds one half-filled node partial sum. Phase 2, Shard AllReduce: InfiniBand lit, one half-filled shard tile rides each inter-node link, and each GPU ends with one green full sum. Phase 3, AllGather: NVLink lit, every GPU holds both green full sums.
context:
: **The Bandwidth Hierarchy**: Per-GPU bandwidth per direction at each tier, the convention of @tbl-interconnect-parameters. NVLink's `{python} CommInfraScenario.nvlink_h100_bw_gb_per_s_str` datasheet figure is the bidirectional total; InfiniBand is one port. The order-of-magnitude gap is what hierarchical algorithms exploit. {#tbl-bandwidth-hierarchy}

A flat ring whose ordering repeatedly crosses node boundaries can leave local NVLink capacity unused while loading scarce inter-node links. Hierarchical AllReduce\index{Hierarchical AllReduce}\index{Hierarchical AllReduce!three-phase decomposition} explicitly partitions the global operation into three stages that align communication volume with the fabric tiers (@fig-hierarchical-allreduce).

title: Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology
caption: **Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology**: In a 2D torus mesh ($4 \times 4$ node grid representing a simplified TPU pod slice), AllReduce proceeds sequentially along orthogonal dimensions. Phase 1 (orange) executes four parallel horizontal rings across the X dimension ($2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). Phase 2 (slate) then executes four parallel vertical rings across the Y dimension ($2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps) on the row-aggregated partial sums. Dashed stubs mark the torus wrap-around links, each leaving one edge of the grid and re-entering at the opposite edge. This dimension-ordered decomposition needs 12 startup rounds against 30 for a 16-rank 1D global ring, a $2.5\times$ reduction, but each axis processes the full message, so its bandwidth time is $3\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth$ for this grid.
alt: Two 4 by 4 grids of nodes with x and y indices 0 to 3. Panel a, Phase 1: horizontal links in each row are amber arrows with dashed wrap-around stubs at both row ends, vertical links are light gray, and every node is a quarter-filled row partial sum. Panel b, Phase 2: vertical links in each column are slate arrows with dashed wrap-around stubs, horizontal links are light gray, and every node is green. Below, a strip of 12 blocks, six amber and six slate, labeled 12 startup rounds for the 2D torus sits above a strip of 30 gray blocks for a 1D ring, drawn to the same scale.
context:
:::

@Fig-torus-reduction maps this dimension-ordered schedule onto a $4 \times 4$ 2D torus grid (16 ranks)\index{Torus Topology!dimension-ordered reduction}. In Phase 1 (orange solid paths), each row executes an independent 4-rank Ring AllReduce across the horizontal X dimension using dashed wrap-around boundary links to close the ring ($2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). Once row partial sums are established, Phase 2 (slate solid paths) executes orthogonal 4-rank vertical Ring AllReduces down the Y dimension ($2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). These phases use direct nearest-neighbor links without multi-hop routing within a logical ring edge. They reduce the startup count from $2(\DeviceCount-1) = 30$ rounds on a flat 16-rank ring to $2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) + 2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 12$ rounds, a $2.5\times$ reduction in the modeled startup term. In this simple form each axis still processes the full message, so the round-count saving comes at a byte cost that the partitioned dimension-wise schedule removes.

title: Endpoint and in-network reduction
caption: **Endpoint and in-network reduction**: The upstream half of a reduction over four GPUs. (a) Switches only forward packets, so every full gradient tensor crosses the upper links and converges on one reducer GPU, which does all the arithmetic. (b) Aggregation-capable switches add their inputs, so each upper link carries one partial sum and the root switch finishes the reduction; the result then travels back down the same tree. A software reduction tree also aggregates along its path, but performs arithmetic at endpoints rather than switches. The diagram compares where arithmetic happens, not measured speedup.
alt: Two panels, each a tree of four GPU cards at the bottom, two switches in the middle, and one box at the top, with arrows pointing upward and each GPU holding its gradient tile g0 to g3. Panel a: gray switches labeled forwards only each send two parallel arrows carrying separate tiles g0 and g1, or g2 and g3, to a blue Reducer GPU that adds all and holds the green full sum. Panel b: amber switches labeled adds each send one arrow carrying a single half-filled tile g0+g1 or g2+g3 to an amber root switch that adds and holds the green full sum.
context:
Hierarchical and dimension-ordered schedules redistribute work across links, but their software reduction stages still require endpoint GPUs to receive and combine contributions. NVIDIA's Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol (SHARP)\index{SHARP!in-network reduction}[^fn-sharp-innetwork-aggregation] moves that intermediate aggregation into the network. Instead of routing each partial sum through a GPU for arithmetic, an aggregation-capable InfiniBand switch combines contributions as packets pass through it.

@Fig-sharp-innetwork contrasts upstream dataflow in a centralized endpoint reduction against in-switch aggregation\index{In-network computing!switch aggregation}. In the endpoint tree of panel (a), intermediate switches merely forward raw packets, forcing all four full gradient tensors ($\LocalGradient_0$ through $\LocalGradient_3$) across the upper links into a single Reducer GPU that executes every addition. In panel (b), SHARP offloads arithmetic to aggregation-capable switch application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)\index{ASIC}\index{Application-Specific Integrated Circuit|see{ASIC}}: each intermediate switch computes partial sums ($\LocalGradient_0+\LocalGradient_1$ and $\LocalGradient_2+\LocalGradient_3$) in-flight, leaving only the combined shards for the root switch to finalize. Moving reduction into the network fabric halves the upper link traffic and relieves accelerator endpoints from coordinating arithmetic steps.

title: Communication-computation overlap
caption: **Communication-computation overlap**: The backward pass runs from the last layer to the first, and each layer's gradient AllReduce launches as soon as that layer finishes, so it runs on the network while the GPU computes the next layer's gradients. The first layer finishes last and has no computation left to hide behind, so its AllReduce is exposed before the optimizer step. Overlap succeeds only when the nonoverlappable overhead ($\SymmetricMessageOverhead$) is small, leaving the bulk transfer free to proceed concurrently. Durations are schematic.
alt: Two-lane timeline over a time axis. The compute lane shows Backward L4, L3, L2, and L1, each followed by a thin solid amber slice labeled o, then a dashed GPU idle box, then an Optimizer block. The network lane shows AllReduce L4, L3, and L2 each starting when its o slice ends and running beneath the next backward block, then AllReduce L1 beneath the idle box. A bracket marks the first three AllReduces as hidden behind backward compute, and a shaded band labeled exposed covers the last o slice and AllReduce L1. A key notes that o is nonoverlappable overhead that occupies the GPU.
context:
Gradient computation during the backward pass proceeds layer by layer, from the output layer back to the input layer. The gradient for layer $\ell$ is available as soon as that layer's backward pass completes, even while layers $\ell-1, \ell-2, \ldots$ are still computing. That ordering lets the gradient for layer $\ell$ start communicating immediately while the GPU computes the gradient for layer $\ell-1$. Over a four-layer backward pass, the transfers for layers 4 through 2 run beneath later backward work, and only the transfer for layer 1, which becomes ready last, is left exposed before the optimizer step (@fig-comm-compute-overlap).

In PyTorch's `DistributedDataParallel`\index{DistributedDataParallel}, this overlap is implemented through gradient hooks\index{Gradient Hook}\index{DistributedDataParallel!gradient hooks}. Each parameter registers a hook that marks its gradient ready. Once all required gradients in a bucket are ready, the reducer can launch an asynchronous AllReduce\index{AllReduce!asynchronous execution}, preserving the same collective order across ranks. Meanwhile, the backward pass continues computing gradients for earlier layers. A transfer is hidden only if it completes before its result is needed; queued communication can consume part of that window, and the last bucket's transfer remains exposed (@sec-communication-overlap-limits).

title: The memory wall
caption: **The memory wall**: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Capacity climbs steadily while demand climbs faster, and the widening gap is why weights, gradients, and optimizer state must be split across devices rather than merely compressed. Training memory assumes 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam state; parameter counts are from @epochai2026notable and capacities are vendor specifications.
alt: Log-scale line chart from 2012 to 2024. A dashed blue series of single-accelerator memory rises from 12 GB (K80) to 180 GB (B200). A red series of the memory needed to train frontier models rises far faster, crossing above accelerator memory between GPT-2 (2019) and GPT-3 (2020), and a light red band labeled split across devices shades the widening gap through Llama 3 in 2024. GPT-3 is circled and annotated as the first plotted model beyond one accelerator, about 35 times the largest of its year. The first signal, memory exhaustion, has a long history, traced in @fig-memory-wall-trend. Among the plotted models, the curves cross in `{python} MemoryWallTrend.crossover_year_str` at GPT-3, whose training state exceeded the largest accelerator then available by about `{python} MemoryWallTrend.crossover_gap_mult_str`. title: The 3D parallelism cube
```
caption: **The 3D parallelism cube**: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its $(\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)$ coordinate, so the cube holds $\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree$ devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis's traffic.
alt: Cube divided into a four-by-four-by-four grid of cells, one cell per GPU, with the tensor axis along the width (within a layer, fast domain), the pipeline axis along the height (stages, activations), and the data axis along the depth (replicas, gradients). The front bottom right cell is solid navy and marked as one GPU. The cells it communicates with are tinted: the rest of its bottom row is labeled tensor group, the rest of its column is labeled pipeline group, and the cells behind it along the depth are labeled data group. A label reads N equals N DP times N PP times N TP.
context:
[^fn-nvlink-intranode-interconnect]: **NVLink**\index{NVLink!distributed training}: NVIDIA's point-to-point GPU interconnect delivers `{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_a100_gb_per_s_str`--`{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str` per-direction bandwidth, roughly `{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_hdr_ratio_low_mult_str`--`{python} DistTrainNvlinkIntro.nvlink_hdr_ratio_high_mult_str` InfiniBand\index{InfiniBand}\index{IB|see{InfiniBand}} HDR per port. This bandwidth gap is why tensor parallelism, which requires AllReduce on every layer, favors the fast NVLink domain, while pipeline and data parallelism can tolerate slower links when their traffic budgets fit. NVLink Switch systems can extend that fast domain beyond one server.

The leap to multi-node training adds network communication overhead, fault tolerance requirements, and cluster orchestration\index{Cluster orchestration!distributed training}. Because each stage compounds the previous one's bottlenecks, single-GPU performance must be optimized before scaling out, so inefficiency does not multiply across the fleet. @Fig-3d-parallelism-cube maps the resulting design space onto a 3D decomposition grid ($\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree$), partitioning cluster execution across tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication), where each individual cell represents a single accelerator coordinate.

title: Data parallelism implementation pipeline
caption: **Data parallelism implementation pipeline**: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients $\MinibatchGradient_i$, (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient $\GlobalBatchGradient$, and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.
alt: Five-stage data-parallel workflow across four GPU swimlanes. A green global batch of B equals 128, drawn as sixteen sample tiles in four groups, sends one group of 32 samples to each GPU. Each GPU card holds an identical four-layer model replica and runs forward and backward passes, producing a small signed bar vector g0 to g3 whose bars differ from lane to lane. All four vectors enter one tall amber AllReduce block labeled g global equals one over N times the sum of g i, ring. Every lane then shows the same averaged bar vector g global feeding an update theta card, with the note identical theta on every GPU.
context:
### Data parallelism implementation {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-data-parallelism-implementation-fa03}

The implementation details matter because the SGD equivalence only holds when each phase preserves the intended aggregate sampling and weighting, complete local gradient contributions, and a single synchronized update. The concrete workflow follows the dataflow from assigning local batches to synchronizing the computed gradients. The five-stage execution pipeline in @fig-dist-train-data-parallelism follows four GPU swimlanes, tracking how identical model replicas ingest disjoint batch shards, compute local gradients ($\MinibatchGradient_0$--$\MinibatchGradient_3$), and synchronize through a ring AllReduce collective before applying uniform parameter updates.

title: Communication patterns and their costs
caption: **Communication patterns and their costs**: Ring AllReduce and a parameter server illustrate two ways to aggregate updates. All-to-All instead routes distinct data to each peer; the complete graph shows logical destinations, not a requirement for dedicated physical links. A switched fabric can carry this traffic, with cost determined by message size, routes, and contention.
alt: Three panels. Ring AllReduce: four GPUs, each holding its gradient as four chunk cells, pass one numbered chunk to the next neighbor around a ring, with equal-weight arrows on every link, labeled 2 times N minus 1 over N times M per GPU, load spread over all links. Parameter server: four workers exchange data with a shared bus that feeds one thick red trunk into a highlighted red server NIC beneath the server, labeled 2M per worker, all traffic through one NIC. Logical All-to-All: four GPUs with four chunk cells each, joined by twelve directed arrows, one per ordered pair, labeled N times N minus 1 messages, logical pairs rather than physical wires.
context:
:::

Across the wider design space, @fig-coll-comm compares three synchronization topologies: the bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce that circulates chunks along neighbor links ($2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ volume), the centralized parameter server constrained by network interface card (NIC) saturation at the server node, and the dense mesh of logical All-to-All peer traffic ($\DeviceCount(\DeviceCount-1)$ messages). In dense synchronous data-parallel settings, ring AllReduce avoids a single reducer bottleneck by distributing traffic evenly across participating links, as Baidu's implementation illustrates [@gibiansky2017baidu].

title: Distributed synchronization models
caption: **Distributed synchronization models**: The timelines compare three synchronization strategies. Top: bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) forces all workers to wait at a global barrier every step. Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to $\StalenessBound$ steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.
alt: Timeline diagram with three panels of four worker rows, in which worker W3 takes longer per iteration than the others. Top, BSP: after every iteration the faster workers sit in red-hatched wait blocks until W3, labeled slow in red, reaches a global barrier. Middle, SSP with s equal to 1: the faster workers run freely until they would lead W3 by more than one iteration, then pause briefly. Bottom, ASP: every worker runs without waiting, so the faster workers finish eight iterations while W3 finishes six.
context:
:::

@Fig-sync-model-timeline sequences execution traces for four workers across BSP, SSP, and ASP, isolating how global barriers force faster workers into idle wait blocks while straggler W3 completes, how bounded slack ($\StalenessBound=1$) throttles drift with brief pauses, and how asynchronous updates remove the global barrier without imposing a finite staleness bound. Communication and resource contention can still leave workers waiting.

title: ZeRO memory reduction
caption: **ZeRO memory reduction**: Standard data parallelism (DDP) replicates all model states across every GPU. ZeRO progressively partitions these states: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradient sharding, and ZeRO-3 shards the parameters themselves; each dashed outline marks the replicated stack a stage no longer holds. ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling, enabling models with 100B+ parameters to fit on accelerators that could not hold the replicated state.
alt: Stacked bar chart of per-GPU memory for optimizer state, gradients, and weights, shaded from darker to lighter blue, under DDP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3. Totals fall from 112 GB to 29.3, 15.5, and 1.75 GB; a red dashed line at 80 GB accelerator memory, with the region above it washed light red, shows that only DDP exceeds it. Behind each ZeRO bar a dashed gray outline at the 112 GB DDP height marks the replicated state that stage no longer holds on the GPU.

:::

ZeRO reaches that result in stages, and the intermediate stages matter because each one buys memory with a different communication pattern. Optimizer sharding alone (ZeRO-1) already brings the replicated footprint of the same model under the accelerator ceiling, because optimizer state is three-quarters of it; gradient sharding (ZeRO-2) and parameter sharding (ZeRO-3/FSDP) continue toward the fully sharded figure (@fig-zero-memory). @Tbl-zero-stages pairs each stage with the collectives it uses.

title: ZeRO state partitioning across GPU ranks
caption: **ZeRO state partitioning across GPU ranks**: Which copy of each training state every GPU holds, for 4 workers. A filled full-width tile is a replicated copy; a quarter-width segment inside a dashed outline is that GPU's shard, stepping one quarter per rank. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4$), ZeRO-2 adds gradients ($\GradientMemory/4$), and ZeRO-3 shards parameters too ($\WeightMemory/4$). The footers give per-worker communication volume relative to DDP: only ZeRO-3 pays more, for the parameter AllGathers.
alt: Four panels, DDP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3 / FSDP, each with four GPU rows and three columns, W, G, and O, drawn in light to darker blue. A replicated state is a filled full-width tile; a sharded state is a dashed outline with only one quarter filled, at the first quarter for GPU 0 through the last quarter for GPU 3, forming a staircase down the rows. DDP fills every tile; ZeRO-1 shards O; ZeRO-2 shards G and O; ZeRO-3 shards W, G, and O. Footers read communication volume 1, 1, 1, and 1.5 times.
section: Segment labels where the segments are tall enough to hold text.
context:
ZeRO-2\index{ZeRO-2!gradient sharding} additionally shards gradients. ReduceScatter leaves each GPU with its $1/\DeviceCount$ shard of reduced gradients. Each worker updates its $1/\DeviceCount$ parameter partition using the corresponding optimizer state, then AllGather restores the updated parameter replicas. In the ideal ring accounting, each phase transfers $\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ elements per worker, for $2\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount$ across both phases. This matches DDP's byte volume ($1\times$) when gradient and parameter communication widths match. Replicated parameters avoid forward parameter gathers, although model operations may still communicate. Under the FP16-gradient convention, gradient storage falls from $2\DeviceCount$ bytes per parameter across $\DeviceCount$ workers to $2$ bytes per parameter in total, or $2/\DeviceCount$ per GPU, apart from transient buffers.

ZeRO-3\index{ZeRO-3!parameter sharding} and FSDP\index{FSDP!parameter sharding} also partition parameters, leaving each GPU with a $1/\DeviceCount$ persistent slice. The full-shard schedule considered here gathers each unit before forward computation, releases its unsharded parameters, and gathers them again for backward. ReduceScatter distributes the completed gradients for local shard updates. @Fig-zero-partitioning contrasts the stored state across four ranks. Under matching communication widths, ZeRO-1 ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4$) and ZeRO-2 ($\OptimizerStateMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4$) retain baseline $1\times$ communication volume; ZeRO-3 ($\WeightMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4, \OptimizerStateMemory/4$) adds the second parameter gather, yielding $1.5\times$ the baseline volume in this accounting.

title: The scaling tax
caption: **The scaling tax**: Effective speedup $\DeviceCount/(1+(\DeviceCount-1)\SerialFraction)$ against GPU count on log-log axes, for illustrative fixed residual fractions $\SerialFraction$ of baseline step time. Ideal scaling (dashed) is linear. Each curve bends away from it and flattens near $1/\SerialFraction$: at 512 GPUs, $\SerialFraction$ = 0.1 percent still delivers about two-thirds of ideal speedup, 1 percent about one-sixth, and 10 percent under 10$\times$ in total. Darker curves carry larger $\SerialFraction$.
alt: Log-log line chart of effective speedup against GPU count from 1 to 512. A dashed diagonal marks ideal linear speedup. Three curves for r of 0.1, 1, and 10 percent bend below it and flatten, the darker curves flattening earlier and lower. Dotted horizontal lines mark the ceilings 1 over r equals 10 and 100 that the 10 percent and 1 percent curves approach, and a pale amber band between ideal and the 10 percent curve is labeled scaling tax at r equals 10 percent.
context:
That baseline fraction is not the synchronization share a profiler reports for a distributed step (the distributed Amdahl pitfall of @sec-vol2-introduction-fleet-law), because the compute share has been divided by $\DeviceCount$ while the residual has not. A residual of `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.r_pct_str` of the single-device step occupies about `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.share_pct_str` of each step on `{python} AmdahlObservedShare.n_str`. Reading the observed share as $\SerialFraction$ would therefore overstate the residual many times over and predict a far lower speedup ceiling than the model implies.

@Fig-scaling-tax illustrates this scaling tax\index{Scaling tax!communication overhead} up to 512 GPUs on log-log axes, complementing the scaling efficiency bound (principle \ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}). In this illustrative fixed-residual model, a small baseline fraction ($\SerialFraction= 0.1\%$) stays closer to ideal scaling than a larger fraction ($\SerialFraction= 1\%$). A residual equal to a tenth of baseline time ($\SerialFraction= 0.10$) limits asymptotic speedup to $1/\SerialFraction= 10\times$. Actual collective and coordination costs can change with worker count, so predicting a training run requires the more explicit Fleet Law below.
```

title: Statistical cost of larger batches
caption: **Statistical cost of larger batches**: A normalized illustration of the gradient-noise trade-off model, with batch size divided by the fitted critical batch. Optimization steps approach a lower limit as batches grow, while total examples processed increase. The crossover is not a hardware-throughput optimum or a measured threshold for a particular model [@mccandlish2018empirical].
alt: Two curves on logarithmic axes. Normalized optimization steps decrease toward one as normalized batch increases; normalized sample use increases from one. Both curves equal two at batch divided by critical batch equal to one, marked as the crossover. The region above the critical batch is shaded light gray; labels name the two regimes, steps falling almost proportionally with few extra samples below the critical batch, and steps flattening toward the minimum while samples keep climbing above it. Each curve is labeled directly.
section: Critical batch size and diminishing returns {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-critical-batch-size-parallelism-hurt-4961}
context:
The gradient-noise model separates statistical efficiency from hardware efficiency. Well below $\CriticalBatchSize$\index{Critical batch size!scaling regimes}, increasing batch size can reduce optimization steps almost proportionally while preserving similar total sample use. Near $\CriticalBatchSize$, the trade-off between fewer updates and more samples becomes material. Above it, step count approaches a lower limit while sample use continues to increase. Neither maximum samples per second nor minimum training time necessarily occurs at $\CriticalBatchSize$: those objectives also depend on device utilization, communication, and the validated learning-rate schedule.

@Fig-critical-batch-size plots this gradient-noise trade-off on log-log axes, tracking the divergence between optimization step count and total sample consumption. Below the critical threshold ($\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize< 1$), increasing batch size yields near-linear reductions in optimization steps with negligible sample waste; past the crossover point at $\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize= 1$ (where both normalized costs equal 2), the step count curve asymptotically flattens toward 1 while total examples processed climb steeply along the $1 + \BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize$ trajectory.

title: Layer-wise model parallelism
caption: **Layer-wise model parallelism**: (a) A 16-layer transformer placed four consecutive layers per GPU, cutting each GPU's weight footprint to one-quarter of the model. Forward activations cross each stage boundary left to right; gradients return right to left. (b) Without microbatching, one batch visits the stages in turn, forward (F) and then backward (B) in reverse, in equal schematic time slots, so each GPU works in only 2 of 8 slots. The microbatched schedule in @fig-pipeline-parallelism fills much of that idle time.

A small bar beside each row splits into 2 busy and 6 idle segments, labeled busy 2 of 8.

#### Layer-wise partitioning {#sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-layerwise-partitioning-cf6a}

Layer-wise partitioning is the least invasive model cut. It saves memory by assigning consecutive layers to separate devices, but it preserves the model's sequential dependence. In transformer architectures, this translates to specific devices managing defined sets of attention and feed-forward blocks. For a 16-layer transformer on four GPUs (@fig-dist-layers-blocks), panel (a) maps the weight footprint reduction to one-quarter per device alongside forward activation and backward gradient transfers across stage boundaries, while panel (b) charts the resulting execution timeline, revealing that each GPU remains idle for six of eight time slots without microbatch pipelining.

title: Pipeline parallelism schedule
caption: **Pipeline parallelism schedule**: A 4-stage pipeline processes 4 microbatches with all forward passes (F) before any backward pass (B), as in GPipe. Rows are pipeline stages and columns are equal time slots. Each backward pass enters a stage only after the next stage has produced that microbatch's gradient, so every stage idles $\PipelineParallelDegree-1$ slots in the forward phase and $\PipelineParallelDegree-1$ in the backward phase, 6 of 14 slots in all.
alt: Pipeline schedule grid with four GPU rows and fourteen time slots. Light blue forward cells for microbatches 1 to 4 step diagonally down and right; darker blue backward cells in reverse microbatch order step diagonally up and right from the last stage; the idle bubble cells that fill the rest of the grid are hatched red, forming triangles at the start and end of the schedule and a diamond in the middle, with the fill slots t1 to t3 and drain slots t12 to t14 bracketed below. At the right, a small bar per stage splits into 8 busy and 6 idle segments, labeled 6 of 14 idle. A legend identifies forward, backward, and idle cells.
context:
:::

In the GPipe schedule of @fig-pipeline-parallelism, a four-stage pipeline processes four microbatches ($\PipelineParallelDegree=4, \MicrobatchCount=4$), and dividing the global batch into discrete microbatches allows forward passes to overlap diagonally across stages before backward passes unfold in reverse order. While microbatching raises hardware utilization above naive sequential placement, pipeline fill ($\PipelineTimeSlot_1$--$\PipelineTimeSlot_3$) and drain ($\PipelineTimeSlot_{12}$--$\PipelineTimeSlot_{14}$) bubbles still leave each device idle for 6 of 14 time slots.

title: Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism
caption: **Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism**: A Megatron-LM layer pair on two GPUs, read left to right. The first layer (for example, QKV or the first feed-forward layer) is split by columns, $\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix = [\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_1 \mid \ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each GPU computes its own slice $\LayerOutputMatrix_i$ of the replicated input's output. The second layer is split by rows, $\RowParallelWeightMatrix = [\RowParallelWeightMatrix_1 ; \RowParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each slice feeds its matching shard on the same GPU without communication. The only collective is the amber AllReduce that sums the partial outputs $\RowParallelOutputMatrix_1 + \RowParallelOutputMatrix_2$, leaving the full result on both GPUs.
alt: Two GPU lanes, each written as a matrix equation with rectangles drawn to shape. On each lane a replicated input matrix X multiplies weight matrix A, of which the GPU holds only one column half, A1 or A2, the other half dashed. The result is one column slice, Y1 or Y2, which multiplies the matching row half of B, B1 on top for GPU 0 and B2 below for GPU 1, giving a full-size partial sum Z1 or Z2; a note between the lanes reads no communication. Both partial sums enter one amber AllReduce bar spanning the lanes, which outputs the full Z on each GPU.
context:
Each GPU computes its partition independently. The concatenation in the equation is logical, because when the next operation is row-parallel, each output shard remains on its producing device and feeds the matching weight shard without an AllGather. The row-parallel half\index{Tensor parallelism!row-parallel linear layer} of the pattern splits weights along rows, $\WeightMatrix= \begin{bmatrix} \WeightMatrix_1 \\ \WeightMatrix_2 \end{bmatrix}$:
$$\LayerOutputMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix= \LayerInputMatrix_1 \WeightMatrix_1 + \LayerInputMatrix_2 \WeightMatrix_2$$
Each GPU computes a partial sum, and the system pays one AllReduce to combine the partial outputs.

title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing
caption: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing**: Expert parallelism on four ranks, one expert per rank, read left to right and drawn for top-1 routing with one token traced. Each rank's gate picks the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts for its tokens; the first All-to-All dispatches every token to the rank that hosts its expert, the experts compute, and a second All-to-All returns the results so each rank can form the gate-weighted sum for its own tokens. In both exchanges every rank may send to every other rank, which is why the pattern stresses the fabric's bisection bandwidth.
alt: Five columns over four rows. On the left, ranks 0 to 3 each hold four token chips lettered a to p. An amber dispatch band carries one line per token to the blue expert box on the rank its gate chose, so Expert 0 holds tokens b, g, i, p, Expert 1 holds d, e, k, n, Expert 2 holds a, h, j, o, and Expert 3 holds c, f, l, m, one token from every rank. A second amber return band carries each token back to its home rank, where the four chips reappear in their original order shaded blue. The route of token a, from rank 0 to Expert 2 and back, is drawn heavier.
context:
While tensor parallelism splits dense operations, expert parallelism\index{Expert parallelism!conditional computation} distributes model capacity that is used selectively. In an MoE\index{MoE!routing}\index{Mixture of experts|see{MoE}} architecture [@shazeer2017outrageously], a feed-forward layer contains $\ExpertCount$ "experts" (independent feed-forward networks). A gating network selects a small subset, often top-1 or top-2, for each token. Increasing expert count while holding expert shape and the number selected fixed increases stored parameters without proportionally increasing expert FLOPs per token; routing and communication still add work.

In a distributed setting, experts are partitioned across workers, with each rank hosting a disjoint subset of expert networks. @Fig-moe-all-to-all-routing traces this token routing cycle across four ranks: after top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ gating selects destination experts, an All-to-All dispatch shuffles tokens across the fabric to the hosting ranks, expert FFNs compute locally, and a second All-to-All return routes the processed activations back to the originating ranks to form the gate-weighted sum. The backward pass repeats both exchanges in reverse order, sending output gradients to the ranks hosting the experts and returning input gradients to the ranks that own the tokens.
