A projected MFU needs comparison with measured execution. @Fig-mfu-progression places reported MFU\index{Model FLOPs Utilization!distributed training} from 2020–2024 systems against an illustrative 50 percent reference line. GPT-3's `{python} MfuProgression.gpt3_mfu_str` and PaLM's `{python} MfuProgression.palm_mfu_str`\index{PaLM!MFU efficiency} describe different hardware and workload configurations; their difference does not isolate the effect of parallelism or overlap. Llama 3's reported result at `{python} MfuProgression.llama3_16k_gpus_str` H100 GPUs (`{python} MfuProgression.llama3_16k_mfu_str`) is lower than at `{python} MfuProgression.llama3_8k_gpus_str` GPUs (`{python} MfuProgression.llama3_8k_mfu_str`)\index{Llama 3!MFU scaling tax}. Interpreting that change requires the batch, configuration, precision convention, and measurement window alongside device count.

title: One PPO-style RLHF step
caption: **One PPO-style RLHF step**: The policy generates responses to a batch of prompts. The frozen reference model supplies log-probabilities for the KL penalty, the frozen reward model supplies a scalar score, and the trained value model supplies value estimates. The penalized reward and value estimates form advantages, which update the policy and value models. Blue cards carry gradients and optimizer state; slate cards run forward passes only and hold weights alone, as each card's weight, gradient, and optimizer-state strip shows; strip widths follow the 2, 2, and 12 bytes per parameter of mixed-precision Adam, unlike the equal-width columns of @fig-zero-partitioning. That asymmetry drives placement.
alt: Flow diagram. Prompts feed a blue Policy card, whose responses fan out to three cards: Reference (slate, log-probs for KL), Reward model (slate, scalar score r), and Value model (blue, value estimates). Each card carries a strip of weight, gradient, and optimizer-state tiles sized 2 to 2 to 12: the blue Policy and Value cards fill all three tiles, while the slate Reference and Reward cards fill only the weight tile and show gradients and optimizer state as dashed empty outlines. The three scoring outputs merge into an Advantages box labeled r minus beta KL, GAE, and a blue return line labeled PPO update feeds gradients back to the Policy and Value cards only.
context:
### The multi-model coordination problem {#sec-distributed-training-rlhf-coordination}

The single-model pretraining baseline becomes a multi-role loop in PPO\index{Proximal policy optimization!model asymmetry}\index{PPO|see{Proximal policy optimization}} [@schulman2017proximal], as used in InstructGPT-style systems [@ouyang2022instructgpt]. @Tbl-rlhf-model-coordination-roles separates policy, reference, reward, and value roles by execution mode and memory burden. In @fig-rlhf-ppo-step, the policy $\Policy$ generates responses for scoring by the frozen reference and reward models and evaluation by the value model $\CriticModel$. The penalized reward ($\ResponseReward- \KlPenaltyCoefficient\,\text{KL}$) subtracts a Kullback–Leibler divergence penalty, weighted by a coefficient $\KlPenaltyCoefficient$ unrelated to link bandwidth $\LinkBandwidth$, to discourage drift from the reference. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) combines rewards and value estimates to judge how much better a response was than expected. Those estimates guide policy updates; the value model learns to predict returns, the cumulative discounted reward that follows each generated token. Reference and reward models remain forward-only in this loop, and shared-backbone implementations can combine roles without changing their distinct responsibilities.

title: Parallelism strategy decision framework
caption: **Parallelism strategy decision framework**: A selection guide that begins with memory fit. For a model that fits on one device, evaluate data parallelism against the throughput target and input-delivery budget; the complete dataset need not fit in accelerator memory. A model that does not fit is routed by the structure that breaks the budget, with sequential depth leading to pipeline parallelism, an oversized single layer to tensor parallelism, and otherwise sharded data parallelism (FSDP/ZeRO). Combine parallelism axes when the workload requires them. Peak memory, global batch, bandwidth, and workload imbalance constrain every candidate.
alt: Decision tree flowchart. From the workload profile, diamonds ask whether the model fits on one GPU, whether one GPU meets the target, whether the layer stack is deep, and whether a single layer is too large. Outcomes are single device, data parallel, pipeline parallel, tensor parallel, or sharded data parallel (FSDP, ZeRO), each with a small glyph of layer bars inside GPU frames: one full stack for a single device, three full copies for data parallel, two frames holding upper and lower layer groups for pipeline parallel, two frames each holding one half of every layer for tensor parallel, and three frames each holding a different one-third slice of every layer, the rest dashed, for sharded data parallel. Dashed lines from the four parallel outcomes lead to a box that combines axes as TP times PP times DP.
context:
: **Parallel Training Strategies**: Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism form the canonical 3D core. Sequence/context parallelism extends the partition along token positions, while expert parallelism extends it across sparse model capacity. Strategy selection remains an engineering feasibility test: identify the binding constraint, the communication primitive it creates, the placement decision it forces, and the measurement that proves the strategy is helping. {#tbl-parallelism-compare tbl-colwidths="[15,22,20,23,20]"}

@Fig-parallelism-flowchart condenses the table into a decision path that starts from memory fit and then asks which structure breaks the budget. Before accepting any branch, check peak memory, global batch, communication service time, and load balance together; bandwidth is a feasibility constraint throughout the decision, not an afterthought.

title: The rise of fleet-scale training
caption: **The rise of fleet-scale training**: Accelerator count for state-of-the-art training runs from 2012 to 2024, with system mean time between failures on the opposing axis. Cluster size rises about four orders of magnitude and system MTBF falls correspondingly, which is what turns fault tolerance from a reliability feature into a scheduling constraint. Counts are published values except the hollow marker, an estimate of the 2020 Microsoft/OpenAI machine size; MTBF applies one per-device planning rate.
alt: Log-scale scatter of training cluster accelerator count from 2012 (AlexNet, 2 GPUs) through Megatron-LM, an estimated GPT-3-era machine (hollow marker), PaLM, LLaMA, and DeepSeek-V3 to 2024 (Llama 3, 16,384 GPUs), with a second axis for system mean time between failures. A red-shaded band with a dashed boundary marks the region where system MTBF falls under 10 hours; PaLM, the GPT-3-era machine, and Llama 3 sit inside it. A double-headed arrow at the right spans AlexNet to Llama 3 and is labeled about 10 to the 4th times.
context:
The consequence is a gap between failure cadence and job length. At `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str`, the GPU-only calculation gives an expected interval of `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.hours_between_str`, so a training run measured in weeks accumulates dozens of expected failures and one measured in months accumulates hundreds. These are planning averages, not a schedule of incidents; a shorter job can finish without failure even when its expected failure count exceeds one. Once the expected time between failures falls below the length of the job, fault tolerance becomes part of the execution budget for long-running fleet work.

Scale and reliability diverge sharply across training generations. By pairing accelerator counts (left axis, log scale) with modeled system MTBF (opposing right axis), @fig-cluster-scaling-trend tracks how training fleets expanded by four orders of magnitude from 2012 (AlexNet on two GPUs) to 2024 (Llama 3 on over 16,000 GPUs), driven by the compute budgets that scaling laws reward (@sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043). Applying the same per-device planning rate across those sizes compresses system MTBF from tens of thousands of hours to under ten hours. The opposing axis illustrates the scaling model rather than a history of measured failure rates, showing why recovery becomes an active scheduling constraint.

title: Published failure rates from production clusters
caption: **Published failure rates from production clusters**: Measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's RSC clusters [@kokolis2025] plotted with Llama 3 training measurements [@dubey2024llama] against the theoretical 1/N curve. At 16,384 GPUs, the Kokolis projection and the Llama 3 empirical measurement bracket a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours (the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement), confirming that fault tolerance is a mathematical necessity, not an edge case. Data sources: Kokolis et al., arXiv:2410.21680; Meta, arXiv:2407.21783.
alt: Log-log scatter plot of mean time to failure in hours versus GPU count with a dashed theoretical 50,000 hours over N line. Filled blue dots mark measured Meta RSC values at 8 and 1,024 GPUs, hollow blue dots mark projections at 16,384 and 131K GPUs, and a dark diamond marks the Llama 3 measurement of 3.1 hours. A short light red band at 16,384 GPUs spans 1.8 to 3.1 hours, labeled failure every 2 to 3 h. Dotted gray reference lines mark 1 day, 1 week, and 3 months.
context:
```

Production measurements confirm the $1/\AcceleratorCount$ trend of @tbl-cluster-mtbf-scaling and show that the GPU-only line is optimistic. Plotted on log-log axes, measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta's clusters follow the slope of the $50{,}000\,\text{h}/\AcceleratorCount$ line across more than three orders of magnitude in job size but sit below it, because a job can be interrupted by far more than its GPUs (@fig-published-failure-rates). The @kokolis2025 study of Meta's Research SuperCluster reported measured MTTF values for observed RSC job sizes and projected a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` MTTF for `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU jobs. That projection lands next to the Llama 3\index{Llama-3!failure report} run recounted in @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment, whose `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_interruptions_str` unexpected interruptions across a `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_days_str`-day snapshot on `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str` H100 GPUs give an observed MTTF of about `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_str`. Together, the measured Llama run and Kokolis projection put `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_gpus_str`-GPU training on a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours, bracketed by the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.kokolis_16k_mttf_attr_str` projection and the `{python} PublishedFailureRates.llama_mttf_attr_str` measurement. This evidence turns the idealized $1/\AcceleratorCount$ relation into an engineering constraint that determines checkpoint frequency, recovery architecture, and infrastructure investment.

title: Root Causes of Training Interruptions
caption: **Root Causes of Training Interruptions**: The 419 unexpected interruptions recorded over 54 days of Llama 3 405B pretraining on 16,384 H100 GPUs, by root-cause component and colored by category. GPU components dominate; silent data corruption appears only where it was detected. Counts are from Table 5 of @dubey2024llama; one percentage in that table (Faulty GPU) disagrees with its count, so shares here are computed from the counts.
alt: Horizontal bar chart of 18 root-cause components sorted by count, colored by category. Faulty GPU leads with 148 interruptions, then GPU HBM3 memory 72, software bug 54, network switch or cable 35, host maintenance 32, GPU SRAM memory 19, and GPU system processor 17. The remaining components each caused 7 or fewer, including NIC 7, NCCL watchdog timeouts 7, silent data corruption 6, and GPU thermal interface and sensor 6.
context:
```

Production logs show which of these failures a large run actually meets. During a `{python} InterruptionCauses.days_str`-day period of Llama 3 405B pretraining on `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpus_str` H100 GPUs, Meta traced each of `{python} InterruptionCauses.total_str` unexpected interruptions to a root cause [@dubey2024llama]. Grouped by cause in @fig-llama3-interruptions, GPU components account for `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_count_str` of them, about `{python} InterruptionCauses.gpu_share_pct_str`, led by `{python} InterruptionCauses.faulty_gpu_str` faulty GPUs and `{python} InterruptionCauses.hbm_str` HBM memory failures. Software bugs caused `{python} InterruptionCauses.software_str`, network switches and cables `{python} InterruptionCauses.network_str`, and the remaining host hardware, from NICs to power supplies, `{python} InterruptionCauses.host_str` between them. Only `{python} InterruptionCauses.sdc_str` interruptions were attributed to silent data corruption, and that count includes only corruption that was caught. Most fault-tolerance effort therefore goes to frequent, detectable accelerator failures, while the rare silent ones demand a different kind of defense.

title: Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures
caption: **Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line, each showing four worker message streams along a time axis with a liveness column at the right. Left, fail-stop: W1, W3, and W4 emit regular violet heartbeat ticks and get green checks; W2's ticks stop at a red X, a bracket labeled silence runs to a violet diamond labeled timeout, and W2 gets a red X for liveness. Caption text reads silence is the evidence. Right, Byzantine: W5 to W8 send amber gradient squares on the same schedule and all four get green checks, but partway along W6's row its squares turn red. Text reads on time, but wrong.
context:
Where a fail-stop component ceases to participate, a value-corrupting component can keep running while returning incorrect results, as when a GPU returns wrong gradients without raising an error, a link delivers a corrupted packet whose error pattern the CRC happens not to cover, or a worker computes different results for identical inputs and state. Byzantine failures\index{Byzantine failure!classification} allow arbitrary behavior, including inconsistent messages to different participants [@lamport1982byzantine]. ML systems can encounter this broader failure model through silent data corruption\index{Silent data corruption!mechanism} or adversarial corruption. Numerical instability\index{Numerical instability!Byzantine failure} and determinism violations\index{Determinism!violation} also require validation when they break the execution contract, but ordinary rounding differences or intentionally stochastic outputs are not themselves evidence of a faulty worker. The recovery concern is a participant whose accepted contribution can corrupt shared state without a visible crash.

The two models leave different evidence (@fig-failure-types). A fail-stop worker such as W2 falls silent, and its missing heartbeats make it suspect. A Byzantine worker such as W6 keeps sending messages on schedule, so it passes every liveness check while the values it sends are wrong.

title: Hierarchy of failure domains
caption: **Hierarchy of failure domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. A node failure affects `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.node_gpus_str` GPUs. A rack switch failure affects 32--64 GPUs (each rack is drawn with only two of its four to eight nodes). A power distribution unit (PDU) failure may affect multiple racks. The red rack shows one such correlated failure: a single top-of-rack switch fault removes every GPU it contains, while the neighboring rack is untouched, which is why replicas must span independent domains (for example, different racks or rows).
alt: Nested rectangles: a datacenter labeled blast radius all GPUs contains a power and network domain spanning several racks, which contains two racks, each drawn with two of its eight-GPU nodes. The left rack is outlined in red, labeled ToR switch fails and 32 to 64 GPUs, and all its GPU squares are red; the right rack is labeled unaffected and its GPUs are blue.
context:
: **Failure Domains in ML Infrastructure**: Understanding failure domain boundaries enables placement of redundant components across independent domains, preventing correlated failures from defeating redundancy strategies. {#tbl-failure-domains}

The nesting of failure domains in @tbl-failure-domains has direct consequences for redundancy placement. Placing replicas within the same domain provides zero protection against that domain's failure mode.

title: The bathtub curve
caption: **The bathtub curve**: Hardware failure rates $\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)$ vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment.
alt: Line graph of failure rate versus component age from days to end of life, showing a bathtub shape across three shaded regions separated by dashed lines: (1) infant mortality in red with a falling rate from manufacturing defects screened by burn-in, (2) useful life in green with a constant rate whose flat floor is highlighted and labeled h equals 1 over MTTF, with MTTF about 50,000 hours, and (3) wear-out in red with a rising rate from electromigration and thermal fatigue.
section: The Bathtub Curve and Hardware Lifecycle {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-bathtub-curve-hardware-lifecycle-7d8a}
context:
[^fn-electromigration-silicon-wearout]: **Electromigration**\index{Electromigration!wear-out mechanism}: Gradual displacement of metal atoms in conductors by electron momentum transfer, first characterized in early electromigration studies and later modeled in Black's reliability equation [@black1969electromigration]. Mean time to failure decreases with higher current density and higher temperature, so sustained high-power accelerator workloads make thermal management a direct determinant of fleet lifespan.

The practical implication for ML systems is that fleet-wide failure rates can depend on age distribution. Under the bathtub model, a new cohort passes through elevated early-life risk, a relatively stable period, and eventual wear-out. Screening, operating conditions, and replacement policy determine how much of that pattern appears in field data. Mixed-age fleets combine cohorts at different stages, so their aggregate hazard need not follow the curve of a single cohort.

title: The ML failure spectrum
caption: **The ML failure spectrum**: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress.
alt: An arrow labeled fault persistence runs from clears on its own to lasts until repaired above three panels: transient, intermittent, and permanent. Each panel shows a row of eight attempt squares over time, green when an attempt completes and red when it faults. Transient: one red square among greens. Intermittent: gray load bars above the row, and the two attempts under the tallest load bars are red. Permanent: two green squares then all red. Below each row are a typical cause (particle strike, cracked solder joint, stuck-at fault or wear-out) and a response box (retry or roll back, drain and stress-test, replace and restore).
section: Fault persistence and the fleet response {#sec-ft-fault-persistence-response}
context:
### Fault persistence and the fleet response {#sec-ft-fault-persistence-response}

Each persistence class from the taxonomy maps to a different fleet action, from retry for a fault that leaves nothing to repair, through quarantine for one that returns under load, to replacement for one that repeats on every attempt (@fig-fault-tolerance-failure-spectrum). A transient fault\index{Transient fault!fleet response}, as @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-transient-failures-57b4 established, leaves no lasting defect from that event, so the fleet's question is only whether its effect escaped. A single-event upset, a voltage droop on an unstable power path [@reddi2013], a timing violation, or a soft error in combinational logic [@mukherjee2005] can corrupt a tensor, packet, or instruction. Detection and correction can prevent propagation; affected state may otherwise require rollback. During training, an undetected error in weights or gradients can compromise convergence and contaminate subsequent checkpoints [@he2023]. During stateless inference, an activation error can remain confined to one request [@mahmoud2020]. If that activation enters retained state such as a KV cache, later outputs can also depend on it.

title: Silent data corruption propagation
caption: **Silent data corruption propagation**: A hardware bit flip moves left to right from one wrong tensor value through the backward pass and the weight update, surfacing only at the final stage as degraded model quality. The two timelines below contrast a detected error, which traps within milliseconds and restarts from the last checkpoint, with silent corruption, which is saved into checkpoints for hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a rollback; the gap between the two is the cost of silence.
alt: Top, a left-to-right chain linked by red arrows: an 8-bit word with one red bit under a lightning mark labeled bit flip in memory or ALU; a 5 by 5 tensor grid with one red cell labeled wrong value in one tensor entry; a gradient grid where the red cell's row and column are tinted red, labeled backward pass taints gradients; a weight grid whose whole row and column are red, labeled weight update commits to weights; and a small plot whose rising quality curve turns red and falls, labeled quality drops seen at evaluation. Below, two timelines share a time axis marked t equals zero, milliseconds, and hours to days. Detected error: a fault dot, a trap dot, then a green restart from checkpoint box. Silent corruption: a fault dot, a long red dashed span labeled corrupt state saved containing three crossed-out checkpoint squares, an alert dot, then a green roll back box.
context:
Digital hardware implements *deterministic* operations, but physical fault occurrence requires a *probabilistic* reliability model. Two mechanisms illustrate the distinction. Single-event upsets (SEUs)\index{SEU!mechanism}\index{Single-event upset|see{SEU}}, the particle strikes introduced with transient failures, create fleet exposure that grows with device count and operating time even when the per-device rate is low. Manufacturing variances\index{Manufacturing variance!silicon margin} can leave "marginal" chips that pass initial QA but fail under particular inputs or operating conditions. Voltage and temperature margins matter, including supply disturbances during rapid current changes ($d\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent/d\TimeInstant$). These defects can produce repeatable errors, so a probabilistic fleet model does not imply that every individual fault is random.

Facebook documented a pervasive SDC issue where a hardware fault caused a valid file to be reported as "size zero" during decompression [@dixit2021silent]; the system "worked" without crashing, but data was silently deleted. In ML, the same failure manifests as valid-looking but numerically corrupted gradients. The pipeline trace in @fig-sdc-example follows a single ALU or memory bit flip as it corrupts an individual tensor entry, taints gradient reduction during the backward pass, commits into weights, and finally surfaces as degraded quality at evaluation. The comparative timelines beneath contrast this silent latency with a standard detected error: while a hardware trap halts within milliseconds to restart cleanly from the last checkpoint, silent corruption commits contaminated state into checkpoints over hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a costly rollback.

title: Silent data corruption at scale
caption: **Silent data corruption at scale**: Jeff Dean presents on silent data corruption (SDC) at MLSys 2024, arguing that at the scale of large ML training jobs hardware errors occur routinely, and that incorrect computations from one buggy chip can propagate and infect an entire training run. Source: Jeff Dean, MLSys 2024 keynote (Google).
alt: Photograph of Jeff Dean giving a keynote at MLSys 2024. On stage he stands at a podium; a projected slide titled 'Silent Data Corruption errors (SDCs)' explains that ML-scale hardware errors can propagate and infect the entire training system.
context:
:::

Telemetry from production training fleets shows this corruption is routine rather than anomalous. At modern training scales, hardware bit flips occur regularly, and erroneous computations from a single malfunctioning accelerator can propagate into the global model state, as Jeff Dean documented in his MLSys 2024 keynote on silent data corruption [@dean2024mlsys] (@fig-sdc-jeffdean).

title: Gradient norm deviation
caption: **Gradient norm deviation**: Transient hardware faults, such as silent data corruption (SDC), can disrupt optimization by causing abrupt changes in gradient norms. Google's production examples show SDC anomalies surfacing as visible gradient-norm spikes. Source: [@dean2024mlsys].
alt: Line graph of gradient norm over training time showing smooth baseline with sudden spike anomaly caused by silent data corruption event.
context:
:::

In the Google training telemetry presented by @dean2024mlsys, @fig-sdc-training-fault identifies an abrupt gradient-norm anomaly as an SDC event. The plot shows the symptom without identifying the damaged bit or circuit. Corrupting a floating-point exponent is one mechanism that can greatly change a tensor value and subsequent updates. Gradient clipping can limit update magnitude, but it does not reconstruct the correct gradient; an anomaly detector must trigger validation or recovery before suspect state is accepted.

title: Hot-spare failover
caption: **Hot-spare failover**: An $\DeviceCount+1$ pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google's data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results [@dean2024mlsys]. The standing cost is the idle spare.
alt: Three panels left to right, each a row of five GPU slots. Panel 1: G0, G1, and G3 active in blue, G2 outlined in red and labeled suspect, and a dashed green spare S. Panel 2: G2 dashed gray and labeled isolated, and S solid blue and labeled active. Panel 3: a new dashed green spare S prime occupies the G2 slot, labeled new spare, with G2 sent to repair.
context:
Full replication protects a broader computation path at a correspondingly high resource cost. Dual modular redundancy\index{DMR!fleet contrast} runs every computation twice and compares the results, and triple modular redundancy\index{TMR!fleet contrast} runs it three times and takes a majority vote, paying 100 and 200 percent hardware overhead to detect or mask a fault within a single control deadline [@sheaffer2007; @arifeen2020]. These guarantees depend on the replicas avoiding a shared fault. The price is justified in safety-critical embedded control, such as a vehicle's onboard computers, where one wrong output can endanger people and the replicated hardware is a small computer. For fleet training, duplicating every step of a run on `{python} FleetReliabilityRates.fleet_gpus_str` doubles the compute devoted to those steps, before comparison and coordination costs. When corruption is rare and rollback can recover valid state, selective redundancy can protect useful progress at lower cost. Screening removes suspect devices, statistical checks run continuously, standby pools absorb drained nodes, and periodic or triggered recomputation checks selected execution paths.

Google's reactive hot-spare protocol shows how those pieces combine in three stages (@fig-sdc-controller). When runtime monitors flag an anomalous gradient and replay implicates a suspect accelerator (G2), the scheduler isolates that device, promotes a standby hot spare (S) into the active ring, and provisions a replacement spare (S') while the suspect unit undergoes hardware diagnostics [@dean2024mlsys]. The fleet pays in advance for one idle device per pool rather than for a duplicate of every computation, and the protocol shifts the burden of correctness from unverified hardware to system-level auditing.

title: Error masking
caption: **Error masking**: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system's true resilience to transient errors.
alt: Flowchart starting at a soft error. A decision diamond asks whether corrupted data is read; No leads to masked in the microarchitecture. Yes leads to a second diamond asking whether output is incorrect or the system crashes; No leads to masked in software, Yes leads to failure. Beside each masked outcome, three masking causes are listed: unused component, overwritten value, and squashed speculation for the microarchitecture; dead instruction, logical or compare op, and uninfluential branch for software. The failure path, Yes and then Yes from soft error to failure, is drawn as a heavy red spine; the No exits are thin gray arrows. A dashed arrow labeled software fault injection enters the spine after the first diamond, and a shaded region below that point, labeled view of software fault injection, encloses only the second diamond, its masked exit, and the failure.
context:
The injection level determines which propagation paths the experiment includes. A register-level bit flip in a simulator such as gem5 [@binkert2011] can expose effects that a mutation of a PyTorch weight tensor omits. Conversely, hardware may mask an injected fault before software observes it. Location and propagation therefore matter when comparing results across fault models [@sangchoolie2017; @papadimitriou2021].

This divergence comes from the multi-tier filtering formalized as error masking [@mohanram2003]. A physical soft error becomes an observable failure only if it passes two screens in turn (@fig-error-masking-ft). The corrupted data must first be read, and the value read must then produce incorrect output or a crash. A hardware disturbance that hits an unused functional unit, is overwritten prior to use, or lands in dynamically dead instructions is silently absorbed within the microarchitecture or runtime [@ko2021]. Because tensor-level mutations inject perturbations downstream of these architectural filters, their empirical error rates must be evaluated at that higher abstraction level.

title: The checkpoint trade-off
caption: **The checkpoint trade-off**: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter's 175B running example on its `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, with a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_s_str` checkpoint write and a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h_str` full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal.
alt: Plot of share of wall time wasted against checkpoint interval in minutes. A dashed blue save-overhead curve falls hyperbolically, a dashed red expected-rework line rises linearly, and a solid dark total curve has a shallow minimum marked with a green dot at about 14 minutes and 5.9 percent wasted. A dotted dropline from the minimum passes through an open circle where the two dashed terms cross, labeled terms equal. The background left of the optimum is tinted blue and labeled writes dominate; the background to the right is tinted red and labeled rework dominates. Each curve carries a direct label.
context:
:::

The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately `{python} YoungDalyOptimal.overhead_pct_str` of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (@fig-checkpoint-tradeoff). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. An interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule.

title: Checkpoint-recovery timeline
caption: **Checkpoint-recovery timeline**: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.
alt: Top, a horizontal timeline: blue compute, green save, blue compute, green save, a red-hatched block labeled lost that ends at a red vertical line, a red recover block, and a final blue compute block. A bracket above the lost and recover blocks reads cost of one failure; brackets below label T ckpt, T write, rework, and T recovery. Bottom, a progress line on the same time axis rises during compute and stays flat during each save, with green dots marking durable progress at the end of each save. During the lost block the line rises in red, then at the failure a red dashed arrow drops it back to the last durable level, it stays flat through recovery, and it climbs again.
section: Young-Daly optimum: green dot with a dropline; the two dashed terms cross on the dropline
context:
:::

Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals ($\CheckpointInterval$) with synchronous save barriers ($\CheckpointWriteTime$), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (@fig-checkpoint-recovery-timeline). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency ($\FailureRecoveryTime$) to reload state and warm up execution pipelines follows before useful work resumes.

title: Distributed checkpoint architecture
caption: **Distributed checkpoint architecture**: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, centralized: four workers send red arrows that merge into one coordinator box labeled ingress limit, which writes to shared storage; beneath, a timing strip shows the four workers' green shard writes in a staircase, one after another, with a red bracket reading blocking write grows with workers. Right, distributed: each of four workers writes with a green arrow to its own NVMe drive, and dashed arrows drain the drives to an object store labeled background; beneath, the four green shard writes start together and end together under a green bracket labeled blocking, followed by dashed gray bars under a bracket labeled drain in background.
context:
#### Distributed checkpointing {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-distributed-checkpointing-5dcc}

Distributed checkpointing eliminates this coordinator funnel by having each worker persist its own shard directly. @Fig-distributed-checkpoint-architecture contrasts the dataflow topologies: the centralized pattern concentrates traffic at the coordinator's ingress, while the distributed pattern writes in parallel to local NVMe and drains the shards to remote object storage in the background. With fixed per-worker shard sizes and sufficient independent staging bandwidth, adding workers need not lengthen the local write pause. Shared drain capacity and completion coordination can still limit scaling. A coordinator signals when to checkpoint and confirms completion, but state flows directly from workers to storage without aggregation.

title: Elastic training recovery
caption: **Elastic training recovery**: Read the three phases top to bottom. Rather than restoring the original worker count before resuming, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the $\DeviceCount-1$ survivors, and redistributes the failed node's data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown.
alt: Three stacked phase panels joined by downward arrows, each with a ring of nodes at left, columns of data-shard tiles in the middle, and a throughput bar at right. Phase 1: nodes N0 to N3 in an amber ring, three shard tiles per node, throughput bar full at 100 percent. Phase 2: N3 is red, the ring links touching it are red and dashed, N3's three shard tiles are red, a violet box over the surviving columns reads rendezvous plus reload, and the empty throughput bar reads paused. Phase 3: N0, N1, and N2 form a three-node ring, each column holds four tiles with the new top tile in green, a label reads plus 1 shard each (plus 33 percent), N3's column is an empty dashed outline, and the throughput bar is three-quarters full at 75 percent.
context:
:::

A small example shows the lifecycle in three phases (@fig-elastic-flow). Execution begins with a balanced four-node AllReduce ring at full throughput. When Node 3 drops out, the survivors pause at a rendezvous barrier and reload the last consistent checkpoint. The group then contracts into a three-node ring in which each worker takes a one-third larger data shard, resuming productive training at 75 percent throughput if the per-worker rate remains unchanged.

title: Serving redundancy strategies
caption: **Serving redundancy strategies**: Active-active (left) splits traffic across three replicas, each carrying about one-third, which uses every device but requires enough headroom for the survivors to absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive (right) sends all traffic to one primary and keeps a warm standby with weights already loaded, which simplifies failover at the cost of capacity that serves nothing while the primary is healthy.
alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line. Each replica card holds a blue weights bar and a load gauge whose green fill shows traffic served. Left, active-active: a load balancer splits requests along three violet arrows labeled one third to replicas 1, 2, and 3; each gauge is one-third full, and a bracket under the empty part of the first gauge reads headroom absorbs a failed share. Right, active-passive: a load balancer sends a solid arrow labeled all traffic to a primary whose gauge is full and labeled traffic, and a dashed arrow labeled on failure to a dashed warm standby whose weights are loaded but whose gauge is empty and labeled idle; text below reads loaded, serves nothing.
context:
#### Replication strategies {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replication-strategies-aaa2}

The availability equation says how much redundancy can help; the replication topology determines how that redundancy behaves under normal execution and sudden hardware loss. Two fundamental designs make opposite bets (@fig-serving-redundancy). Active-active replication splits ingress traffic evenly across live replicas, one-third each for three, which keeps every device busy but requires spare headroom so the survivors can absorb a failed replica's share. Active-passive replication sends all traffic to a designated primary and keeps a pre-warmed standby whose weights remain loaded in accelerator memory, which makes failover fast at the expense of a device that serves nothing while the primary is healthy.

title: The three pillars of observability
caption: **The three pillars of observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures can combine three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces expose the *request path* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). A single signal can justify immediate mitigation; joining signals on shared identifiers strengthens diagnosis without proving the cause.
alt: Three panels draw each signal in its native form. Metrics, labeled when and where: a GPU utilization time series that runs level and then drops sharply in red. Logs, labeled what happened: a stream of gray log lines with one red monospace line reading OOM exception. Traces, labeled request path: a waterfall of nested span bars with one long span outlined in red. In each panel a dashed violet connector leaves the red anomaly, the end of the utilization drop, the end of the OOM line, and the end of the red span, and runs down as an arrow into a bar reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart, roll back, or degrade.

title: Training failure signatures
caption: **Training failure signatures**: Common patterns of model loss over time that indicate underlying system or algorithmic failures. (A) Normal training. (B) Gradient explosion. (C) Loss plateau. (D) NaN divergence, ending where a nonfinite-value check halts the run; without such a check the process can keep running on NaN values rather than crash. Identifying these signatures automatically is essential for rapid recovery in autonomous training pipelines. The curves are synthetic illustrations of each pattern, not logs from a training run.
alt: Four loss-versus-steps panels in a two-by-two grid on a shared loss axis. (A) Normal training: a green curve descending smoothly. Panels B to D repeat that healthy curve as a faint green reference line behind each pathology. (B) Gradient explosion: a descending curve with a red spike segment midway that then rejoins the healthy reference, labeled healthy. (C) Loss plateau: a curve that flattens early, with the gap between it and the healthy reference shaded red and labeled gap to healthy. (D) NaN divergence: a curve that pulls away above the healthy reference, oscillating with growing amplitude, then climbs steeply to a red X labeled NaN check halts run.
context:
#### Training failures {#sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-training-failures-bc3a}

A training-loss signature is useful because it narrows the hypotheses that recovery must test. The trajectories in @fig-training-failure-signatures illustrate symptoms, including nonfinite values that need not crash the process. @Tbl-training-failure-response-map pairs spike, plateau, and divergence patterns, plus the silent hang a loss curve cannot show, with a candidate cause and a first response. That pairing guides investigation without treating the curve as a unique diagnosis.

caption: **Jobs versus GPU Time by Job Size**: Cumulative share of GPU jobs (gray) and of GPU time (red) against the number of GPUs each job requested, for the Kalos LLM-development cluster from March to August 2023. Almost every job is small, while almost all GPU time goes to jobs of 256 GPUs or more. Data from the AcmeTrace release of @hu2024characterization.

The red curve, cumulative share of GPU time, stays below 5 percent through 128 GPUs, then climbs at 256, 504, 512, and 1,024 GPUs to reach 100 percent. A shaded region marks jobs of 256 GPUs or more.
context:
```

Production traces show that this mix is the normal case rather than a contrived one. In the Kalos cluster that Shanghai AI Laboratory used for language-model development in 2023, `{python} JobSizeMix.single_job_pct_str` of `{python} JobSizeMix.job_count_str` GPU jobs requested a single GPU, yet together they consumed `{python} JobSizeMix.single_time_pct_str` of the cluster's GPU time. Jobs of `{python} JobSizeMix.large_threshold_str` GPUs or more made up `{python} JobSizeMix.large_job_pct_str` of submissions and consumed `{python} JobSizeMix.large_time_pct_str` of GPU time [@hu2024characterization], two distributions that @fig-acme-job-size plots side by side. Counted by jobs, the cluster is a stream of small experiments; counted by GPU-hours, it is a few percent of jobs that hold nearly all the accelerators. A scheduler must serve both views at once, which is why fairness, packing, and preemption policies cannot be judged by either count alone.

title: Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives
caption: **Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives**: A four-way trade-off diamond (Throughput, Latency, Fairness, Cost Efficiency) illustrates the tensions governing cluster scheduling. Throughput favors long, unbroken runs; Latency favors aggressive preemption for interactive jobs; Resource-share fairness can constrain placement to equalize shares; and Cost Efficiency uses discounted, interruptible capacity. Each vertex sketches a four-GPU pool over time as that objective would schedule it and names a possible cost of favoring it; the conflicts depend on workload and available capacity.
alt: Four violet-outlined cards arranged as a diamond and joined by dashed edges, each holding a small strip of a four-GPU pool against time, with strip height standing for GPUs, and a line naming what that objective gives up. Throughput, at top: one large gang block runs unbroken across the whole strip while three small jobs wait stacked in a dashed queue column to its left; gives up small jobs, which starve. Cost efficiency, at left: three spot blocks separated by two red preemption ticks, each tick followed by a red hatched stretch of redone work; gives up preemption overhead. Fairness, at right: team A holds half the pool for the whole period, team B holds the other half briefly and the rest of its share sits idle with a dashed outline; gives up peak utilization. Latency, at bottom: the gang block is cut by two red preemption ticks so short gray jobs can start, leaving the gang in fragments; gives up large gangs, which fragment. The center reads a scheduling policy sets the weights.
context:
Fairness requires an outcome metric rather than an input quota rule alone. For job $\JobIndex$, **slowdown**\index{Slowdown!definition} $\JobSlowdown_j=(\JobQueueWaitTime_j+\IsolatedJobRunTime_j)/\IsolatedJobRunTime_j$ compares its queueing-plus-running time with its isolated runtime $\IsolatedJobRunTime_j$, assuming the running time is unchanged by sharing; a one-hour job that waits nine hours has $\JobSlowdown_j=10$, even if its team eventually receives its nominal GPU share. When contention or resizing changes execution time, the numerator must instead use the observed queueing-plus-running duration while the denominator retains the isolated baseline. A scheduler should report the distribution of slowdown by user and job class, together with the age of the oldest pending feasible job. Dominant-share parity detects unequal resource allocation, slowdown exposes unequal delay, and the maximum feasible wait exposes starvation risk. These metrics separate a policy that is fair in allocated GPU-hours from one that is fair in the time users wait to obtain useful results.

The trade-off diamond in @fig-fleet-orchestration-scheduling-tradeoffs illustrates these operational tensions among throughput, latency, fairness, and cost efficiency. Favoring a large unbroken allocation can delay short experiments, while repeatedly admitting short jobs can prevent a large gang from assembling. These conflicts depend on the workload and available capacity; improving one objective does not necessarily worsen every other objective. Resource-share fairness and completion-delay fairness therefore need separate measurements.

title: The fragmentation problem
caption: **The fragmentation problem**: A snapshot of an 8-node cluster (rows) with 8 GPUs each (columns). Blue blocks mark the slots each active job holds (J1 to J15); dashed white cells are free, and the count at the right of each row gives that node's free slots. Although 19 GPUs, roughly 30 percent of capacity, are free, every node still holds at least one busy slot, so the pending job above the grid, which needs a full node, cannot be placed. Fragmentation, not total capacity, sets what the scheduler can admit.
alt: Eight-by-eight grid of GPU slots, rows labeled node 0 to node 7 and columns labeled slot 0 to 7. Each active job, J1 to J15, is a light blue block spanning its slots; free slots are white with dashed outlines, scattered across every row. A column at the right lists free slots per node, between 1 and 3, totaling 19 free, 30 percent. Above the grid, a queue row holds a red dashed bar spanning all eight columns labeled pending job, 8 GPUs on one node, with the note blocked, no node fits.
context:
Periodic **defragmentation**\index{Defragmentation!definition} migrates or preempts low-priority jobs to consolidate free resources into contiguous blocks, analogous to memory compaction in operating systems. The scheduler identifies nodes where partial allocations leave stranded resources, preempts the jobs occupying those resources, and re-schedules them on nodes where they can be packed more efficiently. The cost includes state transfer and restart, plus replay of work not captured by a valid checkpoint. A graceful checkpoint can preserve recent progress, but still takes time and storage bandwidth. The scheduler must weigh these costs against the benefit of starting large jobs sooner. Low-demand periods reduce the number of competing jobs affected by the move.

A third strategy, **over-subscription**\index{Over-subscription!definition}, admits more demand than a capacity dimension can sustain simultaneously, but only where the resource is divisible and the scheduler can bound interference. Average activity of a GPU's streaming multiprocessors (SMs), its compute units, does not create fractional whole GPUs. A job that reserves device memory, requires an exclusive CUDA context, or belongs to a rigid gang still occupies its assigned device while kernels are idle. Statistical multiplexing can be safe for explicitly shareable CPU, network, storage, or partitioned GPU capacity when tenants have measured, weakly correlated peaks and enforceable limits. It is unsafe to convert 70 percent average GPU utilization into a 1.4$\times$ device overcommit ratio. Whole-device capacity should instead be recovered through preemption, elastic resizing, or an isolation mechanism such as Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) hardware partitioning or NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), which lets several processes' kernels share one device, provided the scheduler models each mechanism's memory, compute, and fault-sharing contract explicitly. Both reappear with the serving workloads they suit best in @sec-fleet-orchestration-resource-isolation.

title: The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)
caption: **The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)**: In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire $\DeviceCount$-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.
alt: Two panels, each with a queue lane above eight GPU rows against a time axis. Left, partial allocation: J1 holds GPU rows 0 to 3 and J2 holds rows 4 to 7, both drawn as red hatched blocks labeled holds 4 of 8 that extend past the right edge with dashed ends; two curved red arrows form a cycle between them labeled waits, and the panel reads 8 GPUs held, none computing. Right, gang scheduling: a blue J1 block spans all eight rows, then a blue J2 block spans all eight rows after it, each labeled all 8 at once; above them, J2 waits in the queue in a dashed violet box labeled holds 0 until an arrow labeled J1 finishes drops it into the GPUs. The panel reads no partial holds, no deadlock.
context:
### Gang scheduling {#sec-fleet-orchestration-gang-scheduling}

Partial allocation of rigid multi-GPU jobs creates a distributed scheduling failure mode in which two jobs each hold half the resources they need and block each other indefinitely while every allocated GPU sits idle. In the left panel of @fig-gang-scheduling-deadlock, jobs J1 and J2 each hold 4 of the 8 GPUs they require, and the whole pool stalls. Atomic gang scheduling\index{Gang Scheduling!atomic allocation} (right panel) instead grants J1 all 8 GPUs as one allocation while J2 waits without holding any, which prevents this allocation deadlock.

title: Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes
caption: **Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes**: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (`slurmctld`) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Kubernetes (right) uses a declarative service model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state in `etcd` against desired state specifications.
alt: Two columns. Left, Slurm, drawn as a straight one-way line: a job script with an sbatch command flows down once to slurmctld, then to slurmd on each node, whose connectors end on one dashed violet outline enclosing four nodes; the note reads all nodes granted at once, or the job waits. Right, Kubernetes, drawn as a closed loop: a desired-state file applied with kubectl flows into the API server and etcd, which holds two slots reading desired 4 pods and observed 3. Three violet arrows then form a cycle labeled reconcile loop: watch, from etcd down to the controllers, which act on the gap; recreate, from the controllers to a group of four pods, of which Pod 3 is drawn red and dashed and labeled failed; and status, from the pods back up into etcd. The note reads observed state is reconciled continuously.
context:
A pending gang and a queue of small backfill jobs need both a policy for sharing capacity and a control plane that can enforce it. The policies just developed apply across platforms; the orchestration paradigm determines how the platform represents allocations and recovers when observed state diverges from them. Slurm, shaped by HPC batch systems, favors explicit resource requests and predictable allocation. Kubernetes, shaped by cloud-native service management, favors declared desired state and continuous reconciliation. The choice is therefore not Slurm vs. Kubernetes as products; it is which control model best matches the workload mix, failure behavior, and operational culture of the fleet.

The control-plane architectures in @fig-fleet-orchestration-slurm-vs-k8s contrast two control models. Slurm follows an imperative batch model: the user states the resources a job needs, and the central slurmctld dispatches that allocation through per-node slurmd daemons. Kubernetes follows a declarative model: the user states what should be running, and controllers reconcile observed state toward that declaration through the API server and node agents. Both platforms accept explicit resource requirements and track execution state, so the useful distinction is which lifecycle the platform manages directly: an allocated batch job or a collection of workloads maintained by controllers. That distinction shapes how ML workloads are admitted, monitored, and recovered from failure, and distributed training still needs framework-level coordination under either model.

title: Physical topology hierarchy and bandwidth cliffs
caption: **Physical topology hierarchy and bandwidth cliffs**: Hardware boundaries dictate communication performance across three distinct domains. The example compares a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` per-direction NVLink endpoint budget with a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` per-direction external port. Under balanced load saturating a `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ratio_hi_str`:1 to `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ratio_lo_str`:1 oversubscribed spine, the external per-endpoint share falls to approximately `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str`. A non-blocking spine need not impose this reduction. The bar in each domain's header draws its bandwidth on one shared linear scale.
alt: Nested boxes. A pod of spine switches contains a rack under one leaf switch, which contains a node of eight GPUs, G0 to G7, each wired to an NVSwitch. Beside the rack's node sit three smaller gray nodes labeled more nodes, and beside the rack sit three gray racks labeled more racks, each holding a column of miniature gray nodes drawn like the sibling nodes. Each domain header carries a solid amber bar of its per-direction bandwidth, all starting at the same position on one linear scale: the node bar for NVLink at 450 GB/s is long, the rack bar at 50 GB/s is short, and the pod bar at about 12.5 to 25 GB/s per endpoint, oversubscribed, is a sliver with a dashed extension.
context:
A 64-GPU job within one rack can avoid cross-rack paths that a spread allocation must use. It outperforms the spread allocation only when those paths add exposed latency or bandwidth contention; a non-blocking, uncongested spine need not reduce sustained throughput. The performance difference stems directly from the hierarchical communication analysis in @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-hierarchical-allreduce-1338: a flat ring AllReduce runs at the speed of the slowest link in the ring, and cross-rack hops introduce both higher latency and increased contention risk. For synchronous training, every iteration waits for the slowest worker to complete its AllReduce, so even occasional cross-rack congestion inflates the Fleet Law's communication term $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ (@eq-fleet-law) on every step it touches.

The scheduler must therefore model the cluster as a hierarchical graph with discrete bandwidth boundaries (@fig-fleet-orchestration-topology-hierarchy). In the illustrated H100 fleet, per-direction bandwidth steps down from `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` across the NVSwitch inside a node to `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` per port under a leaf switch, and to roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str` per endpoint when balanced traffic saturates an oversubscribed spine. A node boundary can introduce a large bandwidth reduction, but a non-blocking rack or pod boundary need not reduce per-endpoint bandwidth. Oversubscription adds a separate constraint when traffic saturates shared uplinks. Topology-aware placement minimizes the communication cost of the job's actual traffic pattern rather than applying a fixed penalty to every boundary.

title: Topology-unaware vs. topology-aware placement
caption: **Topology-unaware vs. topology-aware placement**: An illustrative 4-GPU job that permits inter-node placement and uses an oversubscribed cross-rack fabric, placed across two racks (left, topology-unaware) must traverse leaf-spine-leaf hops: 3 switch hops per AllReduce message at about `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_gb_per_s_str` effective bandwidth. The same 4-GPU job packed within one rack (right, topology-aware) uses a single leaf switch: 1 hop at about `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`, roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.rack_vs_spine_mult_str` faster. Blue squares are the job's GPUs; gray squares are GPUs held by other jobs.
alt: Two panels, each with a spine switch above two racks of four GPUs under a leaf switch; line width encodes per-GPU bandwidth, and GPUs held by other jobs are filled gray. Left, topology-unaware: GPUs G0 and G1 sit in Rack A and G2 and G3 in Rack B. A thin amber path runs from Rack A's leaf switch up through the spine switch and down to Rack B's leaf switch, inside pale shared-uplink channels that also carry gray flows from other jobs; the three traversed switches are tinted amber and numbered 1, 2, 3, labeled 3 hops at about 12.5 GB/s per GPU. Right, topology-aware: all four job GPUs sit in Rack A, joined to one green leaf switch numbered 1 by thick green links; the spine switch is gray and not crossed, and the label reads 1 hop at about 50 GB/s per GPU.
context:
:::

For a 4-GPU collective group, the routing paths make that cost concrete (@fig-topology-placement-paths). In the illustrated contended fabric, scattering ranks across Rack A and Rack B forces a 3-hop leaf-spine-leaf path with about `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_gb_per_s_str` of effective bandwidth per endpoint, a share of contended uplinks rather than a physical link rate. Consolidating all four ranks (G0–G3) under Rack A's leaf switch avoids those shared uplinks and provides about `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` per GPU under the example's load assumptions.

title: Topology placement impact
caption: **Topology placement impact**: Assumed AllReduce latency across four placement strategies (Random, Rack-Aware, Rail-Optimized, and Topology-Optimal) for a 0.5 GB gradient sync on 64 GPUs. The assumed latency falls from 120 ms to 25 ms, a 4.8$\times$ ratio. Labels report payload divided by completion time (algorithm throughput), not physical link bandwidth. The dashed ghost above each bar names the source of delay that strategy removes.
alt: Bar chart of AllReduce latency for four placement strategies: random at 120 ms, rack-aware at 85 ms, and rail-optimized at 40 ms in gray, and topology-optimal at 25 ms in light green. Each bar carries its latency and algorithm throughput inside its top. Above each bar after the first, a dashed hatched ghost reaches up to the previous bar's height and names the delay that strategy removes: spine hops, cross-rail hops, and contended leaf ports, joined by dotted steps into a staircase. A dashed line carries the 120 ms level across the chart, and a green double arrow between it and the top of the topology-optimal bar is labeled 4.8 times lower.
context:
```

Applied to a whole job, the same reasoning ranks placement strategies. The latencies in this comparison are illustrative, not derived. They are constructed to stay above the ring-AllReduce bandwidth bound for the payload, and they show the order in which placement removes delay rather than values a reader could recompute from topology names. For a 0.5 GB gradient synchronization on `{python} TopologyPlacement.n_gpus_str` GPUs, random placement spans multiple racks and spine switches and takes an assumed `{python} TopologyPlacement.random_placement_latency_ms_str`. Each successive strategy removes a source of delay that the previous one leaves. Confining the group to a single rack removes spine hops and reduces latency to `{python} TopologyPlacement.rack_aware_latency_ms_str`. Rail-optimized alignment maps ranks so that every member of each collective group sits at the same local GPU index and therefore on the same network rail (developed in @sec-fleet-orchestration-rail-optimized). Traffic that previously hopped between rails through the spine now stays within one rail's switches, which cuts latency to `{python} TopologyPlacement.rail_optimized_latency_ms_str`. Topology-optimal placement additionally avoids leaf ports that other jobs are using and reaches `{python} TopologyPlacement.optimal_latency_ms_str`, a `{python} TopologyPlacement.speedup_mult_str` reduction (@fig-topology-placement, where each bar also carries its algorithm throughput). This ratio compares whole collectives under four assumed placements, so it need not match the link-bandwidth ratio of the two-rack paths above.

title: Hierarchical placement for 3D parallelism
caption: **Hierarchical placement for 3D parallelism**: This placement example maps distributed training dimensions to physical interconnect layers. Tensor parallelism (TP), which exchanges activations at every layer, stays inside a node on NVLink (`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str`); pipeline parallelism (PP) maps across adjacent nodes under one leaf switch (`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`); and data parallelism (DP), which exchanges gradients only once per step, spans racks through the oversubscribed spine. Bandwidths are per direction, as in @fig-fleet-orchestration-topology-hierarchy.
alt: Physical layout of one 3D-parallel job. Two racks, Rack 1 replica 1 and Rack N replica N, separated by an ellipsis, each contain a leaf switch above three nodes labeled stage 0, stage 1, and stage 2. Each node is a blue box of eight GPUs in two rows of four with a thick amber NVSwitch bar between them, and small amber arrows near the bottom of the nodes, below the NVSwitch bars, hand off from stage 0 to stage 1 to stage 2. Above the racks, an amber spine switch labeled oversubscribed joins the two leaf switches by an undirected dashed amber path labeled DP gradients once per step, about 12.5 to 25 GB/s. A bracket under one node of Rack 1 reads TP every layer, NVLink 450 GB/s, and a bracket under the three nodes of Rack N reads PP stage boundaries, leaf 50 GB/s.
context:
Within a node it is a rank-mapping decision. The launcher or framework must give every member of a data-parallel group the same local GPU index on its node, which is what removes the cross-rail hops in the placement comparison above; a mapping that puts shard $\LocalRankIndex$ at index $\LocalRankIndex$ on one node and at another index elsewhere sends that group's traffic between rails. Across nodes it constrains the scheduler only when allocations are smaller than a node. When each replica's pipeline stage occupies a complete node and every node wires local GPU $\LocalRankIndex$ to rail $\LocalRankIndex$, any free node already offers every rail, so rail alignment does not narrow which racks the scheduler can choose. With partial-node allocations, a job can receive different local indices on different nodes, and the scheduler must then choose GPU positions as well as nodes so that each group's members share a rail. Those positions can conflict with the tensor-parallel budget and the paths between pipeline stages when only particular GPU positions remain free, so the packing cost follows the allocation granularity and the available topology rather than an inherent conflict among the three parallelism dimensions.

Resolving these conflicts means matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (@fig-fleet-orchestration-hierarchical-placement). Per-layer tensor-parallel activation exchanges stay on intra-node NVLink at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str`, pipeline stage boundaries cross intra-rack leaf switches at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`, and the once-per-step data-parallel gradient synchronization spans the oversubscribed spine at roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str`. Even a single-node allocation can have meaningful topology constraints when GPUs occupy different interconnect, PCIe, or non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains. Packing efficiency should therefore be optimized only among placements that satisfy the job's local and external communication contract.

title: Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine
caption: **Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine**: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.
alt: State machine with a central active training state that has a step completion self-loop. Solid arrows lead from it to scale up on idle GPUs, to scale down on preemption, and to replace worker on host timeout or ECC error. Dashed arrows return to active training labeled group rebuilt, ranks released, and spare joined. A red dashed arrow labeled spot reclaim deadline runs from scale down to replace worker.
context:
### The scheduler-framework contract {#sec-fleet-orchestration-elastic-contract}

Elastic scheduling requires a well-defined contract between the scheduler and the training framework. For planned resizing, the scheduler and framework coordinate resource release through defined signals and an agreed adaptation window. Unexpected failures can bypass that window, so the framework must also recover from valid saved state. Its recovery path reconstructs communication groups and either preserves the global batch or applies a validated batch-size and learning-rate policy. The worker-membership lifecycle therefore behaves as a state machine centered on active training (@fig-fleet-orchestration-elastic-state-machine). Idle GPUs trigger scale-up, preemptions trigger scale-down, and host timeouts or ECC errors divert ranks to worker replacement; each path returns to active training once the communication group is rebuilt or a spare node joins.

title: Modeled scaling efficiency and elastic operating range
caption: **Modeled scaling efficiency and elastic operating range**: (a) Scaling efficiency ($\ScalingEfficiency$) of the 175B reference job from 64 to 4,096 GPUs, computed with `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.tp_str`-way tensor parallelism within each DGX H100 node, `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.pp_str` pipeline stages, HDR InfiniBand, and a fixed global batch of `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.batch_seqs_str` sequences. The shaded window is an assumed admission policy; efficiency alone establishes neither its minimum nor its maximum. (b) Share of each step lost to tensor-parallel communication, pipeline bubble, and exposed gradient synchronization. Lower efficiency does not imply that adding workers reduces throughput.
alt: Two stacked panels sharing a GPU-count axis. Top, a line of modeled scaling efficiency against GPU count on a log scale from 64 to 4,096 GPUs, declining gently and then more steeply, with a shaded policy window from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Bottom, stacked bars of the share of step time lost at each GPU count, labeled directly beside the 4,096-GPU bar from bottom to top as tensor-parallel communication, pipeline bubble, and exposed gradient synchronization; the tensor-parallel share stays nearly flat while the pipeline bubble grows fastest.
context: its scaling efficiency falls from `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.eff_min_str` at `{python} ElasticNodeRange.min_gpus_str` GPUs to `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.eff_max_str` at `{python} ElasticNodeRange.max_gpus_str` GPUs and `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.eff_top_str` at `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.top_gpus_str` (@fig-fleet-orchestration-scaling-efficiency-curve, panel a). Efficiency falls, yet quadrupling from `{python} ElasticNodeRange.max_gpus_str` to `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.top_gpus_str` still raises throughput `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.thr_gain_mult_str`, so a lower efficiency is a declining marginal return rather than a slowdown. Panel (b) locates the loss. Tensor-parallel communication shrinks along with each worker's computation, so its share of the step never rises above `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.tp_share_str`. The decline comes instead from pipeline fill and drain and unhidden gradient synchronization, which take roughly fixed time per step while each worker's share of the batch shrinks. The pipeline bubble grows fastest of the three, for a reason the bubble fraction $(\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)$ of @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-pipeline-parallelism-8748 makes explicit. With the global batch fixed, each added replica takes a share of the sequences, so the microbatch count $\MicrobatchCount$ per replica falls while the stage count stays at `{python} ElasticScalingCurve.pp_str`, and the idle fraction rises. The shaded window from `{python} ElasticNodeRange.min_gpus_str` to `{python} ElasticNodeRange.max_gpus_str` GPUs is therefore a policy choice, not an interval derived from these efficiencies alone. A minimum allocation could follow from a completion deadline or the job's declared resource contract. It does not follow from insufficient per-worker computation at smaller scale, since with fixed global work fewer workers generally perform more work each. The upper limit likewise requires comparing additional useful progress with resize cost and the value of serving queued jobs. A real scheduler must obtain those inputs from profiling and the workload's quality target.

title: Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization
caption: **Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization**: This constructed portfolio combines reserved physical capacity, on-demand acquisitions, and interruptible workers. Reserved capacity covers the steady 60 percent base, on-demand the next 20 percent, and spot the peak; these shares and the demand curve are scenario assumptions. A discount commitment alone does not reserve capacity, and on-demand admission is not instantaneous. Schedulers map steady-state baseline demand to reserved capacity, diurnal spikes to on-demand instances, and restart-tolerant training to discounted spot pools. Hatching marks reserved capacity that is held while demand sits below it.
alt: Chart of share of peak capacity over one day with three horizontal tiers separated by dashed lines: reserved from 0 to 60 percent, steady base load; on-demand from 60 to 80 percent, bursts that can wait; and spot from 80 to 100 percent, restart-tolerant work. A constructed demand curve starts near 40 percent, peaks near 92 percent inside the spot tier, and settles near 50 percent. The area under the curve is filled with the color of the tier that serves it: blue below 60 percent, yellow between 60 and 80, and green above 80. Inside the reserved tier, the area above the curve is hatched and labeled reserved, idle, while the on-demand and spot tiers stay white wherever demand does not reach them.
context:
: **Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers**: Capacity tiers trade cost and commitment against availability guarantees and interruption risk, giving the scheduler a price ladder for routing workloads by urgency and restart tolerance. {#tbl-cloud-capacity-reservation-tiers tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

The constructed portfolio in @fig-fleet-orchestration-capacity-reservation divides capacity into a reserved tier covering the steady 60 percent baseline, an on-demand band between 60 and 80 percent, and an interruptible spot tier serving peaks up to 92 percent. An organization with 60 percent steady-state utilization and 40 percent burst demand might reserve capacity for 60 percent of peak need, use on-demand for bursts whose deadlines tolerate admission and startup delay, and use spot for restart-tolerant work. These shares illustrate a policy rather than establish an optimal portfolio. The scheduler must match each workload's deadline and recovery contract to the capacity tier: reserved capacity can support the steady serving load or a training job's base allocation, while spot can support elastic replicas or independent experiments that tolerate reclamation. A peak in urgent demand cannot automatically be assigned to spot merely because it lies above the reserved band.
