Freezing weights removes their gradients and optimizer state from $\TrainableStateMemory$, but it does not make the frozen base or every backward dependency disappear.

```
title: The edge inference landscape
caption: **The edge inference landscape**: Published inference latency and energy measurements from MLPerf Tiny and official benchmarks reveal three distinct hardware tiers separated by approximately 100$\times$ in energy per inference; because the tiers run different workloads (keyword spotting and small-image tasks versus ResNet-50), the gap mixes hardware efficiency with workload size. Dedicated neural processors (Syntiant, STM32N6) achieve keyword spotting in under 5 ms at 30--160 microjoules, while edge GPUs (Jetson Orin) deliver sub-millisecond latency at 15 mJ.
alt: Log-log scatter plot of inference latency in milliseconds against energy per inference in microjoules. A light gray band labeled MCU/ASIC tier holds Syntiant Core 2 and STM32N6 NPU points from tens to a few hundred microjoules; a slightly darker gray band labeled edge accelerator tier holds Google Coral Edge TPU at a few thousand microjoules; the darkest gray band, labeled edge GPU tier, holds Jetson AGX Orin running ResNet-50 near 15000 microjoules at under one millisecond. A double-headed arrow at the left spanning the bands is labeled about 100 times energy gap.
context:
[^fn-neuralengine-hardware-evolution]: **Apple Neural Engine**\index{Apple Neural Engine!definition}\index{Neural Engine!on-device training}: Apple's dedicated neural accelerator, first shipped in the A11 Bionic in 2017; its rating growth through the A17 Pro is tracked in @fig-edge-npu-tops. Which of an update's operators actually reach it, rather than falling back to the CPU or GPU, is the runtime question worked through in @sec-edge-intelligence-mobile-ai-accelerator-optimization-67fe.

Published benchmark results from MLPerf Tiny and vendor data illustrate the range of edge inference costs in @fig-edge-inference-landscape. The plotted tiers span roughly 100$\times$ in energy per inference. Dedicated neural processors such as the Syntiant Core 2 and STM32N6 NPU occupy the sub-millijoule MCU and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) band (30 to 444 $\Glyph{\mu}$J per inference across keyword spotting, visual wake words, and small-image classification, with keyword spotting finishing in under 5 ms), Google Coral appears near 4.8 mJ, and the Jetson AGX Orin appears near 15 mJ for ResNet-50. The roughly 100$\times$ gap mixes different workloads with different hardware, so it is not a matched-task efficiency comparison. Energy per inference does not determine battery lifetime on its own, because inference frequency, sleep power, sensing, radio use, and usable battery capacity also enter that budget. For a learning device the figure sets the scale against which an update must be judged. One evaluation costs microjoules to millijoules, while each second of training inside the `{python} EdgeMobilePowerEnvelope.sustained_range_str` sustained envelope spends joules, more than a thousand keyword-spotting evaluations at the plotted 30 to 160 $\Glyph{\mu}$J. An update can therefore be a substantial energy cost, but its share of the device budget depends on how often training and inference run. Both paths need measurement over the same operating period.

title: TinyTL adaptation paths
caption: **TinyTL adaptation paths**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every weight and retains the state needed for their gradients. (B) TinyTL freezes the backbone weights (gray) and trains only each block's bias vector ($\BiasVector$), small lite residual modules beside the blocks, and the classifier (blue). The backward pass still traverses every frozen block to reach those biases, so the saving comes from what must stay live for it, not from a shorter backward path; the activation and normalization choices determine that state.
alt: Two panels. Panel A, full fine-tuning: input, three blue trainable blocks, and a blue classifier, with a dashed backward arrow spanning all blocks; to the left of each block a wide hatched input tile and a narrow mask tile mark the state kept or recomputed. Panel B, TinyTL: input, three gray frozen blocks each with a small blue bias chip labeled b and a blue lite residual module to its right, and a blue classifier, with a dashed backward arrow also spanning all blocks; to the left of each block the input tile shrinks to a small square for the downsampled residual input, while the mask tile stays the same. Both classifiers keep the same tile. Legend: frozen weights, trainable, backward pass, state kept or recomputed.
section: Enable gradients for bias parameters only
context:
Tiny Transfer Learning (TinyTL) [@cai2020tinytl] targets the activation term of @eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory as well as trainable state. It builds on the derivative argument above. Frozen linear layers drop their saved inputs, so what remains is the backward state of nonlinearities and normalization. TinyTL combines bias adaptation with activation and normalization choices that reduce that state; optional lite residual modules restore some adaptation capacity at an additional memory cost.

Full fine-tuning (Panel A of @fig-tinytl-architecture) computes gradients for every intermediate layer weight, whereas TinyTL\index{TinyTL!memory optimization} (Panel B) freezes the convolutional backbone (gray blocks) and confines parameter updates to lightweight residual side-paths and bias vectors $\BiasVector$ (blue blocks). The dashed backward-pass arrow spans the full network depth in both architectures. TinyTL's memory reduction therefore stems not from truncating the backward pass but from avoiding the storage of intermediate feature maps needed to compute weight gradients.

title: LoRA architecture
caption: **LoRA architecture**: The input $\LayerInputVector$ passes through the frozen base matrix $\WeightMatrix_0$ and, in parallel, through a trainable low-rank path: down-projection $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ ($\AdapterRank \times \HiddenDimension$) and up-projection $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ ($\HiddenDimension \times \AdapterRank$), which play the roles of $\LowRankRightFactor^T$ and $\LowRankLeftFactor$ in the low-rank update above. Only $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ and $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ carry gradients and optimizer state. For serving, the product $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ can be folded into $\WeightMatrix_0$, removing the separate adapter operations when the merged representation is supported. End-to-end latency still needs measurement.
alt: Matrices drawn to proportion. Input vector x of length d splits into two paths. The upper path passes through a large gray frozen square W0 of size d by d to the vector W0 x. The lower path passes through a short wide blue matrix A of size r by d, a tiny vector of length r, and a tall thin blue matrix B of size d by r to the vector BA x. The two vectors add at a plus node to give output h of length d. To the right, a separate panel labeled for serving shows one d by d matrix W0 plus BA with the adapter folded in. A legend marks gray as frozen, with no gradients or optimizer state, and blue as trainable.
section: │ Scope: chapter-anchor — LoRA section and federated sync prose share base-model footprint.
context:
[^fn-lora-adapter-efficiency]: **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)**\index{LoRA!definition}: @hu2021lora learn rank-$\AdapterRank$ decomposition matrices $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ and $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ instead of updating full weight matrices, reporting a 10,000$\times$ reduction in trainable parameters for their GPT-3 comparison. That reduction does not apply to the full model footprint: a model with `{python} EdgeLoraParameterEfficiency.base_model_params_b_str` parameters has about a `{python} EdgeLoraParameterEfficiency.fp16_weight_footprint_gb_str` FP16 weight footprint before gradients, optimizer state, and activations. Even at rank `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.mid_tier_lora_rank_str`, adapter storage depends on the dimensions and number of adapted matrices, and deployment must still accommodate the frozen base model.

@Fig-adapter-lora-arch traces the parallel dataflow of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA): input $\LayerInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^\HiddenDimension$ passes through a frozen base matrix $\WeightMatrix_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension\times \HiddenDimension}$ and a trainable path with down-projection $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank\times \HiddenDimension}$ and up-projection $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension\times \AdapterRank}$. Their outputs sum to $\HiddenActivation= \WeightMatrix_0 \LayerInputVector+ \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\LayerInputVector$, with the update restricted to rank $\AdapterRank\ll \HiddenDimension$. The base weights need no parameter gradients or optimizer state, although backward computation may still traverse the base path. Folding the product into the base weights ($\WeightMatrix_0 + \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$) removes separate adapter arithmetic for that merged model. Numerical compatibility, any requantization, and the cost of retaining merged copies determine whether this is the appropriate serving representation.

title: Selective on-device fine-tuning
caption: **Selective on-device fine-tuning**: (1) The full network is meta-trained in the cloud on generic data. (2) Each layer or channel group is ranked by its expected adaptation benefit per unit of device cost, and the device's data, compute, and memory budget sets the cut. (3) On the device, only units above the cut are updated on local data while the rest stay frozen. Scores and cut position are schematic.
alt: Three stages. Stage 1, meta-train in the cloud on generic data: layers 1 to 3 and a head, all blue and trainable. An arrow labeled theta leads to stage 2, rank by benefit per unit device cost: a bar chart whose bar heights are benefit per unit cost and whose bar widths are device cost, sorted from head, layer 3, layer 2, to layer 1 along a cumulative device cost axis. A red dashed line labeled device budget, data, compute, memory cuts the axis after the head and layer 3, which are blue; layers 2 and 1 beyond the cut are gray. An arrow labeled mask leads to stage 3, update on device with local data: layers 1 and 2 gray and frozen, layer 3 and head blue and trainable.
context:
This layer-wise profiling yields a candidate ranking from which $\SelectedLayerSet$ can be constructed subject to a memory budget. Gains measured one layer at a time need not add when layers train together, and shared backward dependencies change the combined cost. The selected set therefore needs a joint quality and resource check, with the profiling cost included in the adaptation budget.

@Fig-ondevice-pretraining places that ranking inside a complete selective fine-tuning\index{Fine-Tuning!selective, on-device} pipeline. Stage 1 meta-trains the network in the cloud, which means training its initial weights so that a few later updates on new data adapt it well (the idea behind model-agnostic meta-learning, taken up in @sec-edge-intelligence-federated-personalization-3c73). Stage 2 ranks layers or channel groups by adaptation benefit per unit of device cost and lets the device budget set the cut, and Stage 3 updates only the units above the cut on local data. Freezing the units below the cut removes their gradient and optimizer state, but the backward pass still runs through any frozen layer that lies between the loss and a selected one, so the selected set must be costed under the complete execution schedule.

title: Federated averaging protocol
caption: **Federated averaging protocol**: One FedAvg round in four steps. (1) The coordinator selects a cohort, over-selecting to absorb dropouts, and broadcasts the global model $\ModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}$. (2) Each client runs $\LocalEpochCount$ local epochs on its private data. (3) Clients that finish before the round deadline upload $\ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}$; a straggler that misses the deadline is dropped. (4) The coordinator forms the example-weighted average of @eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation, which becomes the next global model.
alt: A round drawn on a time axis. A coordinator lane at the top holds step 1, select cohort and broadcast theta t, and step 4, aggregate as a sum of n k over n round times theta k at t plus 1. A gray broadcast line feeds five client lanes. Each client lane shows a green local data block whose width reflects its example count, then a blue bar of E local epochs and an amber upload block. Circled step numbers 2 and 3 sit above the first client's epoch bar and upload block. Clients 1 to 4 finish before a red dashed round deadline, and their uploads join an amber line into the aggregate step. Client 5's bar runs past the deadline into a red hatched segment marked with a cross and labeled dropped.
context:
This formula optimizes an *example-weighted* objective, in which a client with ten times as many local examples receives ten times the influence. That choice is appropriate when every example should contribute equally, but it can let prolific users or large institutions dominate the model. A *user-weighted* objective instead assigns each participating client weight $1/\ParticipatingClientCount$, optionally capping or normalizing each client's local contribution before aggregation. Neither choice is universally fair. The system must declare whether its unit of interest is an example, a user, an organization, or a deployment cohort, then evaluate that population rather than inherit $\ClientSampleCount_k/\RoundSampleCount$ as an implementation default.

A deployed round wraps the averaging rule in policy that the equation leaves unstated (@fig-federated-averaging-cycle)\index{FedAvg!coordination cycle}. @Eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation fixes how completed models combine, but not which clients are invited, how long the coordinator waits, or how few completions force a round to be abandoned. Those protocol choices decide which contributions enter the sum. A client that misses the deadline contributes nothing, and its examples are absent from $\RoundSampleCount$ for that round. Over-selection and its population-coverage trade-off are developed in @sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675.

title: Measuring the local-work trade-off
caption: **Measuring the local-work trade-off**: The local-work setting $\LocalEpochCount$ acts through two opposing paths. More local epochs lengthen each round, $\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)$, while reducing how often clients synchronize, which can lower the rounds to target, $\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)$, unless client drift raises it. Only their combination, the measured time to target $\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount)$, ranks candidate settings, and a setting is admissible only if it also fits the client energy and population-coverage budgets.
alt: Three rows on a common wall-clock time axis, for small, moderate, and large E. Each row is a sequence of rounds, each a blue local-epochs segment followed by an amber upload and sync segment. The small-E row has many short rounds with thin blue segments; the moderate-E row has fewer, longer rounds; the large-E row has three long rounds plus one more round added by drift, its local-epochs segment gray hatched and still ending in an amber sync segment. A bracket over the first row is labeled rounds to target R of E, and a bracket under one large-E round is labeled round duration t r of E. Each row ends at a tick labeled T target of E; the moderate row ends first and its tick is green.
context:
##### Communication-computation trade-off {#sec-edge-intelligence-communicationcomputation-tradeoff-6e31}

@Fig-comm-compute-tradeoff lays out the opposing systems paths governed by local work $\LocalEpochCount$ as a timeline of rounds: increasing local epochs lengthens per-round execution duration $\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)$ (the width of each round) while reducing synchronization frequency (the number of rounds in a row), which can lower the required rounds $\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)$ until client drift penalizes convergence. Both paths combine into the cumulative time to target $\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount)$, where each row ends, which remains admissible only if total consumption fits within client energy and fleet-coverage budgets. A setting that requires fewer rounds can still prolong total wall-clock duration. Selecting $\LocalEpochCount$ therefore requires comparing measured times to target against physical admission constraints, rather than relying on ungrounded heuristics.

title: Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning
caption: **Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning**: As network bandwidth decreases from fast to slow, the time-minimizing number of local epochs shifts rightward because additional local computation amortizes more communication. The curves come from an illustrative cost model in relative units, not measurements; its growing local-work term stands in for the longer rounds and added drift that make excessive local work counterproductive.
alt: Log-scale plot of total training time in relative units against local epochs per round, with three violet curves labeled at their right ends: fast network dotted, medium network dashed, slow network solid. Each curve has a marked minimum with a dropline to the horizontal axis, labeled E star equals 10, 20, and 40 for the fast, medium, and slow networks. An arrow in a band beneath the plotting area, under the feet of the droplines, runs from E star equals 10 to E star equals 40 and is labeled slower network, larger E star.
context:
:::

The operating point depends on the deployment. Larger local updates can amortize transfer overhead, but they also change drift, completion time, and which clients finish. The network alone can move the optimum, as a cost model in relative units shows (@fig-fl-communication-computation). Its minimum $\LocalEpochCount^*$ shifts from $\LocalEpochCount=10$ on the fast-network curve to $\LocalEpochCount=40$ on the slow-network curve because amortizing expensive transfers justifies more local work. These curves are not measured convergence results. A deployment must establish whether additional local work actually reduces time to target after drift and client completion are counted, and adaptive epoch policies need the same outcome and coverage checks as fixed settings.

title: Gradient compression techniques
caption: **Gradient compression techniques**: Standard updates transmit full-precision values; quantization maps values to lower-precision buckets, such as FP32 to INT8; and sparsification transmits only the most significant top-$\Glyph{k}$ gradients. The latter two mechanisms reduce bytes transferred but introduce representation error or residual state that the training algorithm must manage.
alt: Three rows, each showing a four-value gradient vector on the left and its upload payload as a horizontal bar on the right. Row A, FP32: values plus 0.50, minus 0.20, plus 0.01, plus 0.80, each 32 bits, giving a 128-bit bar. Row B, INT8 with scale s about 0.0063: values plus 79, minus 32, plus 2, plus 127, each 8 bits, giving a bar one quarter as long plus a small hatched scale segment. Row C, top-k with k equal to 2: values at index 0 and 3 are kept, the two dropped values are dashed and flow down into a residual e box kept on the device, and the bar holds two values plus a hatched index segment.
context:
:::

The local-work schedule and update encoding jointly determine communication cost. @Fig-gradient-compression compares uncompressed 32-bit values (Panel A) with uniform 8-bit quantization (Panel B), which gives a $4\times$ reduction in value bytes before scales and other metadata are counted. Top-$k$ sparsification with retained error feedback (Panel C) must encode coordinate identities as well as selected values. Error feedback retains one residual value per update coordinate between transmissions. Its storage depends on the update size and residual precision and must fit the device allowance alongside training and replay state. The receiving path must reconstruct or aggregate these encodings consistently, with separate compatibility requirements when secure aggregation hides individual updates.

title: Federated personalization architectures
caption: **Federated personalization architectures**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every layer; (B) head-only adaptation freezes the feature extractor and trains only the task head; (C) adapter-based learning, such as LoRA, inserts small trainable modules beside a frozen backbone. The dashed arrow marks how far the backward pass must reach. Adapters shrink trainable state, but because they sit at every depth their gradients still traverse the backbone, so the required backward state must be retained or recomputed. In this comparison, head-only adaptation truncates the backward pass at the feature extractor.
alt: Three columns of four layer boxes above a task head. Column A: all layers and the head are blue and trainable, with a dashed backward arrow spanning the whole column. Column B: layers are gray and frozen, the head is blue, and a short dashed arrow spans only the head. Column C: layers are gray and frozen with a small blue adapter box beside each, the head is blue, and the dashed arrow spans the whole column. To the left of each column, hatched tiles mark where backward state is kept or recomputed: beside every layer and the head in columns A and C, beside the head only in column B. A legend marks gray as frozen, blue as trainable, the dashed arrow as backward pass extent, and the hatched tile as state kept or recomputed.
context:
: **Personalization Trade-Offs**: Federated learning strategies balance personalization with compute, information exposure, and adaptation latency. Data locality narrows exposure but does not by itself provide a privacy guarantee. {#tbl-personalization-strategies}

Selecting an on-device personalization strategy requires balancing adaptation capacity against memory residency. @Fig-personalization-arch contrasts the structural footprint of three fine-tuning paradigms: full fine-tuning of every backbone layer (Column A), head-only adaptation that freezes feature extractors (Column B), and parameter-efficient adapters inserted alongside frozen backbone blocks (Column C).

title: Secure aggregation protocol
caption: **Secure aggregation protocol**: A simplified two-client view of pairwise masking. Clients A and B agree on a shared random mask $\PairwiseMaskSecret$; A uploads $\FirstClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \PairwiseMaskSecret$ and B uploads $\SecondClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters - \PairwiseMaskSecret$, so each upload alone looks random to the server. Summing them cancels the mask and yields exactly $\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters$. The server learns only the aggregate, which can still leak information unless differential privacy bounds it.
alt: Each update is drawn as a row of six shaded cells. Client A's update delta theta A, a smooth pattern of blue cells, passes through a plus s node to produce y A, an irregular pattern of amber cells labeled looks random; client B's update delta theta B passes through a minus s node to produce y B, also labeled looks random, whose cells are lightest where the mask is darkest and y A's cells are darkest. Between the clients, a row of irregular gray cells is the shared mask s from key agreement, linked by dashed lines to both mask nodes. Amber uplinks cross a dashed boundary from on device to visible to server. Inside the aggregation server, y A and y B are added like a column sum, giving a row of green cells equal to delta theta A plus delta theta B, with the note masks cancel, s minus s equals 0.

title: Measured AI Performance across Phone Processors
caption: **Measured AI Performance across Phone Processors**: Aggregate AI Benchmark score of mobile systems-on-chip by release year on a logarithmic axis, colored by processor family. The shaded window marks processors from 2020 onward that a client fleet can still contain; the bracket gives the spread of scores within it. Scores measure inference through each processor's software acceleration path, not training speed. Data from @ethz2026aibenchmark, method of @ignatov2019aibenchmark.
alt: Log-scale scatter of AI Benchmark score from about 1 to 23,000 against release years 2010 to 2026, colored by family: Snapdragon, MediaTek Dimensity, Exynos, Google Tensor, Kirin, and others. Scores rise by more than four orders of magnitude over the period. A shaded window from 2020 to 2026 contains scores from about 55 to about 22,600, labeled as roughly 400 times. Google Tensor G4 in 2024 sits far below the Snapdragon and Dimensity flagships of the same years.
context:
```

Measured scores show a spread of the same order among phones alone, without counting microcontrollers. The AI Benchmark from ETH Zurich runs a fixed suite of quantized and floating-point inference workloads on each phone processor through its Android acceleration path [@ignatov2019aibenchmark; @ethz2026aibenchmark]. Among processors released from `{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_first_str` on, which a client fleet can still contain, the scores span about `{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_spread_mult_str`, from the `{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_lo_name_str` (`{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_lo_year_str`) to the `{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_hi_name_str` (`{python} MobileAISpread.fleet_hi_year_str`), and @fig-mobile-ai-spread plots every processor in the ranking. Even flagships of the same generation differ by `{python} MobileAISpread.gen_spread_mult_str`, with the `{python} MobileAISpread.gen_lo_name_str` scoring that far below the `{python} MobileAISpread.gen_hi_name_str`, largely because each score reflects the processor's software path as well as its silicon; the Tensor G4 result runs through Android's generic neural-network interface, while the leaders use their vendors' own runtimes. These are inference scores, not training speeds, but they bound the problem from the side that matters for scheduling. No single local-work quota fits devices that differ by two orders of magnitude in measured throughput.

title: Tiered adaptation strategy
caption: **Tiered adaptation strategy**: The flowchart routes a deployment by the adaptation the local change needs, then by whether a larger update is needed for the quality target and fits the measured device budget, then by whether updates are valuable across devices. Bias-only updates, adapters or LoRA, and partial or full fine-tuning are candidates for increasingly demanding changes on increasingly capable devices, subject to measured resource and quality budgets. The federated card names one common configuration; whether differential privacy is required depends on the deployment's threat model.
alt: Flowchart starting at deploy on-device learning. Diamond one asks whether heavy adaptation is needed: no leads down to the first of three adaptation cards lined up left to right; yes leads to diamond two, compute and energy sufficient, whose no branch leads to the second card and whose yes branch leads to the third. Each card carries a small branch tag at its top, lightweight, moderate, and full from left to right, and is drawn around a large four-layer stack whose blue trainable share grows from left to right: bias-only BitFit on microcontrollers shows gray layers each holding a small blue chip labeled b; adapters or LoRA on mobile NPUs shows gray layers each with a blue adapter beside it; partial or full fine-tuning on wall-powered edge servers and high-end GPUs shows all four layers blue. All three cards join into diamond three, updates valuable across devices: no leads to a local-only adaptation card, shadow validation and drift monitoring, marked by one device with a self-loop arrow; yes leads to a violet federated card, FedAvg plus differential privacy, fleet model synchronization, marked by three devices sending amber arrows up to a global theta box.
context:
: **Edge-Learning Integration Controls**: A tiered edge-learning deployment needs explicit controls for capability matching, graceful degradation, resource conflicts, and validation across device and network combinations. {#tbl-edge-integration-controls}

@Fig-tiered-adaptation condenses the same reasoning into three questions. The first asks how much adaptation the local change needs, so a light change stays on bias-only updates whatever the device. The second asks whether meeting the declared quality target requires a larger update and whether that candidate fits the measured device budget, and the third asks whether the updates are valuable across devices, which decides between local-only learning and federation. The cards distinguish lightweight and moderate adaptation from a larger update candidate; these labels describe adaptation demand rather than the Tier 1--3 device classes, and the device names on each card mark typical homes for a branch. In tier terms, Tier 3 devices sit in the lightweight branch, Tier 1 and Tier 2 phones in the moderate branch, and wall-powered edge servers as possible candidates for the larger-update branch. A no answer at the second decision retains adapters because the larger update is unnecessary or does not fit; if that smaller update also misses the quality target, the policy must be revised before deployment. The voice-assistant policy of this section therefore spans the lightweight and moderate branches, with budget phones held to the lightweight branch by a memory limit that the flowchart does not draw. The deployable choice must still satisfy the measured working-set, runtime, and energy constraints while meeting the local quality target, and federation adds the compatibility and population-validation requirements just established.

title: Edge MLOps lifecycle pipeline
caption: **Edge MLOps lifecycle pipeline**: The lifecycle links cloud pretraining and model compression with over-the-air deployment, on-device adaptation, and telemetry governed by explicit privacy controls. Keeping raw user data local does not by itself make the returned metrics private.
alt: Two regions split by a dashed line, cloud above and device fleet below, with five numbered stages. In the cloud: 1 pretrain, base model; 2 compress, with three package squares of decreasing size per tier; 3 staged rollout over the air. A slate gray arrow descends from the rollout into a grid of device tiles grouped as first wave, wider wave, and not yet updated; updated tiles carry a small blue adapter mark and the not-yet-updated tiles are dashed. A panel labeled 4 adapt locally zooms into one device: a gray frozen base model, a blue adapter, and green local data that stays, under the released policy. A dashed amber line labeled no raw data rises from an updated tile in the wider wave through a privacy controls box to 5 telemetry, aggregate metrics, and a dashed violet retrain trigger returns along the top to stage 1.
context:
Integrating on-device learning into machine learning operations (MLOps\index{MLOps!definition}), the practices that version, deploy, monitor, and roll back production models, expands what a release must validate. Backbones, adapters, update policies, and local histories can change on different schedules across heterogeneous devices. Existing integration tests, version registries, and monitoring remain useful, but the released weights no longer fully describe the behavior that will run later. Operations must validate the permitted adaptation process and its recovery path as well as the initial model.

@Fig-edge-mlops-pipeline traces a five-stage edge learning lifecycle: centralized base-model pretraining (Stage 1), per-tier hardware compression (Stage 2), and staged over-the-air rollouts (Stage 3) originate in the cloud, while local adaptation executes on-device under the released update policy (Stage 4). Aggregate telemetry (Stage 5) supplies evidence for deciding whether cloud retraining is warranted. The telemetry needs its own privacy controls; aggregation alone does not establish a privacy guarantee, and a detected change must be distinguished from a quality regression before triggering a new training cycle.

title: On-device shadow validation
caption: **On-device shadow validation**: A frozen baseline runs beside the active model. Their disagreement, confidence, latency, and resource deltas can flag a change without labels; a rollback decision still requires a validated outcome signal or safety invariant.
alt: Eight live inputs, x1 to x8, form columns. In each column the gray frozen baseline, v1 in shadow, and the blue adapted candidate, v1.1 serving, each emit a class letter. A comparator row marks each column equal or, where the letters differ at x4 and x7, a violet not-equal cell; the comparator is label-free. A dashed line leads to a disagreement rate bar whose filled part passes a red tick labeled tau. A red arrow labeled exceeds tau leads to a gate that holds the candidate out of service. A box labeled validated outcome or safety invariant feeds the gate, which resolves either to a green clear, return to service, or a red regression, roll back.
context:
Shadow model\index{Shadow Model!evaluation} evaluation maintains multiple model variants on each device and compares their behavior. Devices can run a frozen, last-known-good model beside a locally adapted version and measure prediction divergence, confidence shifts, latency, and resource use on the same input stream. Without labels or a validated outcome proxy, these comparisons detect change, not performance degradation: agreement can hide a shared error, and disagreement does not reveal which model is correct. A shadow comparison can therefore suspend an update for further evaluation, but automatic rollback requires labeled outcomes, a validated behavioral invariant, or a proxy whose relationship to task quality has been established for the deployment.

The comparator can therefore act only as a gate, never as a judge (@fig-shadow-validation). The live input stream is mirrored to the frozen baseline and the adapted candidate, and the comparator tracks their disagreement, confidence shift, and resource deltas. When disagreement exceeds a tolerance $\ResponseThreshold$, the gate holds the candidate out of service; validated outcome evidence then either clears it or confirms the regression that justifies rollback.

title: The N-models complexity explosion
caption: **The N-models complexity explosion**: The curves show monitoring alerts growing linearly with model count, deployment coordination growing as $\mathcal{O}(\ProductionModelCount \log \ProductionModelCount)$, and dependency conflicts growing quadratically as models share features and data sources. Under these assumed shapes, the total operational load crosses team capacity around 50 models, sketching the transition from artisanal model management to platform-required operations.
alt: Log-log plot of operational load against models in production. A dotted linear monitoring line, a dashed model-count-log-model-count deployment line, and a dash-dot quadratic dependency line sum to a solid total curve that crosses a red dashed team-capacity line at about 50 models, marked with a red dot. Zones labeled Artisanal, Growing pains, and Platform required divide the axis at 10 and 50 models; the last zone is lightly shaded red.
context:
:::

@Fig-n-models-complexity sketches operational load across production model counts on a logarithmic scale, with one assumed growth shape per source of work. Alerts grow linearly because each model brings its own fixed set of monitored metrics. The sketch assigns deployment coordination an intermediate $\ProductionModelCount \log \ProductionModelCount$ growth shape; this is an illustrative assumption rather than a release-scheduling complexity bound. A dense dependency graph motivates the quadratic conflict curve because $\ProductionModelCount$ models form roughly $\ProductionModelCount^2/2$ possible pairs; the recorded dependencies determine which pairs can actually conflict. Under these shapes the total crosses the team-capacity ceiling near 50 models. The shapes are a sketch, not measurements, so the crossing marks where repeated work outgrows a team rather than a threshold a real organization can read off the plot; measured dependency density, engineering effort, and remediation cost decide when platform engineering pays.

title: The platform benefit-cost threshold
caption: **The platform benefit-cost threshold**: Assumed annual benefit divided by annual cost for two platform budgets. Break-even occurs at a ratio of one. With fixed per-model benefit, the ratio grows linearly; a ratio of five corresponds to a net ROI of 400 percent, not 500 percent.
alt: Line plot of platform benefit-cost ratio against production models from 0 to 150, with a right axis giving the same ratio as net ROI in percent, so a ratio of one reads 0 percent and a ratio of five reads 400 percent. A solid blue line for a 2M dollar per year platform crosses the dashed break-even line at 20 models and reaches 5 at 100 models, annotated 5 times benefit-cost equals 400 percent net ROI. A dashed orange line for a 5M dollar per year enterprise platform crosses break-even at 50 models. The band below ratio one is shaded light red as the investment phase and the area above it pale green as the returns phase.
context:
@Fig-platform-roi-threshold charts this benefit-cost trajectory across production model counts for two annual platform budgets, isolating the break-even crossing where each linear benefit ray climbs out of the shaded investment phase into the net-positive returns phase. With a fixed \$100K benefit per model per year, a \$2M/year platform achieves parity at the 20-model marker, whereas a \$5M/year enterprise platform requires 50 models to reach the break-even line. At 100 models, the \$2M platform ascends to a benefit-cost ratio of 5, equivalent to a net ROI of 400 percent. The linear curves assume constant marginal benefit and fixed platform costs; dependency growth, diminishing savings, or higher operating costs change the result. The \$5M platform's 50-model crossing is also a different quantity from the 50-model crossing in @fig-n-models-complexity. That one marks where repeated work outgrows a team; this one marks where a budget pays back.

The figure's budgets are annual running costs, so its \$2M/year platform differs from the worked example's one-time \$2M build, which charges only a third of that amount to each year of its three-year life. The break-even count is therefore not a universal constant; it moves with the two inputs a platform team controls. Raising savings per model steepens the line and moves the crossing left, raising platform cost flattens it and moves the crossing right, and the benefit-cost ratio stays linear in model count.

title: Dependency-aware model registry
caption: **Dependency-aware model registry**: A version bump on embedding model $\Glyph{E}$ starts a traversal of the registry's recorded downstream edges: retrieval $\Glyph{R}$, rankers $\Glyph{K}_1$ to $\Glyph{K}_3$, and ensemble $\Glyph{M}$ form the impact set (dashed region) that must be re-evaluated before $\Glyph{E}$ v3.2 ships. A model with no recorded edge from $\Glyph{E}$, such as fraud model $\Glyph{F}$, is not flagged, which is why an unrecorded dependency is a silent risk. The rankers also consume features derived from $\Glyph{E}$ directly; only the retrieval path is drawn.
alt: A model registry frame holds every model and its recorded edges, with columns labeled hop 0 to hop 3. At hop 0, embedding model E, drawn in violet with a heavier border and labeled v3.1 to v3.2, sends a violet arrow to retrieval model R at hop 1, which fans out to rankers K1, K2, and K3 at hop 2, which merge into ensemble model M at hop 3. R, the three rankers, and M sit inside a dashed violet region labeled impact set, re-evaluate before release. Below E, a gray fraud model F labeled not flagged is joined to E only by a faint dotted line labeled unrecorded.
context:
#### Dependency tracking {#sec-ml-operations-scale-dependency-tracking-1d7e}

Beyond these core requirements, the distinguishing feature of enterprise registries is explicit dependency tracking. When Model A consumes features computed by Model B, that relationship must be recorded and enforced, because the recorded edges are what bound the work an upstream change creates. A version bump on embedding model $\Glyph{E}$ propagates along those edges to an impact set of candidate retrieval, parallel rankers, and an ensemble, all of which must be re-evaluated before release (@fig-model-registry).

title: E-commerce model ecosystem
caption: **E-commerce model ecosystem**: Data sources feed a user embedding and a product embedding. A shared bus carries both embeddings into both mid-tier models, candidate retrieval and price sensitivity, whose outputs merge in the ranking model before business rules apply inventory and promotion constraints. Because every embedding reaches every downstream model, a change to the user embedding requires coordinated evaluation of all four consumers.
alt: Five-tier dependency graph read top to bottom with tier labels Sources, Embeddings, Mid-tier, Ranking, and Rules. Green user behavior logs and product catalog boxes feed a violet user embedding box and a blue product embedding box. Both embeddings drop onto a violet horizontal line labeled shared bus, which feeds blue candidate retrieval and price sensitivity boxes. Their outputs merge into a blue ranking model box labeled pCTR times pBuy, then into a gray business rules box labeled inventory, promotions. All four downstream boxes sit inside a dashed violet region labeled coordinated evaluation, and every edge from the user embedding onward is violet.
context:
The next layer turns shared representations into candidate sets and business signals. A candidate retrieval model uses the embeddings to find relevant products, and a price sensitivity model\index{Ensemble!price sensitivity model} estimates how strongly a user will respond to price changes. A ranking model\index{Ensemble!ranking model} then scores the candidate products using both embedding features and auxiliary signals, while a business rules model applies promotional and inventory constraints before results reach the user.

The resulting graph has five tiers, and its shape decides what a change costs. User and product representations travel over a shared bus into candidate retrieval and price sensitivity, which converge in ranking before business rules apply (@fig-ecommerce-graph).

title: Feature store architecture
caption: **Feature store architecture**: A dual-store architecture resolves the conflict between training (high-throughput batch scans) and serving (low-latency point lookups). One set of feature definitions drives materialization from batch and streaming sources into an offline store, which keeps full history for point-in-time training joins (the throughput path, top), and an online store, which keeps the latest value per entity for serving lookups (the latency path, bottom). Shared definitions support compatible feature meanings; materialization and historical-availability checks must verify that contract.
alt: A violet feature definitions box sends a dashed arrow into a tall green materialization box listing batch, streaming, and on-demand, which batch data and event streams feed from the left. Materialization writes to two green stores. The offline store is drawn as a grid of cells, rows by entity and columns by time, labeled full history with a time arrow; a bracket over all its rows sends an arrow labeled scan to a blue training box labeled point-in-time joins, under the heading throughput path. The online store is drawn as three key cells, each with one latest-value cell; one value cell is outlined and sends an arrow labeled lookup to a blue serving box labeled point lookups, under the heading latency path.
context:
### Feature store architecture {#sec-ml-operations-scale-feature-store-architecture-51da}

The **dual-store architecture**\index{Dual-Store Architecture!definition} resolves the tension between high-throughput batch training scans and low-latency serving lookups by splitting storage while the platform enforces compatible definitions and temporal semantics across both paths. One materialization engine, governed by versioned feature definitions, writes ingested batch and stream data into an offline analytical store for historical joins and an online key-value store for point lookups (@fig-feature-store-architecture).

title: Point-in-time correctness
caption: **Point-in-time correctness**: A training example at noon should see only the clicks already logged by noon (solid green, 4), not the clicks that arrive later (dashed gray). A naive join that reads the midnight batch value of `total_clicks_today` counts all 10 and leaks six future events into the example. A point-in-time join pairs each training event with feature values as they existed *at the event timestamp*, so the example contains only information that would have been available at inference time.
alt: Timeline from 00:00 to 24:00 with a dashed vertical line at 12:00 labeled training example at 12:00 and a dotted line at 24:00 labeled batch job. Four solid green click markers fall before noon and six dashed gray markers after it. A green bracket spans the four early clicks, labeled 4 clicks, with an arrow to a green box reading point-in-time join, total_clicks_today equals 4. A red dashed bracket spans all ten clicks, labeled 10 clicks by midnight, with an arrow to a red box reading naive join, midnight value, total_clicks_today equals 10.
context:
Training data must reconstruct features strictly as they existed at the timestamp of each historical event. @Fig-time-travel sequences this temporal boundary along a 24-hour execution trace: an example generated at 12:00 must observe only the four clicks logged prior to the noon cutoff, whereas an unaligned midnight batch job counts all ten daily clicks and contaminates the training example with six future events. Using unaligned feature values as inputs for historical training examples creates data leakage[^fn-data-leakage-pitfall] that inflates offline metrics but fails in production.

[^fn-data-leakage-pitfall]: **Data Leakage**\index{Data Leakage!feature store risk}: Future information can inflate offline metrics when a model learns signals unavailable at prediction time. Shared feature infrastructure should enforce historical availability boundaries, but model and data owners must still specify the prediction moment and verify how features were computed. A timestamped join cannot remove future information already embedded inside an incorrectly constructed feature.

title: ML CI/CD pipeline
caption: **ML CI/CD pipeline**: Read the top row left to right and the bottom row right to left. Continuous integration checks each commit; continuous training validates data, trains, and evaluates against a metrics gate that either blocks the candidate and raises an alert or registers it. Continuous deployment then moves the registered version through staging, a canary slice of traffic, and full production. Monitoring closes the loop: detected drift returns to data validation and investigation before a decision to retrain.
alt: Two rows of stage boxes. Top row, left to right, under brackets labeled continuous integration and continuous training: commit, unit tests, data validation, training, and evaluate with candidate metrics. Evaluate feeds a large, heavily outlined diamond labeled metrics gate, the decision point of the pipeline; a red arrow labeled fail leads left to a red box reading block, alert, and a green arrow labeled pass leads down to a green registry box. Bottom row, right to left, under a bracket labeled continuous deployment: registry, staging, canary at 5 percent of traffic with a bar filled 5 percent, and production at 100 percent of traffic with a full bar, ending at a violet monitoring box. A dashed violet arrow labeled drift prompts validation runs from monitoring back up to data validation.
context:
#### Pipeline stages {#sec-ml-operations-scale-pipeline-stages-06f5}

@Fig-ml-cicd stages the delivery lifecycle across continuous integration, training, and deployment, with an evaluation gate that blocks or registers a candidate. Monitoring returns drift signals to data validation. A confirmed population change may justify retraining, while a corrupted feature pipeline requires repair before it supplies another training run. The sequence matters because each stage establishes evidence for the next rather than treating every alert as permission to train and deploy.

title: Shadow and canary deployment
caption: **Shadow and canary deployment**: In shadow deployment (A), the proxy mirrors all production traffic to the candidate; users receive only the production response, and both outputs are compared offline. No user sees the candidate's output, but mirroring every request doubles inference load, so the shadow path needs its own capacity and must be isolated so it cannot slow production. In canary deployment (B), the splitter sends a small weighted slice of live traffic to the candidate (here the 5 percent stage) and widens it through the 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent stages as evidence accumulates, rolling back if SLO or error metrics drift.
alt: Two panels. Panel A, shadow deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic proxy. One lane carries a row of 20 solid request ticks labeled every request to the production model, whose output becomes the user response; a second dashed lane carries 20 hollow ticks labeled every request, copied, to a dashed candidate shadow model, labeled 2 times inference load, whose output is logged but not returned. Both outputs feed a violet offline diff box comparing outputs and latency. Panel B, canary deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic splitter. The production lane, labeled 95 percent, carries 19 of the 20 request ticks with one empty slot, and the candidate canary lane, labeled 5 percent, carries the single tick from that slot. Beside it, five bars drawn to scale show canary shares of 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent with the 5 percent bar highlighted, above a red dashed box reading roll back if SLO or error metrics drift.
context:
#### Shadow deployment and traffic replay {#sec-ml-operations-scale-shadow-deployment-traffic-replay-ee4f}

Shadow deployment\index{Shadow deployment!traffic mirroring}\index{Deployment!shadow mode} runs the new model alongside production, receiving copied inputs and logging outputs without returning them to users. @Fig-shadow-deployment contrasts mirroring to an isolated candidate (Panel A) with canary deployment (Panel B), which exposes a controlled share of traffic to candidate responses. Shadow execution can reveal defects absent from offline tests, but its resource consumption and external side effects still require containment. It also cannot reveal how users would react to outputs they never receive.

title: Interleaving vs. A/B testing
caption: **Interleaving vs. A/B testing**: (A) A/B testing splits users into cohorts, and each cohort sees only one ranker's list, so the comparison is between cohort means and must overcome the variation between users. (B) Interleaving has both rankers rank the same query for each user and merges the results into one list (here by team draft); each click is credited to the ranker that contributed the item, so every user supplies a paired, within-user comparison. That pairing can make ranker-preference screening more sample-efficient; it does not measure the full deployment outcome assessed by an A/B test [@netflix2017interleaving].
alt: Two panels. Panel A, A/B testing: a row of eight user circles, four blue labeled cohort 1 at 50 percent and four gray labeled cohort 2 at 50 percent. Cohort 1 sees a list of blue items A1 to A3 labeled ranker A only, cohort 2 sees gray items B1 to B3 labeled ranker B only, and each list leads to its own mean box; a bracket joins the two means above the label compare the two cohorts' means. Panel B, interleaving: a box reading each user, one query feeds ranker A's blue list A1 to A3 and ranker B's gray list B1 to B3, which merge into one middle list labeled merged list alternating A1, B1, A2, B2, with a thin connector from each source item to its merged slot. A click dot on the edge of merged A2 routes to a credit A box and a click dot on the edge of merged B2 routes to a credit B box; a bracket joins them above the label credit each click to its source ranker.
context:
The advantage of interleaving is statistical efficiency. An interleaving experiment can require far fewer samples than A/B testing, and Netflix reports more than 100$\times$ fewer users for some ranking experiments [@netflix2017interleaving], because each user provides direct comparison signals rather than contributing only to aggregate statistics.

In an interleaving workflow, the variants produce ranked lists that a method such as team draft or probabilistic interleaving combines into one presentation. The mixing and credit-assignment rules must control position effects and identify which ranker contributed each item. Engagement with those items supplies a relative preference signal. @Fig-interleaving-vs-ab contrasts the between-cohort comparison of A/B testing (Panel A) with this within-user comparison (Panel B). The latter can screen candidates efficiently, but preference within a blended list does not directly measure the effect of deploying either complete ranking policy on long-term outcomes such as retention. Those outcomes still require an experiment designed to measure them.

title: Hierarchical monitoring architecture
caption: **Hierarchical monitoring architecture**: To prevent alert fatigue, monitoring operates at four levels, each with its own owner. Business and portfolio metrics raise the few alarms that indicate broad impairment and route each incident to the owning model family, while model and infrastructure metrics serve primarily for diagnosis and root-cause analysis.
alt: Four-tier violet pyramid with a left axis labeled impairment scope, component to fleet. From top: business metrics (revenue, conversion, engagement), portfolio metrics (engagement lift, fraud caught, appeal rate), model metrics (task quality, latency, drift, saturation), and infrastructure metrics (accelerator utilization, feature store latency, serving health, network, storage, pipelines). A signals column beside each tier shows one red page dot for business, two red page dots for portfolio, one red dot and eight hollow gray diagnostic-record dots for model, and one red dot and nineteen gray dots for infrastructure. An owner column lists incident lead, domain teams, model owners, and platform team. A key reads page and diagnostic record.
context:
### Hierarchical monitoring architecture {#sec-ml-operations-scale-hierarchical-monitoring-architecture-407d}

The alert fatigue problem motivates coordinated triage. To stem the flood of uncoordinated alarms, @fig-monitoring-pyramid structures telemetry into a four-tier triage pyramid, mapping operational scope from component health at the base up to fleet-wide business impact at the apex. Broad signals reveal fleet impairment, portfolio signals route incidents to the owning model family, and granular model or infrastructure telemetry supports local diagnosis. Routine fluctuations remain diagnostic records, while urgent local failures still page their owners without waiting for a fleet-wide signal. The hierarchy provides context for routing and grouping alerts while preserving those immediate response paths.

title: Build vs. buy TCO
caption: **Build vs. buy TCO**: The curves compare cumulative cost over a `{python} BuildVsBuyFigureScenario.horizon_months_num_str`-month horizon for a high-utilization H100 reference cluster. The gap between the lines is shaded light orange and labeled renting cheaper until a dark dot with a dotted dropline marks where the lines cross, late in the 30-month horizon; after the crossing, the narrow gap is shaded light blue, and a bracket spanning the two end values at month 30 is labeled owning cheaper.

```
title: The TCO iceberg
caption: **The TCO iceberg**: The analysis separates visible infrastructure costs from operational costs that are easier to omit. In this illustrative budget, the hidden operational costs (engineering labor, pipeline maintenance, retraining, monitoring, incident response, and compliance) together constitute half of total cost.
alt: A ten-by-ten grid of square cells, each 1 percent of total cost of ownership, filled row by row from the top. Each category is a rectangular block labeled inside with its name and share, the label sitting on a solid strip of merged cells centered in the block, six cells wide in full-row blocks and three in half-row blocks. All cells are equal squares; blocks are separated by wider white gutters added between cells, and color encodes only visible versus hidden. The top five rows are pale blue: four rows of GPU cloud compute, 40 percent, and one row of object storage, 10 percent, together labeled visible infrastructure, 50 percent of TCO. A dashed waterline separates them from the bottom five rows, all in a darker gray: two rows of engineering labor, 20 percent, one row of data pipeline maintenance, 10 percent, and two rows split in half among retraining, monitoring, incidents, and compliance, 5 percent each, together labeled hidden operational costs, 50 percent of TCO.
context:
Here, $\TrainingCost$ is the initial training and evaluation cost, $\InferenceCost$ is recurring serving cost, $\TotalDataCost$ covers data acquisition, storage, cleaning, and governance, and $\IterationCost$ captures subsequent experimentation and maintenance. The categories require a common accounting horizon and an explicit allocation rule. If retraining compute is charged to $\TrainingCost$, it must be excluded from $\IterationCost$; shared hardware depreciation and energy likewise enter these workload costs once rather than being added again as a separate fleet bill.

Budget projections that count GPU compute and storage can omit substantial operational work. In the illustrative budget of @fig-tco-iceberg, engineering labor (20 percent), pipeline maintenance (10 percent), continuous retraining, monitoring, incident response, and governance together equal the visible infrastructure spend. The example shows what an incomplete budget can miss; its proportions are not universal cost shares. Each organization must measure these obligations within the same accounting horizon as its infrastructure costs.

title: Organizational patterns for ML
caption: **Organizational patterns for ML**: (A) A centralized platform team gives every model team the same infrastructure, but all requests pass through one shared queue, which can become the bottleneck. (B) Embedded teams each build their own tooling, which is fast locally but duplicates infrastructure and lets stacks diverge. (C) A hybrid keeps a core platform and places ML engineers (MLE) inside model teams as liaisons, balancing standardization with responsiveness.
alt: Three panels of the same three blue team boxes. Panel A, centralized: each team sends an arrow up into a red-outlined shared request queue drawn as a row of slots, five filled and one empty, whose single red exit arrow leads into one violet platform team box. Panel B, embedded: a dashed gray outline labeled no shared platform sits where the platform would be; each team box sits under an own tooling label and contains its own stack of violet bars, with bar lengths differing from team to team. Panel C, hybrid: one violet core platform box sends an arrow down into each team box, where it ends at a violet MLE chip inside the team.
context:
### Centralized platform team {#sec-ml-operations-scale-centralized-platform-team-16fc}

A centralized ML platform team\index{Organizational pattern!centralized platform} supports consistency by building and maintaining shared infrastructure while model teams own model development and behavior. @Fig-ml-org-models contrasts three organizational patterns. A shared request queue (Panel A) centralizes prioritization but can become a bottleneck; uniform standards depend on enforced contracts, not the queue itself. Embedded tooling (Panel B) favors local responsiveness while risking duplication. The hybrid pattern (Panel C) places dedicated ML engineers near product teams while retaining a common platform. Self-service interfaces can preserve central standards without routing every routine action through a human queue.

title: ML system attack surface
caption: **ML system attack surface**: Red arrows mark where an adversary enters the system: the training data, the training job and its dependencies, the stored weights, the serving API, and the infrastructure beneath all three layers. Each entry point calls for a different control, so defense spans data collection, training and weights, the serving interface, and the provenance of firmware and hardware.
alt: Pipeline of training data, training job, weights, and serving API in data, model, and interface layer frames, with clients exchanging queries with the API. Training data is a grid of sample tiles with two red poisoned tiles; the training job holds three imported package chips, one red; the weights are a shaded parameter matrix. An infrastructure layer below shows accelerator hosts, network fabric, firmware and drivers, and schedulers and keys. Red arrows enter from above at poisoning and backdoor triggers, tampered packages and frameworks, artifact theft and unsafe loading, and extraction, adversarial inputs, and membership inference, and from below at hardware Trojans, co-tenant leakage, firmware tampering, and side channels.
context:
Learned-information exposure follows from the difference between *transient processing* and *persistent learning*. Many applications process sensitive data without encoding it into learned parameters; machine learning systems can preserve patterns from training data in their model parameters. Sensitive information may then remain in a model after the original processing has ended and become accessible through outputs or systematic interrogation. Queries to a healthcare model may expose memorized patient information, while queries to a proprietary model may reveal enough behavior to train a substitute. The first threatens training-data privacy; the second threatens model confidentiality.

Architectural complexity compounds these challenges. A contemporary ML deployment spans data ingestion pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, model serving systems, and continuous monitoring frameworks, each introducing distinct vulnerabilities as @fig-attack-surface maps across the ML lifecycle. Continuous adaptation at edge nodes and federated coordination protocols add further entry points, each with its own trust assumptions.

title: Stuxnet and the ML supply chain
caption: **Stuxnet and the ML supply chain**: The top row traces the Stuxnet chain from removable media through Windows hosts and Siemens Step7 software to altered PLC logic, which damaged centrifuges while operators saw normal readings. The bottom row places the ML analog under each stage: a compromised public artifact passes through trusted build and training steps into a model whose misbehavior monitoring does not reveal.
alt: Two aligned rows of four stage boxes. Top row, Stuxnet 2010: USB media, Windows hosts, Siemens Step7, PLC logic. Bottom row, ML supply chain: public artifact, build host, training job, model artifact. A red dot inside every stage box marks the hidden payload, and red arrows carry it from box to box. A dashed vertical line between the first and second stages is labeled air gap and trust boundary. Each row ends in a displayed-versus-actual pair: a dashed gray monitor view with a flat line, tapped from the last stage, reads operators see normal or health checks pass, while the red payload arrow enters a red box with a jagged trace reading centrifuges damaged or model misbehaves.
context:
[^fn-air-gapped-isolation]: **Air-Gapped**\index{Air-Gapped!isolation}: Physical network separation does not eliminate transfer paths through removable media or authorized personnel. An isolated ML training cluster still needs a controlled process for admitting frameworks, datasets, and pretrained weights; each transfer must preserve the intended trust boundary.

ML supply chains that ingest public packages, datasets, model weights, or firmware face four analogous vectors: compromised dependencies (malicious packages in PyPI and conda repositories), poisoned datasets on public platforms, backdoored model weights in model repositories, and tampered accelerator firmware. Each can introduce behavior through an artifact the pipeline accepts. Because a model's behavior depends on every contributor to its data, code, weights, and hardware, the model can be trusted only as far as a verifiable record of those contributors extends. That statement is the provenance bound on trust (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}), and it carries the Stuxnet lesson to every artifact an ML pipeline admits. Artifact signatures and immutable provenance logs establish origin and integrity evidence; controlled dependency admission limits which artifacts enter the pipeline. Behavioral testing addresses a different question, because an authentic, unchanged artifact can still contain a backdoor. @Fig-stuxnet maps these parallels between the Stuxnet attack chain and ML supply chain vulnerabilities.

title: Threat prioritization matrix
caption: **Threat prioritization matrix**: Likelihood and impact place each example threat in a quadrant, and the quadrant sets the response. Likely, damaging threats such as federated data poisoning warrant automated defenses; rare but severe threats such as hardware side channels justify preparation in high-value deployments; likely but lower-impact extraction calls for API limits; and membership inference through a public API is monitored and reassessed when the training data is sensitive. Dashed arrows show how deployment assumptions move a threat to another quadrant.
alt: Likelihood and impact plane split into four quadrants, with the high-likelihood, high-impact quadrant shaded red. Each quadrant names a response and holds one example threat as a dot: automate defenses for data poisoning in federated training, prepare where value is high for hardware side channels on cloud-hosted models, limit and shape the API for model extraction via a public API, and monitor and reassess for membership inference via a public API. Two dashed arrows move threats to new positions: side channels shift right toward higher likelihood with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware, and membership inference shifts up toward higher impact with sensitive training data.
context:
[^fn-membership-inference-sec]: **Membership Inference as a Threat**\index{Membership Inference Attack!threat model}\index{Membership Inference Attack!training set membership}: For threat modeling, the relevant variable is what the adversary observes: confidence scores, labels only, or individual client updates [@shokri2017membership]. Attack success depends on the target model, data, outputs, and adversary knowledge. Confirming that an individual's data was in a training set can still create privacy and compliance risk; whether that disclosure violates GDPR, HIPAA, or another rule depends on the data, parties, and deployment context [@gdpr2016; @hhs2003hipaaprivacy].

The framework guides resource allocation, as @fig-threat-matrix summarizes. The example prioritizes accessible model and data threats before more specialized hardware attacks. A deployment with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware may require a different order. The allocation decision depends on the expected harm, the control's effectiveness, and its engineering cost, not on the attack category alone.

title: ML lifecycle threats
caption: **ML lifecycle threats**: Poisoning, backdoor insertion, model theft, and adversarial inputs enter at different lifecycle stages (red arrows), and each stage has its own first control (green gates). Dashed lines show a training-time compromise that passes its gate persisting into every later stage, so a control placed at a different stage cannot intercept the threat before it takes effect.
alt: A left-to-right pipeline of four stage boxes: data collection, training, deployment, inference. Above each stage a red arrow labeled with its threat strikes a green gate box naming that stage's first control: poisoned samples and flipped labels hit data validation and provenance, backdoor insertion hits a secure training environment, model theft by artifact or API hits access control and API design, and adversarial inputs hit input validation. Below the pipeline, two dashed red lines, the first marked if missed, leave the data collection and training boxes, run beneath every later stage, and end under inference at a red bracket labeled compromised model.
context:
@Fig-ml-lifecycle-threats locates these entry points. Upstream, an attacker may inject samples or alter labels in a data source the pipeline accepts. A backdoor can then remain inactive on ordinary evaluation inputs and activate on a chosen trigger. Downstream, deployed files expose an artifact-access boundary, while prediction APIs expose a query boundary. An adversarial input crosses the latter without requiring the attacker to alter the training pipeline.

Controls must act at the relevant entry point and preserve their assumptions through later stages. Data validation limits what enters training, artifact controls authenticate what deployment loads, and serving controls constrain requests and returned information. None establishes behavioral correctness by itself; the threat model determines which attack each control must withstand.

title: Model theft strategies
caption: **Model theft strategies**: Exact artifact theft (left) obtains the model file, checkpoint, registry entry, or device artifact and reconstructs the original model. Approximate behavioral theft (right) uses black-box API queries, output signals, and surrogate training or distillation to clone the model's behavior without direct access to weights.
alt: Two panels. Left, exact artifact theft: a registry, bucket, or device frame holds a shaded weight grid; a red arrow labeled access the file, extract weights leads to a red exact-copy box with an identical grid, captioned same weights, no training cost paid. Right, approximate behavioral theft: a table of recorded x and y pairs sends queries to a dark deployed-API box and receives labels, logits, and scores; a red arrow labeled train surrogate leads to a red behavioral-clone box with a differently shaded grid, captioned different weights, similar outputs.
context:
[^fn-model-serialization-pickle]: **Model Serialization**\index{Model Serialization!security}: Python's pickle format, common in PyTorch checkpoint workflows, can execute arbitrary code during deserialization, so loading an untrusted checkpoint is equivalent to running untrusted code. Formats such as SafeTensors store only tensor data and remove that execution path [@huggingface_safetensors].

@Fig-model-theft-types separates two theft objectives that require different controls. **Exact artifact theft**\index{Exact Artifact Theft!definition} obtains the model file or deployment artifact through storage, registry, or device access. The attacker can reuse the recovered weights without repeating their training. **Approximate behavioral theft**\index{Approximate Behavioral Theft!definition} uses API responses, such as labels, logits, embeddings, or confidence scores, to train a surrogate. It can exploit permitted queries without breaking authentication. The literature names this query-based branch in several ways. *Model extraction* and *model stealing* are synonyms for the attack, while *knockoff modeling* and *model distillation* name its usual training step, in which a surrogate learns from the victim's outputs. Its usual product is a behavioral surrogate, but the same query access can also recover selected internal parameters, a third outcome that the OpenAI results below demonstrate. Encryption, access control, and protected deployment paths restrict artifact access; signatures separately authenticate artifact integrity. Output limits, query budgets, auditing, and pricing constrain behavioral extraction, while watermarking can support attribution after copying.\index{Model Theft!strategies}

title: Data poisoning as bilevel optimization
caption: **Data poisoning as bilevel optimization**: The attacker (outer loop) chooses poisoning data $\PoisoningDataset$ to raise the trained model's loss on a test set, the untargeted form drawn here, or, for a targeted attack, to lower its loss on the attacker's chosen label. The system (inner loop) attempts to minimize its training loss on the combined dataset $\CleanTrainingDataset \cup \PoisoningDataset$. The nested attack objective can require repeated training evaluations or approximations. It does not imply that every poisoning defense must simulate full training.
alt: A red attacker box at top holds the outer objective, maximizing test loss over the poison set subject to a size budget. A red arrow labeled inject leads to a grid of training tiles in which three red poisoned tiles sit among clean tiles, labeled S union S poison. A blue arrow leads to the inner-loop training box with the arg-min training equation and a chain of SGD steps ending at theta star. A theta-star arrow feeds an evaluation box that computes the target test loss, and a red feedback arrow returns the target loss along the right edge to the attacker.
context:
$$ {#eq-targeted-poisoning}

@Fig-data-poisoning-loop connects the nested objectives to the training system. The outer loop is the attacker's proposal step, which optimizes the attack objective, either raising loss on the test set (@eq-untargeted-poisoning) or, for a targeted attack, lowering loss on the chosen label $\ExampleLabel_t$ (@eq-targeted-poisoning). The inner loop is the defender's training process, which minimizes loss on the combined data. The attacker evaluates or approximates this inner effect on training, and uses the resulting target loss to refine the proposal. An attacker without access to the defender's training process must instead rely on a surrogate or other available feedback.

title: Data Poisoning Impact
caption: **Data Poisoning Impact**: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages. In the illustrated successful attack, a poisoned record admitted at ingestion contaminates the training corpus, pulls the optimizer's gradients toward the attacker's trigger, and yields a backdoored model whose clean accuracy can remain intact, so aggregate validation alone can miss it.
alt: Two rows of four panels under the headings ingestion, training corpus, optimization, and trained model, joined by arrows. In the nominal row, three green clean records arrive, the corpus is a grid of green record tiles, a gray step descends into the minimum of a set of loss contours, and a straight decision boundary separates hollow and filled points. In the poisoned row, the middle arriving record is red, one tile of the corpus grid is red, a red step bends away from the contour minimum toward a red trigger diamond while a dashed gray path shows the clean direction, and the same decision boundary now has a small red dashed pocket around a trigger diamond on the filled side, labeled backdoor pocket and clean accuracy intact. The arrows in the poisoned row are red.
context:
Data poisoning attacks differ in their objective and scope [@biggio2012poisoning]. Availability attacks\index{Data Poisoning!availability attack} seek broad degradation of useful performance. Targeted attacks\index{Data Poisoning!targeted attack} seek errors on selected inputs or classes and may leave aggregate accuracy largely unchanged [@shafahi2018poison]. Backdoor attacks\index{Backdoor Attack!trigger patterns}\index{Data Poisoning!backdoor attack}\index{Backdoor Attack!BadNets} associate an attacker-chosen trigger with unwanted behavior; the trigger can be visible, as in a sticker, even when its significance is hidden [@gu2017badnets]. Subpopulation attacks\index{Data Poisoning!subpopulation attack} instead target a group defined by shared features [@jagielski2021subpopulation]. These categories can overlap. Their objectives guide which evaluations are needed beyond aggregate accuracy, including targeted, trigger-specific, and subgroup tests.

The objective classes say what an attacker wants; the attack *mechanism* depends on the attacker's access to the system and knowledge of the data pipeline. Every mechanism shares the shape traced in @fig-poisoning-impact, in which a poisoned record enters the training pipeline alongside clean data and attempts to alter the resulting model's behavior. The most direct mechanism is label modification, where an attacker selects a subset of training samples and alters their labels, flipping $\ExampleLabel= 1$ to $\ExampleLabel= 0$ or reassigning categories in multi-class settings. Even small-scale label corruption can shift decision boundaries.

title: Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation
caption: **Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation**: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during *training* rather than at *inference*.
alt: A violet aggregation server box at the top shows the weighted mean w t plus 1 equals w t plus the sum over k of n k over n times delta w k, and an inset plot of update vectors drawn from the point w t: three amber honest updates point steeply upward in a narrow fan, one red update delta w 2 points nearly sideways, and a thicker violet aggregate arrow sits between them, tilted away from the honest fan. A row of clients sits below: client 1, a red malicious client 2, client 3, an ellipsis, and client N, each holding a row of small green data tiles, with two red tiles in client 2. Each benign client sends an amber update arrow, delta w 1, delta w 3, and delta w N, up to the server, while client 2 sends a red update delta w 2 marked poisoned. Dashed red arrows labeled w t plus 1 run from the server down to each client.
context:
Beyond label modification, the attacker can keep the label intact and corrupt the features instead, the strategy known as **clean-label poisoning**\index{Clean-Label Poisoning!definition}. Because every label is correct, label audits cannot flag these records. Imperceptible image perturbations, subtle shifts in structured fields, and fixed trigger patterns aim for the same outcome.
```
