In each case the training example still appears legitimate, but it bends the learned decision boundary toward a future failure. Generative methods and data-synthesis tools raise the same risk at larger scale because they can create natural-looking examples whose only purpose is to distort what the model learns.

```
Whether those examples become poisoning depends on the data boundary. Web scraping, social media feeds, crowdsourced annotation, and untrusted user submissions all allow poisoned records to enter upstream and pass through weak cleaning checks in a "trusted" form. Physical systems add a second path. A sticker on a road sign is an inference-time adversarial attack when the car sees it, but an image of it harvested into a training corpus becomes a poisoning path only if the contribution serves an attack on the learner; correctly labeled examples of such inputs can instead help train resistance to them. Online learning systems tighten the feedback loop further, allowing an attacker to introduce small increments of malicious data until model behavior drifts without a single obvious anomaly. @Fig-poisoning-attack-example draws the collaborative form of the same boundary, in which one malicious client's update reaches every participant through aggregation. @Sec-security-privacy-gradient-sync-integrity examines the same exposure among the workers of a synchronous data-parallel job.

title: Adversarial arms race
caption: **Adversarial arms race**: Defense evaluation is an iterative engineering cycle of defining the adversary's capabilities, evaluating adaptive attacks against active defenses, revising mechanisms and assumptions, and retesting after system or deployment modifications. The diagram formalizes the review process rather than predicting defense longevity.
alt: Four numbered cards at the corners around a central system, a model box inside a green defense boundary with a gap on its right side. Card 1, specify the adversary, shows white, gray, and black box access and a perturbation budget and goal; a gray arrow leads to card 2, run adaptive attacks, drawn in red, whose red arrow passes through the gap in the defense and strikes the model. A gray arrow labeled results leads to card 3, harden the system, whose green arrow returns to the defense boundary. A gray arrow from the changed system leads to card 4, retest after changes to weights, data, or deployment, where the line earlier evidence is struck through, and a gray arrow returns to card 1.
context:
Adversarial inputs exploit the deployed model's decision behavior under attacker-chosen modifications. Some attacks use small, hard-to-perceive perturbations; others use visible patches or changes allowed by a physical or semantic constraint. The threat model must state those constraints before attack success or defense quality can be measured. This shifts attention from the integrity of upstream training data to the inputs and decisions exposed during inference.

These attacks create real-world risks in domains such as autonomous driving, biometric authentication, and content moderation. Small, visually hard-to-distinguish perturbations can cause image classifiers to make high-confidence errors [@szegedy2013intriguing; @goodfellow2015explaining]. Physical-world work showed that printed adversarial images can survive camera capture and remain misclassified by an ImageNet classifier [@kurakin2018]. Road-sign attacks then showed that small stickers or perturbations can cause signs to be misclassified under realistic viewing conditions [@eykholt2018]. A deployed defense must be evaluated against attacks adapted to its mechanisms. @Fig-adversarial-arms-race shows the resulting review cycle: changing the attacker model or the deployment can invalidate earlier evidence, requiring renewed testing.

title: Adversarial decision boundary
caption: **Adversarial decision boundary**: High-dimensional neural networks often have nonlinear decision boundaries. An adversary seeks to find a minimal perturbation $\Glyph{\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ that pushes a clean data point $\ModelInput$ across the boundary into another class region, subject to an allowed perturbation bound $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. A norm bound alone does not establish perceptual invisibility; physical attacks require separate feasibility constraints.
alt: Two-class input space split by a curved decision boundary, with class A, stop sign, below and class B, speed limit, above. A dashed circle of radius epsilon adv surrounds the clean input x. A red perturbation arrow delta runs from x to a red adversarial point x prime just across the boundary but inside the circle.
context:
Because these attacks succeed against models with high clean accuracy, defenses must act on the attack itself. They divide between runtime controls, such as input validation and anomaly monitoring during inference (@sec-security-privacy-runtime-system-monitoring-a71c), and training-time methods such as adversarial training on deliberately perturbed examples [@madry2018towards]. @Sec-robust-ai-input-attack-detection-defense-19d3 evaluates both against stated threat models.

A small, norm-bounded perturbation can carry a clean input across a curved decision boundary into another class region (@fig-adversarial-boundary), so resilience depends on the geometry of the decision surface rather than on clean validation accuracy alone. The figure and its caption write the perturbation as $\Glyph{\boldsymbol{\delta}}$, which the text writes as $\AdversarialPerturbation$, and bound its size by $\|\AdversarialPerturbation\| \leq \AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. Both symbols belong to the adversarial threat model. The bold $\AdversarialPerturbation$ is a vector in input space, unrelated to the scalar slack $\PrivacyAdditiveSlack$ in the differential privacy guarantee of @sec-security-privacy-differential-privacy-8c2b, and $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ is a radius, not the privacy budget $\PrivacyBudget$.

title: Threat mitigation flow
caption: **Threat mitigation flow**: Threats, assessment evidence, and candidate controls have different roles. Dashed lines link each piece of evidence to every control it can inform, so a signal does not uniquely select a defense, and the listed controls require a stated threat model and validation.
alt: Four threat rows, each with red-dot threat, blue assessment-evidence chips, and green candidate-control chips, with a solid line from each threat to its evidence chips and dashed lines from every evidence chip to every control chip in the row. Model extraction: query telemetry to access and query limits and output restrictions. Data poisoning: provenance audit and targeted evaluations, crossing to intake controls and quarantine and retraining. Adversarial input: adaptive attack tests to adversarial training and input validation. Membership inference: privacy attack audit and privacy accounting to an accounted DP mechanism.
section: Availability abuse and denial of wallet {#sec-security-privacy-availability-denial-wallet}
context:
: **Threat landscape**: Machine learning systems face diverse threats throughout their lifecycle, ranging from data manipulation during training to model theft postdeployment. The table categorizes these threats by lifecycle stage and attack vector, clarifying how vulnerabilities manifest and enabling targeted mitigation strategies. {#tbl-threats-models-summary}

The appropriate defense depends on the attack vector, lifecycle stage, and available evidence. @Fig-threat-mitigation-flow separates assessment evidence from candidate controls. Monitoring can reveal suspicious querying, while watermarking can support attribution after extraction; neither establishes that theft was prevented. Privacy audits measure attack success under tested conditions, whereas an accounted DP mechanism provides a formal bound under its stated assumptions. Each row identifies a design starting point, not a guaranteed detection-to-defense pipeline. The figure's fourth row is membership inference rather than availability abuse. Availability controls were just covered, and membership inference shows most sharply the gap between empirical evidence, such as an audit, and a formal bound from an accounted mechanism.

title: Fault injection attack
caption: **Fault injection attack**: A timed laser pulse that skips the unconditional jump at line 6 forces a positive ReLU activation through the zeroing block at lines 7–10. The fault changes executed control flow without changing the stored model parameters.
alt: Eleven-line ReLU assembly listing with line 6, jmp end, highlighted in red. A dashed arrow from line 6 to line 11 marks the intended jump and is crossed out. Brackets label lines 2 to 3 as positive input with branch not taken, lines 4 to 5 as copying the activation, line 6 as the laser fault skipping the jump, lines 7 to 10 as falling through to zeroing, and line 11 as the intended jump target.
context:
The ML-specific risk is that a small computation fault can become a semantic failure. An embedded classifier running on a microcontroller may misclassify a safety-important input, while a fault in memory or control logic may expose proprietary weights or architecture details. Unlike ordinary random faults, adversarially timed faults are chosen to land on computations the model or security protocol depends on.

The experiments of @breier2018 targeted activation-function implementations on a microcontroller with timed laser faults.\index{Laser Fault Injection} @Fig-injection identifies the vulnerable instruction in the observed ReLU implementation. For a positive accumulator, the copy instructions assign the activation to the output, and the following `jmp end` normally skips the zeroing block. A laser pulse timed to suppress that jump makes execution fall through into the clear instructions, overwriting the positive output with zero and forcing the neuron inactive. The conditional `brge` instruction is not the skipped instruction in this example, and the fault changes executed control flow rather than any stored model weight.\index{Fault Injection Attack!activation manipulation}

title: Side-channel attack vulnerability
caption: **Side-channel attack vulnerability**: Power consumption patterns reveal information about a password comparison; consistent power usage indicates correct password bytes, while abrupt changes signal incorrect input and halted processing. Even without knowing the password, an attacker can infer it by analyzing the device's power usage during authentication attempts. Source: Colin O'Flynn.
alt: Oscilloscope trace showing red serial data line and blue power line. Power remains stable through first three correct bytes, then jumps sharply at fourth incorrect byte, revealing partial password match through timing.
context:
Studies of Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)\index{AES!side-channel vulnerability} implementations showed that an implementation can leak information about a key without an attacker breaking the cipher's mathematical construction. The same distinction between an algorithm and its implementation applies to the ReLU activations, softmax normalizations, and weight-load sequences that constitute a forward pass.

Power analysis of a password check shows the mechanism in its simplest form [@kocher2011]. Consider a device that verifies a 5-byte password (`0x61, 0x52, 0x77, 0x6A, 0x73`) received one byte at a time over a serial interface. With the correct password, the power profile stays stable across all five bytes.\index{Side-Channel Attack!power profile} @Fig-encryption2 shows what happens when only the first three bytes are correct. The power pattern tracks the correct-password profile through the third byte (`0x61, 0x52, 0x77`), then jumps when the device rejects the fourth byte (`0x42`) and halts authentication.\index{Side-Channel Attack!power signature divergence} An entirely wrong password (`0x30` repeated) produces the same jump immediately after the first byte.\index{Side-Channel Attack!power consumption jump}

title: Power traces
caption: **Power traces**: Cryptographic computations reveal subtle, data-dependent variations in power consumption that reflect internal states during specific operations. The traces are schematic: amplitudes are illustrative and follow the Hamming-weight ordering rather than a measured capture.
alt: Two line graphs. Left shows three overlapping power traces over six clock cycles in one orange hue, dotted, dashed, and solid; a gray band, outlined as the region magnified on the right, marks the S-box window where the traces peak. Right zooms into that window, where the peaks separate by weight; labels to the right at each peak's height, each led by a short swatch in its trace's line style, read 1111 wt 4, 0101 wt 2, and 0000 wt 0, and a double arrow marks the amplitude gap delta P between 0000 and 1111.
context:
Machine learning also changes the attacker's side of this analysis. Extracting a key from noisy power traces requires finding signal patterns associated with secret-dependent computations, and a convolutional neural network can learn those patterns from labeled traces, turning part of the analysis into a learned classification task. The attacker still needs suitable measurements and training data, but can reuse the trained model across repeated attempts under compatible conditions. The SCAAML framework (Side-Channel Attacks Assisted with Machine Learning), developed by researchers at Google, is a widely studied and reproducible demonstration of this learned pipeline [@bursztein2024; @burszteindc27].

@Fig-side-channel-curves illustrates data-dependent power consumption during an AES S-box substitution. The left panel places a possible leakage interval within a longer trace; the right panel magnifies a schematic difference between processed values. Hamming weight counts the ones in a binary value: 1111 has weight 4, 0101 has weight 2, and 0000 has weight 0. The drawing orders amplitudes by that weight to illustrate a leakage model, not a measured law of CMOS switching. Actual leakage depends on circuit structure, state transitions, noise, and countermeasures. A classifier must learn a reproducible relationship in measured traces before these differences can support key recovery.\index{Power Traces}

title: STM32F target board
caption: **STM32F target board**: The measurement setup exposes power consumption during AES operations on the microcontroller. Those traces provide the observations from which a side-channel model can infer data-dependent internal behavior.
alt: Photograph of the blue STM32F target board, a CW308 UFO board, seated on a red mainboard. The board is designed for use with a ChipWhisperer for side-channel analysis.
section: Labels at each peak's height, each led by a swatch in its trace's line style
context:
[^fn-sbox-lookup-table]: **S-box (Substitution Box)**\index{S-box}: The nonlinear byte-substitution table in AES. In the first round, its input combines a plaintext byte with a key byte. Predicting its output is a 256-way classification problem; with the corresponding plaintext byte known, the attacker can map predictions back to candidate key bytes and combine evidence across traces.

Capturing these physical signatures requires access to suitable instrumentation. The STM32F target board in @fig-stm32f-board sits on a ChipWhisperer-compatible baseboard with labeled connections for measurement and triggering. Such a setup supports the synchronized power measurements used to train and evaluate a side-channel model. The photograph illustrates the measurement interface; the attack experiment, rather than the board's appearance, establishes which secrets can be recovered and how many traces are needed.

title: Hardware supply chain attack surface
caption: **Hardware supply chain attack surface**: Each lifecycle stage admits its own compromise (red arrows) and needs its own assurance evidence (green gates); no single check covers the chain, and dashed lines carry each missed compromise forward to deployment. Unlike software, which can be patched remotely, a compromise that survives to deployment often requires physical replacement.
alt: A left-to-right pipeline of five stage boxes: design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, deployment. Above each stage a red arrow labeled with its compromise strikes a green gate box naming its assurance check: design flaws or malicious IP hit design review and verification, hardware Trojans hit die inspection by micrography, substituted components hit X-ray screening, cloned or relabeled parts hit provenance and functional tests, and probing and fault injection hit secure boot and attestation. Below the pipeline, dashed red lines marked if missed leave the first four stage boxes and run to deployment, where they end at a red bracket labeled physical replacement.
context:
@Fig-hw-supply-chain maps the full lifecycle through design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, and deployment. Each stage presents opportunities for tampering or substitution: recycled electronic waste can be relabeled as new, distributors can mix cloned parts into legitimate shipments, and insiders at manufacturing facilities can embed hardware trojans that routine functional tests may miss. Micrography, X-ray screening, and functional testing provide different evidence, with coverage and cost determined by the suspected modification. Procurement therefore needs risk-based provenance controls as well as inspection; passing a functional test does not establish a component's origin or exclude dormant malicious behavior.

Fleet procurement changes the shape of this risk. A training cluster is bought in bulk from a small number of part numbers, so each of the `{python} ReferenceClusterAttackSurface.node_count_str` nodes of the reference cluster carries the same accelerators, network adapters, management controller, and firmware images as every other. A compromised shared design, firmware release, or production batch can therefore affect many nodes at once. Replication does not remove a vulnerability shared by the replicas, although one compromised unit is evidence about its part number, not proof that every unit carrying it is affected. The provenance bound on trust (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}) applies to silicon and firmware as much as to data. Supplier, batch, and firmware records help identify the affected population; supplier concentration increases common dependencies even when those records are complete.

title: Layered defense stack
caption: **Layered defense stack**: Controls are grouped by the layer they protect, from the silicon root of trust through platform isolation and model safeguards to data privacy. A compromised component can undermine controls that rely on its execution or stored state. These runtime dependencies must be checked against each control’s threat model; a correctly released differentially private artifact retains its release-level guarantee.
alt: Four stacked tiers of four controls each. From top: data (encryption at rest, provenance tracking, secure aggregation, differential privacy), model (adversarial training, input validation, output monitoring, rate limits), platform (container isolation, network segmentation, access control, runtime telemetry), and hardware (trusted execution, secure boot, HSM key custody, PUF device identity). A red dot on the platform tier marked compromised host sends a dashed red arrow up to the differential privacy block, labeled alters it before release, while a green arrow from differential privacy leads to a separate green released-artifact box.
context:
[^fn-robustness-privacy-tradeoff]: **Robustness-Privacy Trade-Off**\index{Robustness-Privacy Trade-Off!adversarial training}: Adversarial training can increase susceptibility to membership inference in the settings studied by @song2019privacy. The result means that a robustness intervention must be reevaluated against privacy invariants rather than assumed to improve every security property at once.

Layered defense\index{Defense in Depth!layered architecture} (also known as defense in depth) makes these dependencies explicit. Differential privacy bounds what a specified release reveals about an individual's contribution; it does not protect a separate copy of raw training records from theft. Federated learning changes where training data reside but does not, by itself, bound what updates reveal. Hardware isolation can protect execution within its threat model without establishing that an application follows the intended data policy. Combining these mechanisms requires stating each guarantee and checking which assumptions the other layers preserve.

title: Secure enclave architecture
caption: **Secure enclave architecture**: The Secure Enclave is an isolated region of the system on chip with its own processor, random-number generator, public-key accelerator, AES engine, and root keys. The application processor reaches it only through a mailbox, enclave memory in DRAM passes through a memory protection engine, and storage keys go directly to the inline AES engine, so a compromised application processor never holds them. Source: Apple.
alt: Block diagram. A system-on-chip frame holds an application processor and a Secure Enclave region containing an enclave processor, TRNG, memory protection engine, PKA, AES engine, and root keys. Arrows connect the application processor to DRAM and to the enclave through a mailbox, the memory protection engine to an encrypted enclave region of DRAM, the enclave to secure storage over I2C, and the root keys to a storage AES engine that writes encrypted data to NAND flash.
context:
[^fn-trustzone-hardware-security]: **ARM TrustZone**\index{ARM TrustZone!adoption}: Introduced in 2004, TrustZone partitions an ARM processor into secure and normal "worlds" with hardware-enforced isolation. Its presence on a device does not by itself protect an ML deployment: the model, keys, and data path must actually be placed inside the secure world, which depends on whether the device vendor exposes secure-world applications beyond key storage.

@Fig-enclave diagrams the isolation boundaries and bus interfaces of Apple's system-on-chip (SoC) Secure Enclave. Its dedicated processor, true random number generator (TRNG), public key accelerator (PKA), and cryptographic engines operate separately from the application processor, which communicates through a mailbox interface. A memory protection engine encrypts and authenticates the enclave's external memory, while protected key paths support storage encryption [@apple2024secureenclave]. This example demonstrates isolation of designated security operations and state. It does not imply that arbitrary application model weights or activations reside inside the Secure Enclave; their protection depends on the execution and data paths the platform supports.\index{Secure Enclave!architecture}

title: Secure boot sequence
caption: **Secure boot sequence**: Each trusted stage authenticates the next component before use. Extending the chain to a verified model loader permits model-artifact authentication; generic boot verification does not provide that extension automatically. Measured boot records evidence, whereas verification enforces the loading decision.
alt: Horizontal chain of four stages: 1, immutable boot root; 2, verified bootloader; 3, verified OS or loader; 4, authorized ML workload. Green diamonds between stages authenticate the bootloader, the kernel and startup policy, and the manifest and artifact digest; each diamond sends a red fail arrow up to a shared box labeled halt and reject the component. Below, a measurement log row records bootloader hash, kernel hash, and model digest under stages 2 to 4, and a bracket under the last gate and stage reads extension to the model. A dashed after-boot arrow leads to a dashed box reading runtime controls still required.
context:
For machine learning systems, secure boot authenticates the components included in its verification chain. Model artifacts receive this protection only when a verified loader checks their signatures or a signed manifest before loading them; boot verification alone does not authenticate weights read later from storage. Secure update flows must extend the same verification policy to replacement firmware, runtimes, and model artifacts.

Secure boot frequently operates in tandem with hardware-based TEEs to establish an unbroken chain of trust prior to code execution. @Fig-secure-boot sequences this stepped verification handshake, pairing each trusted execution stage with an explicit cryptographic authentication gate [@nist2018sp800193]. Execution proceeds from an immutable boot root through a verified bootloader and operating system, halting and rejecting the component if any signature check fails. For machine learning pipelines, Stage 3 extends this chain beyond conventional system software: the verified OS or loader authenticates the model manifest and artifact digest before launching the authorized ML workload. The terminal stage emphasizes that while boot-time authentication blocks unauthorized or tampered binaries, dynamic runtime controls remain necessary to guard against post-boot attacks and data-dependent exploits.\index{Secure Boot!sequence}

title: Physical unclonable functions
caption: **Physical unclonable functions**: Each panel turns uncontrolled manufacturing variation into a device-specific response. Two chips of the same design answer the same challenge differently (A); a laser challenge scattered by a random token yields a speckle response (B); a challenge sets each arbiter stage straight or crossed, and the faster of two racing edges sets the response bit (C); and threshold-voltage mismatch decides the value a cross-coupled SRAM cell settles to at power-up (D).
alt: Four panels. A: two chip squares with different dot patterns produce response R1 and response R2, marked not equal. B: a tilted laser sends a beam at a marked angle into a token filled with scattered particles, and diverging rays reach a speckle image. C: two signal paths pass through switch stages C1, C2, and Ck, crossing in one stage, into an arbiter that outputs bit r. D: two cross-coupled inverters between nodes A and B, one drawn heavier and labeled threshold-voltage mismatch, with node A settling to 0 and node B to 1.
context:
For ML fleets, a PUF can reduce the need to inject and persistently store a unique secret in each device. The phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) and the cameras and drones of edge deployments still need enrollment: the verifier must associate a device with trusted authentication evidence and manage its admission and revocation. A PUF-derived key can encrypt the on-device model at rest, so copying the stored file does not yield the device-bound key that decrypts it. Authentication can use enrolled challenge-response information or a credential backed by a derived key, depending on the design. Both protections have limits. Plaintext weights extracted during execution expose the shared model regardless of how the storage key was generated, and successful authentication establishes which device is speaking, not that its runtime software is uncompromised.

@Fig-puf diagrams physical unclonable function architectures that turn manufacturing variation into device-dependent responses [@gao2020]. Panel A illustrates the challenge-response abstraction: two devices of the same design respond to challenge $\PufChallenge$ with different responses ($\PufResponse_1 \ne \PufResponse_2$). The remaining panels show different physical mechanisms. Optical PUFs illuminate random scattering tokens to produce speckle patterns (Panel B). Arbiter PUFs send a signal along paths configured by challenge bits ($\PufChallenge_1$ through $\PufChallenge_k$), with the relative arrival times determining the response bit $\PufResponseBit$ (Panel C). SRAM PUFs exploit transistor mismatches that bias memory cells toward preferred startup states (Panel D). These preferences are not perfectly repeatable under every operating condition, which motivates the error correction and calibration discussed next.\index{Physical Unclonable Function!arbiter PUF}\index{Physical Unclonable Function!SRAM PUF}

title: Adversarial prompt evasion
caption: **Adversarial prompt evasion**: Implicitly adversarial prompts bypass typical content filters by triggering unintended generations, revealing limitations of solely relying on pregeneration safety checks. These examples underscore the necessity of post-hoc content analysis as a complementary defense layer for robust generative AI systems.
alt: Three deliberately blurred images generated by a text-to-image model, each showing graphic red content resembling blood or injury.
context:
However, prompt filtering alone is insufficient for safety. Research has shown that text-to-image systems can be manipulated through implicitly adversarial prompts, which are queries that appear benign but lead to policy-violating outputs. The Adversarial Nibbler project introduces an open red teaming methodology that identifies such prompts and demonstrates how models like Stable Diffusion can produce unintended content despite the absence of explicit trigger phrases [@quaye2024; @parrish2023adversarial]. These failure cases often bypass prompt filters because their risk arises from model behavior during generation, not from syntactic or lexical cues.

The red-teaming gallery in @fig-adversarial-nibbler presents three blurred generated images with red content suggestive of blood or injury. These examples illustrate why an output needs assessment against the application's policy even when the prompt appears acceptable. The images alone cannot reveal which input filter was active, how a prompt bypassed it, or which internal generation mechanism caused the result. Diagnosing those failures requires prompt, model, and filter records alongside the outputs. Output classifiers provide a complementary check, whose own errors must also be evaluated.\index{Adversarial Attack!prompt evasion}

title: Differential privacy and output distributions
caption: **Differential privacy and output distributions**: These illustrative densities show how outputs can overlap without having identical likelihoods. Differential privacy bounds how much the output distribution can change between adjacent datasets $\NeighboringDataset$ and $\AdjacentNeighboringDataset$. The privacy parameters limit, rather than eliminate, the information an observer can gain about any one individual's inclusion.
alt: Two overlapping bell curves over the mechanism output space, blue for the mechanism on dataset X and orange for the mechanism on adjacent dataset X prime, each labeled directly. A gray region marks their overlap, and a vertical double arrow at outcome o marks the difference between the two density values there.
context:
uses the central model of differential privacy. Each person supplies a bounded salary to a trusted analyst; the analyst computes the sum, adds one Laplace draw calibrated to the sum's global sensitivity, and divides by the fixed, public group size. The example protects a salary replacement within a public roster. If participation itself is private, adjacency must be add/remove, meaning adjacent datasets differ by the presence or absence of one person's records rather than by a change to one value. Under that relation the count becomes data dependent and needs its own privacy treatment, so division by that count is not automatically safe post-processing. This differs from local differential privacy, in which each person randomizes a value before submission and the analyst aggregates the randomized reports. Both models compare output distributions on adjacent inputs, but their mechanisms, trust assumptions, and utility are not interchangeable.

@Fig-differential-privacy illustrates output densities of a randomized mechanism $\RandomizedMechanism$ evaluated across adjacent datasets $\NeighboringDataset$ (blue curve) and $\AdjacentNeighboringDataset$ (orange curve). Overlap means that either dataset can produce outcomes in the same region; it does not make the distributions identical. For a discrete outcome $\MechanismOutcome$ in $\text{Range}(\RandomizedMechanism)$, relative likelihood can be expressed as $\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome] / \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome]$ when the denominator is positive. Continuous curves instead depict densities, whose ratio is not their vertical difference. The $(\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)$ guarantee applies to probabilities of measurable output sets: it bounds one probability by $e^{\PrivacyBudget}$ times the other plus $\PrivacyAdditiveSlack$. For a continuous output, those probabilities are areas under the curves over the selected set. The definition therefore constrains distributional change across all such sets, rather than declaring an overlapping region private or treating additive slack as a pointwise density-ratio allowance.

title: Published privacy-utility results
caption: **Published privacy-utility results**: Accuracy at selected privacy budgets from [@abadi2016deep; @bu2020gaussian; @de2022dp]. MNIST stays comparatively accurate under single-digit epsilon budgets in these experiments, while CIFAR-10 trained from scratch without extra data remains harder, with De et al. reporting 81.4 percent at $\PrivacyBudget = 8$. Comparisons require the full mechanism, accountant, adjacency relation, training regime, and data rather than epsilon alone.
alt: Test accuracy versus privacy budget epsilon on a log axis. A blue line of MNIST results from Bu 2020 rises from 95 to 98 percent, blue triangles mark MNIST results from Abadi 2016, and orange markers at epsilon 8 mark CIFAR-10 results from Abadi 2016 at 73.0 percent and De 2022 at 81.4 percent. Dashed lines mark the nonprivate baselines, 98.3 percent for MNIST and 93.0 percent for CIFAR-10, each labeled directly. A double arrow at epsilon 8 spans from the CIFAR-10 baseline down to the lower result and is labeled roughly 12 to 20 points below its baseline.
context:
The parameter $\PrivacyBudget$ quantifies the privacy budget\index{Differential Privacy!privacy budget epsilon}. In the pure-DP definition above, smaller values of $\PrivacyBudget$ impose a tighter likelihood-ratio bound; achieving that bound may require more noise or a different mechanism. No universal $\PrivacyBudget$ value denotes "strong," "moderate," or acceptable privacy: interpretation depends on adjacency, the additive slack $\PrivacyAdditiveSlack$ in approximate DP, composition, and the consequences of inference. Under pure DP, the multiplicative factor $e^{\PrivacyBudget}$ bounds ratios of probabilities for the same output event on adjacent datasets. Approximate DP relaxes that event-probability inequality with additive slack, as developed below.

@Fig-privacy-utility-frontier plots classification accuracy against privacy budget $\PrivacyBudget$ on a logarithmic scale across published MNIST and CIFAR-10 benchmarks [@abadi2016deep; @bu2020gaussian; @de2022dp]. These comparisons show setting-specific utility costs; differences in architectures and training procedures prevent isolating task complexity alone. The plotted MNIST results stay within about 3.5 percentage points of the 98.3 percent nonprivate baseline at budgets in the range $\PrivacyBudget\in [1, 2]$. For CIFAR-10 without extra data, the plotted results reach 73.0 percent in @abadi2016deep and 81.4 percent in @de2022dp at $\PrivacyBudget= 8$, roughly 12 to 20 points below the displayed 93.0 percent nonprivate reference, so these CIFAR-10 settings pay several times the MNIST accuracy cost at a budget four times looser. That reference is a comparison point, not a ceiling on achievable accuracy. Selecting a budget therefore requires the full training regime, adjacency relation, additive slack, accountant, and utility requirements rather than the horizontal coordinate alone.

title: Clean Predictions and Perturbation Robustness
caption: **Clean Predictions and Perturbation Robustness**: Two illustrative two-dimensional classifiers demonstrate the distinction between clean-data accuracy and certified robustness. Both decision boundaries correctly separate the labeled clean inputs. Dashed circles delimit identical perturbation neighborhoods around each point. Boundary A maintains separation outside both circles, whereas boundary B intersects them, allowing a small adversarial perturbation to change the classification. Agreement on clean inputs does not establish resilience under attack.
alt: Two panels show the same negative and positive inputs surrounded by dashed circles. A vertical decision boundary in panel A lies outside the circles. A sloped boundary in panel B crosses both circles. The same arrow moves the positive input within its circle, crossing only boundary B.
context:
:::

Two models can agree on every clean input and still differ in how far an input can move before its label flips. In @fig-clean-vs-robust-classification, each labeled point is surrounded by the same perturbation radius, the largest input change the evaluation allows. Vertical boundary A keeps every allowed change on the correct side, while oblique boundary B cuts through the neighborhood around $\PositiveClassInput$, so a small displacement $\AdversarialPerturbation$ flips the predicted class. The adversarial defenses of @sec-robust-ai-input-attack-detection-defense-19d3 turn that distance into a measured quantity and, under stated assumptions, a certified one.

title: Autopilot-Involved Barrier Crash (2018)
caption: **Autopilot-Involved Barrier Crash (2018)**: This Model X collision with a highway barrier in Mountain View, California, a later incident than the 2016 crossing-trailer crash, shows the safety risks of relying on machine learning for perception in autonomous systems, where failures to correctly interpret the scene can lead to catastrophic outcomes. The incident underscores the need for robust validation, redundancy, and failsafe mechanisms in self-driving vehicle designs to mitigate the impact of imperfect AI models. Source: BBC News.
alt: Photograph of a dark-blue Tesla after a highway collision. The front-left of the vehicle is heavily damaged; emergency crews and barrier wreckage are visible on scene, consistent with an Autopilot-involved impact.
context:
:::

[^fn-autopilot-perception-safety]: **Autopilot**\index{Autopilot!perception failure}: The 2016 crash involved Tesla's then-current SAE Level 2 driver-assistance system and Mobileye-era perception stack, not the later 8-camera full-self-driving hardware or dual FSD-chip computer. Later Tesla vehicles introduced expanded camera coverage and dedicated FSD compute, but the robustness lesson is the same: fleet-scale data collection does not automatically cover rare scenarios such as a white trailer against a bright sky.

title: Robotic Lander on Mars
caption: **Robotic Lander on Mars**: An artist's rendering of NASA's Mars Polar Lander on the Martian surface. Remote robotic missions exemplify the class of systems in which software or sensor faults cannot be recovered by human intervention, motivating the rigorous validation and failure-mode analysis that ML components in the decision loop must also satisfy. Source: Slashgear.
alt: Artist rendering of NASA's Mars Polar Lander on the Martian surface with solar panels and robotic arm extended, illustrative of robotic planetary landers whose autonomous decision loops demand rigorous validation.
context:
Embedded systems can operate through critical intervals in which external intervention is too slow. Remote maintenance may remain possible between those intervals, but an autonomous landing or control maneuver needs a local response before its deadline. Validation must therefore cover both the component's failure modes and the system behavior that follows, including any ML model in the decision loop.

The loss of NASA's Mars Polar Lander in 1999, attributed by the review board to premature touchdown detection that likely shut the engines off before landing [@nasa2000mpl], illustrates the consequences of a false sensor indication during autonomous descent. The planetary deployment illustrated in @fig-nasa-example places the response inside the vehicle rather than with a remote operator. For a learned component in such a control loop, validation must connect plausible input and sensor failures to the actions they can trigger; exhaustive testing of every possible input is not a feasible safety argument.

title: Weight Corruption via Bit Flip
caption: **Weight Corruption via Bit Flip**: (a) One corrupted weight $\CorruptedModelWeight$ drives hidden unit $\HiddenUnitOutput_2$, whose output feeds every downstream logit. (b) For an illustrative trained weight $\ModelWeight = 0.042 \approx 1.34 \times 2^{-5}$, flipping bit 30, the most significant exponent bit of the FP32 word, raises the stored exponent from $2^{-5}$ to $2^{123}$. In general, flipping an exponent bit with place value $2^{\ExponentBitIndex}$ scales the value by $2^{\pm 2^{\ExponentBitIndex}}$; here the factor is $2^{128}$, giving $\CorruptedModelWeight \approx 1.4 \times 10^{37}$. The result is still finite, so NaN and infinity checks never fire, yet it can produce extreme downstream activations, depending on the input, activation function, and downstream weights. A range check $|\ModelWeight| \le \WeightRangeBound$ against the trained weight distribution catches it cheaply.
alt: Left: a small network with four inputs, three hidden units, and two outputs; one input-to-hidden weight is drawn thick and red, and dashed red arrows run from the affected hidden unit to both outputs. Right: two FP32 bit rows showing sign, eight exponent bits, and a collapsed mantissa. The top row encodes w = 0.042 with exponent bits 01111010; an arrow labeled bit 30 flips 0 to 1, value times 2 to the 128 leads to the bottom row, whose first exponent bit is red and set to 1, labeled w prime approximately 1.4 times 10 to the 37.
section: From ML performance to system reliability {#sec-robust-ai-ml-performance-system-reliability-7d42}
context:
Once silent failure becomes a systems property, accuracy, latency, and throughput no longer describe the full reliability envelope. The deployed model also depends on the computational substrate that executes it, and that substrate can corrupt a correct model without producing a visible service failure.

@Fig-weight-corruption traces how a physical bit flip cascades through neural inference. In panel (b), flipping bit 30 of an FP32 weight scales its magnitude by $2^{128}$, transforming a modest weight ($\ModelWeight= 0.042$) into an extreme outlier ($\CorruptedModelWeight\approx 1.4 \times 10^{37}$). Panel (a) traces the affected path through hidden unit $\HiddenUnitOutput_2$ to output logits ($\NetworkOutput_1, \NetworkOutput_2$). The corrupted weight is finite and can evade NaN or infinity checks; whether it dominates those outputs depends on the input, activation function, and downstream weights. Targeted bit-flip attacks deliberately select vulnerable weight bits, so their results should not be interpreted as the effect of one random hardware upset. Memory subsystem failures during training can likewise corrupt gradient updates and prevent model convergence. Scale turns one corrupted value into a persistent exposure. Every forward pass of a dense GPT-3-class model reads all `{python} RobustAISetup.gpt3_params_b_str` of its parameters, so a corrupted weight resident in memory participates in every request that replica serves until something detects it. Estimating how often such corruption occurs requires a sourced, device-specific error rate with its stored capacity and time basis, which is the role of the fleet-scale probability model below.

title: Silent Error Probability at Scale
caption: **Silent Error Probability at Scale**: Probability of at least one silent data corruption event per hour as a function of cluster size, for three illustrative per-device error rates. The curves are analytical, $\Pr(\geq 1) = 1 - (1-\DeviceSilentCorruptionProbability)^\DeviceCount$, and show how quickly cluster-scale probabilities compound as per-device rates increase; fleet observations of silent corruption [@dixit2021silent] motivate stress-testing at rates above soft-error predictions.
alt: Semilog plot showing three S-curves, solid, dashed, and dotted, labeled with per-device SDC rates of 1e-3, 1e-4, and 1e-5. A red band above probability 0.95 is labeled effectively certain, and a dashed line at 0.5 is labeled more likely than not. The 1e-3 and 1e-4 curves enter the red band and approach probability 1.0 by 100000 devices, with a dot marking 0.63 at 10K on the 1e-4 curve; the 1e-5 curve rises to about 0.63.
context:
n_gpus_certain_str = fmt(n_gpus_certain_val, precision=0)
```
Scale also compounds the chance that such corruption occurs somewhere. Under the fleet model of @sec-ft-sdc-verification, a fleet of $\DeviceCount$ devices\index{Silent data corruption!cluster-scale probability}, each with independent residual-error probability $\DeviceSilentCorruptionProbability$ over the same interval, sees at least one silent error with probability $\Pr(\geq 1) = 1 - (1 - \DeviceSilentCorruptionProbability)^\DeviceCount$; bit flips that hardware corrects are not silent errors. @Fig-silent-error-probability plots that curve for three illustrative per-device rates. At `{python} SilentErrorProbability.p_per_hr_prose_str` per device-hour, a `{python} SilentErrorProbability.n_gpus_large_str`-device cluster sees some corruption within an hour with probability `{python} SilentErrorProbability.p_total_large_str`, and corruption becomes nearly certain at roughly `{python} SilentErrorProbability.n_gpus_certain_str` devices. The rates are stress-test assumptions rather than measured device rates, although Meta's SDC report confirms corruption at observable fleet scale [@dixit2021silent].

title: The Robustness Taxonomy
caption: **The Robustness Taxonomy**: Environmental shifts, input-level attacks, and system-level faults decomposed into concrete failure subtypes (dark), each paired with its principal defense (green). Each pillar descends onto a defense wall at the point where it enters the ML pipeline, the data stream, the model's inputs and training data, or the weights and accelerators. Software and pipeline defects originate in the system layer, but they are drawn as the cross-cutting pipeline rail on which all three walls sit because their symptoms can amplify or imitate any of the pillars.
alt: Three side-by-side pillar columns sit above one horizontal dashed pipeline band that runs left to right from data in to output and is labeled software and pipeline defects, cross-cutting; inside the band, a labeled icon sits centered under each column. Each column holds four white failure chips, each naming a failure in dark text and its defense in green. A red arrow from each column's chips ends on a solid green wall bar resting on the pipeline band, directly above the component that pillar strikes: a data stream of sample dots under environmental shifts, a grid of input and training data tiles under input-level attacks, and an accelerator chip holding weight cells under system-level faults. Environmental shifts: covariate shift to importance weighting, concept drift to retraining on fresh labels, label shift to prior re-estimation and recalibration, domain shift to domain adaptation and fine-tuning. Input-level attacks: evasion (FGSM, PGD) to adversarial training, C and W and boundary attacks to certified defenses, data and backdoor poisoning to provenance and spectral filtering, physical perturbations to transformation-robust training. System-level faults: silent data corruption to redundant execution and fleet screening, memory and weight bit flips to ECC and weight range checks, underflow overflow and NaN to loss scaling and NaN guards, distributed training desync to checkpoint rollback and watchdogs.
section: The three pillars of robust AI {#sec-robust-ai-three-pillars-robust-ai-2626}
context:
### The three pillars of robust AI {#sec-robust-ai-three-pillars-robust-ai-2626}

An engineer must decide which failure signal is present before choosing a defense. Each of the three pillars named at the start of the chapter decomposes into concrete failure subtypes, and each subtype pairs with the defense that targets it (@fig-robustness-taxonomy).

title: Types of Distribution Shift
caption: **Types of Distribution Shift**: (a) Under covariate shift, deployment inputs move to a new region of feature space while the labeling rule, and so the correct boundary, stays fixed. (b) Under label shift, class frequencies change while each class's inputs look the same; the bar heights are illustrative. (c) Under concept drift, the same inputs acquire new labels, so points between the old and new boundaries become errors. Covariate shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$ fixed, label shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput \mid \ExampleLabel)$ fixed, and concept drift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$; the distinction determines whether reweighting, recalibration, or model adaptation is appropriate.
alt: Three panels with a shared key for class 0 (filled) and class 1 (open) points and red label-changed points. Panel a, covariate shift: blue training points labeled train, of two classes, sit on either side of a dashed boundary, and an arrow points to amber deployment points labeled deploy, of the same two classes in a new region, still on the correct sides of the unchanged boundary. Panel b, label shift: paired blue train and amber deploy bars for y equals 0 and y equals 1; training bars are equal, and the deployment bar for y equals 1 is much taller than for y equals 0. Panel c, concept drift: the same points with a dashed boundary labeled old and a solid green boundary labeled new crossing it; points between the two boundaries are red to mark changed labels.
context:
Consider a medical diagnosis model trained on X-ray images from one hospital and deployed in a clinic with different imaging equipment\index{Distribution Shift!clinical imaging}. Even for the same medical conditions, acquisition settings can change the image characteristics. This difference between training and deployment populations is **distribution shift**\index{Distribution Shift!definition}; whether it reduces diagnostic accuracy requires evaluation on the clinic's data. A move to a different source altogether, such as a new hospital, sensor, or region, is often called domain shift\index{Domain Shift}, and it can combine several of the shift types distinguished below.

@Fig-shift-types partitions distribution shift into three geometric and statistical regimes: inputs can migrate to an unfamiliar region of feature space (panel a), label priors can skew (panel b), or the underlying mapping itself can invert (panel c). Here, $\ModelInput$ denotes an input and $\ExampleLabel$ its outcome label. Input-only monitors can detect changes in $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$; distinguishing changes in label frequencies or in $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel\mid \ModelInput)$ generally requires outcome evidence or additional assumptions.

title: Accuracy on a Fresh Test Set from the Same Recipe
caption: **Accuracy on a Fresh Test Set from the Same Recipe**: Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-V2, a test set rebuilt by following the original ImageNet collection protocol, against accuracy on the original ImageNet validation set, for testbed models that reach at least 55 percent on the original. Every point lies below the dashed line of equal accuracy, and the red least-squares line shows that the loss tracks accuracy almost linearly. ImageNet-V2 is from @recht2019imagenet; model evaluations from the testbed of @taori2020measuring.
alt: Scatter plot of ImageNet-V2 top-1 accuracy from about 43 to 81 percent against original ImageNet accuracy from about 56 to 88 percent. A dashed diagonal marks equal accuracy; all points lie 7 to 14 points below it. A red fitted line runs through the points. AlexNet near 56.5 and 43, VGG-16 near 72 and 59, ResNet-50 near 76 and 63, and EfficientNet-L2 Noisy Student near 88 and 81 are labeled.
context:
```

Even a shift that was designed to be no shift at all costs accuracy. @recht2019imagenet rebuilt the ImageNet validation set a decade after the original by following the original collection and labeling protocol, then evaluated existing models on the new images. In the larger testbed of @taori2020measuring, every one of the `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.model_count_str` models that reach at least `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.val_floor_str` percent on the original set scores lower on the new one, by `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_min_str` to `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_max_str` points with a median of `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_median_str` (@fig-imagenet-v2-shift). The loss follows a nearly straight line, so a model that is better on the original set is better on the new one, yet no architecture, training recipe, or amount of extra data closes the gap. Whatever separates the two sets is not an obvious visual change, yet it is costly to every model. For a fleet, accuracy measured on held-out data from the training distribution is therefore an optimistic estimate of accuracy on the next population of inputs, not a prediction of it.

title: A Calibrated Distribution-Shift Workflow
caption: **A Calibrated Distribution-Shift Workflow**: In this synthetic service, PSI enters the warning zone as user behavior shifts and crosses the service's escalation threshold at week 32. Following investigation and validation of the changed operating population, the service versions a new input reference at week 41. Values on either side of that reference change use different comparison populations; the drop is not evidence of model recovery.
alt: Line plot of weekly PSI over 52 weeks with service-calibrated green, orange, and red alert zones labeled stable, warning, and major shift. Drift crosses the escalation threshold at week 32. A gray band from week 32 to week 41 is labeled investigation and validation, and a discontinuity at week 41 is labeled approved reference change, after which PSI uses the new reference.
context:
: **PSI Alert Bands**: The fleet convention bands can initialize alert severity, but each service must validate them against its binning, baseline, sample size, predictive features, and response cost. {#tbl-robust-ai-psi-thresholds}

Binning and the treatment of empty bins change what PSI can see, so the bin boundaries chosen on the reference sample must be reused for the comparison population. An empty bin is handled with a smoothing constant\index{Population Stability Index!smoothing constant} $\PopulationStabilitySmoothingConstant$ and renormalization; because that choice can materially change PSI on sparse bins, the monitoring configuration records it alongside the reference. Monitoring population stability index over time as plotted in @fig-distribution-shift-detector reveals when the input population moves from the stable band into the warning band and then the major-shift band, triggering an escalation path that may lead to retraining after performance correlation. At week 41, the service approves and versions a new input reference after validating the changed operating population. The lower PSI thereafter compares traffic with that new reference, not the original one. Changing model weights alone would not reduce input PSI against a fixed reference, and the discontinuity does not establish improved predictions.

title: Imperceptible Misclassification in GoogLeNet
caption: **Imperceptible Misclassification in GoogLeNet**: Adding a perturbation of $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007$ in the sign direction of the loss gradient changes GoogLeNet's prediction from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence), although the two images look identical to a person. The attack does not merely flip the label; it leaves the model more confident in the wrong answer than it was in the right one. Source: [@goodfellow2015explaining].
alt: Three-panel demonstration: a panda photograph labeled panda, plus a faint noise pattern scaled by 0.007, equals a visually identical photograph that GoogLeNet labels gibbon.
context:
:::

Adversarial attack categories encode access and cost. A white-box attacker can use gradients directly, a black-box attacker uses surrogate transfer or queries to the target, and a physical attacker must survive cameras, lighting, and distance. @Fig-adversarial-googlenet demonstrates this vulnerability on an image-classification network: adding an imperceptible perturbation that follows the sign of the loss gradient ($\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007$), the fast gradient sign method defined below, flips GoogLeNet's prediction from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence), leaving the classifier paradoxically more confident in the erroneous label than the ground truth.

title: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry
caption: **Gradient-Based Attack Geometry**: Around a correctly classified input $\ModelInput$, the dashed square marks every perturbation allowed by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. FGSM moves each coordinate by the full budget in the sign direction of the loss gradient $\nabla_\ModelInput \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$, which lands $\AdversarialExample$ on a corner of that square, the allowed point that maximizes the first-order increase in loss. A step no larger than $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ in any coordinate therefore carries the input across the decision boundary. The class labels are illustrative.
alt: Two-dimensional input space divided by a solid diagonal decision boundary into a true-class region and an other-class region. A clean input x sits inside a dashed square labeled allowed set. A short blue arrow labeled gradient of L points up and to the left from x; a longer red arrow runs from x to the square's upper-left corner, marked x adv equals x plus epsilon times sign of the gradient, which lies across the boundary. A bracket under the square marks its half-width epsilon adv.
context:
In this formulation, $\ModelInput$ denotes the original input, $\AdversarialExample$ is the generated adversarial example, and $\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$ represents the prediction loss evaluated at model parameters $\ModelParameters$ and true label $\ExampleLabel$. The gradient term $\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction$ describes local loss sensitivity, $\text{sign}(\cdot)$ extracts each component's sign to maximize the linearized loss within the coordinate-wise budget, and the scalar $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ bounds the maximum allowable perturbation magnitude under the $\ell_\infty$ norm. This single step need not maximize the nonlinear loss or cause misclassification. Image implementations also clip the perturbed input to its valid pixel range. The subscript distinguishes this adversarial radius from other uses of $\Glyph{\epsilon}$ in the book, such as the differential-privacy budget.

Geometrically, moving along the sign vector of $\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$ carries input $\ModelInput$ to a corner of the bounding cube defined by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$, producing $\AdversarialExample$; in the illustration of @fig-gradient-attack, that corner lies across the decision boundary in the adjacent class region. A different boundary or gradient need not produce a successful attack within the same budget.

title: Adversarial stickers
caption: **Adversarial stickers**: In the cited study, the modified signs achieved targeted misclassification on all tested laboratory images and 84.8 percent of moving-vehicle field-test frames. The gap between those conditions shows why physical attacks must be evaluated across the actual sensing path.
alt: Photo of stop signs with small black and white stickers applied. The signs remain recognizable as stop signs to a person but cause the evaluated classifier to predict a targeted speed-limit class.

title: Physically Realizable Road-Sign Perturbations
caption: **Physically Realizable Road-Sign Perturbations**: Physically realizable modifications can cause machine learning models to make incorrect predictions. The three panels show perturbations from the original study, from a subtle full-sign poster to conspicuous graffiti-style camouflage and black-and-white sticker patches that look like ordinary vandalism yet trigger misclassification [@eykholt2018robust].
alt: Photographs of stop signs with conspicuous vandalism-style markings applied, illustrating physical adversarial perturbation as a category.
context:
:::

Physical perturbations also need not be subtle to matter. The perturbations in @fig-graffiti range from a poster covering the whole sign to graffiti-style markings and sticker patches that pass for ordinary vandalism. The associated study evaluates whether these physical modifications induce misclassification through the camera pipeline without digital access to the captured input [@eykholt2018robust].

title: Dirty-Label Data Poisoning
caption: **Dirty-Label Data Poisoning**: Mismatched image-text pairs represent a dirty-label poisoning attack where cat images are paired with misleading 'dog' captions in training data. Incorporating these corrupted pairs can cause models to learn incorrect multimodal associations.
alt: Three panels labeled 'Dirty-label poison data', each showing a cat image paired with a misleading text caption that calls the image a dog: 'A dog on the grass', 'Animal art dog pencil drawings', and 'Dog digital art...'.
context:
:::

The attack class runs from early formulations against support-vector machines\index{Data Poisoning!support-vector machines} [@biggio2012poisoning] to web-scale and generative-model data pipelines [@shan2024]. The dirty-label attack sampled in @fig-dirty-label-example pairs cat images with misleading 'dog' captions, attempting to induce false associations during multimodal pretraining.

title: Concept Poisoning Dose-Response
caption: **Concept Poisoning Dose-Response**: Stable Diffusion XL outputs across four poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300 samples) and eight source prompts (dog, car, handbag, hat, fantasy art, cubism, cartoon, concept art). As the dose grows, outputs morph from the intended source concept toward the attacker's destination concept, demonstrating Nightshade-style concept poisoning of a pretrained model.
alt: 4x8 grid of Stable Diffusion XL outputs. Rows are poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300); columns are source prompts (Dog, Car, Handbag, Hat, Fantasy art, Cubism, Cartoon, Concept Art). Outputs morph toward destination concepts as dose grows.
section: Art protection via poisoning case study {#sec-robust-ai-case-study-art-protection-via-poisoning-6106}
context:
Nightshade, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, aims to deter unauthorized training by poisoning images that a scraper may collect [@shan2024]. It does not block scraping itself. Its perturbations preserve the apparent image content while changing how a model learns from it; the reported experiments show targeted concept corruption when the modified images enter the tested training pipelines.

The dose-response matrix in @fig-poisoning charts this progressive corruption across four poison doses (0 to 300 samples) and eight prompt concepts. As the dose increases, Stable Diffusion XL outputs morph away from source concepts (generating cows for "car" or cats for "dog") under the tested training conditions. These outputs demonstrate changed behavior without, by themselves, identifying the internal representation that caused it. The experiment demonstrates concept poisoning\index{Data Poisoning!concept poisoning}: poisoned samples distort a model's semantic associations.

title: Standardized Robustness Evaluation of Published Defenses
caption: **Standardized Robustness Evaluation of Published Defenses**: Clean accuracy (gray) and accuracy under AutoAttack (red) for CIFAR-10 defenses on the RobustBench leaderboard by publication year, at a perturbation budget of 8/255 in the $\ell_\infty$ norm. Filled red points trained only on CIFAR-10; hollow points used additional data. The line tracks the best robust accuracy published by each year. Points near zero are defenses that do not withstand the standardized attack. Data from @croce2021robustbench.
alt: Scatter plot of CIFAR-10 accuracy from 0 to 100 percent against publication years 2018 to 2024. Gray clean-accuracy points cluster between about 80 and 95 percent. Red robust-accuracy points spread lower, between about 30 and 75 percent, with a stepped line for the best so far rising from 44 percent in 2018 to about 66 percent in 2020 and 75 percent in 2024. Four red points sit near zero in 2019 and 2020.
context:
```

RobustBench approximates that discipline at scale with one standardized, parameter-free attack ensemble, AutoAttack, applied to every published defense under one fixed threat model, which for CIFAR-10 is a perturbation of at most 8/255 per pixel in the $\ell_\infty$ norm [@croce2021robustbench; @croce2020autoattack]. @Fig-robustbench-progress plots the `{python} RobustBenchProgress.entry_count_str` dated entries. The best accuracy under attack rose from `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_first_pct_str` in 2018 to `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_pct_str` in 2024, while the same model kept `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_clean_pct_str` accuracy on clean images, so even the strongest defense still fails on about `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_fail_pct_str` of attacked inputs. The four entries at the bottom of the plot are published defenses that keep high clean accuracy yet fall below `{python} RobustBenchProgress.broken_floor_str` accuracy under the standardized attack, the result an evaluation that is not adaptive to the defense can miss.

title: Data Poisoning and Interception Workflow
caption: **Data Poisoning and Interception Workflow**: Adversaries inject malicious rows into a user-item rating matrix to manipulate model behavior. A defense layer analyzes contributed data and removes suspected malicious records before training. This can reduce poisoning risk but does not guarantee an uncorrupted model.
alt: A rating matrix with four user rows and two red sybil rows that rate item 3 as 1 and item 4 as 5. A gray bracket spans every row of the matrix, and a single line leaves its midpoint and forks. The upper branch, a dashed red arrow labeled no filter, reaches a red compromised model box in which item 3 is buried and item 4 boosted. The lower branch, a gray arrow, enters a green interception box labeled spectral scores, influence audit. Inside it, six scored rows drawn as small cell strips split: four plain rows pass to a kept stack, and the two red rows are diverted into a dashed red quarantine tray. A green arrow labeled filtered carries the kept rows to a candidate model box marked validate before release.
context:
Each layer covers a distinct point along the data path, and no single detector can substitute for end-to-end controls. While representation learning broadens defense to handle ordinary distribution shift, it cannot prove that the training corpus is uncompromised.

For the recommendation system, the interception layer in @fig-adversarial-attack-injection examines contributed ratings before they reach training. Its decisions must preserve provenance so later model failures can be traced back to the accepted records.

title: Autoencoder Ingestion Gate
caption: **Autoencoder Ingestion Gate**: An autoencoder trained on trusted data learns to compress inputs through a narrow latent layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$ and reconstruct them. Reconstruction error supplies an anomaly score, not proof that an input is poisoned. The gate accepts records whose reconstruction error $\AutoencoderReconstructionError$ stays at or below a threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ calibrated on held-out clean data and quarantines the rest.
alt: Symmetric hourglass network: an encoder narrows seven input units through five and three hidden units to a two-unit latent layer, and a decoder expands back to seven reconstructed outputs. An arrow from the output leads to a reconstruction error panel, L rec equals the squared norm of x minus x hat, containing a horizontal score axis labeled L rec at its arrow end and split by a dashed threshold tau. Left of tau is a green accept zone, L rec at most tau, holding a stacked cluster of green record dots at low scores; right of tau is a red quarantine zone, L rec greater than tau, holding two red record dots at high scores.
context:
After the source boundary, anomaly detection asks whether a candidate training example belongs to the distribution that the pipeline intended to learn from. The cheapest tests compare each record against the bulk distribution: Z-score filtering, Tukey's method, and Mahalanobis distance flag examples whose feature values sit far from normal ranges. These tests are useful because they are fast enough to run at ingestion, but they catch only poisons that look like statistical outliers in raw feature space. For high-dimensional or multimodal data, raw-feature distances are a weak signal: a manipulated image or caption that passes raw-feature checks may separate from clean examples in a pretrained vision or language model's embedding space. That separation depends on the encoder and attack, so it must be measured rather than inferred from the use of a learned representation. Applying Mahalanobis distance\index{Mahalanobis Distance!latent representation filtering} or clustering to those representations tests a different hypothesis from raw-feature screening. The pipeline must check whether the resulting outliers correspond to malicious contributions or to legitimate variation it needs to retain.

More coordinated attacks require structure-aware checks. Clustering methods such as K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering look for anomalous groups or isolated points rather than single extreme values. The autoencoder ingestion gate diagrammed in @fig-autoencoder adds a learned representation to the screening pipeline: the model compresses inputs through a bottleneck layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$, accepting records whose reconstruction error $\AutoencoderReconstructionError$ falls below threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ and quarantining anomalous outliers. Each method has a failure mode. Clean-label poisons need not be statistical outliers. Clustering depends on the representation, and autoencoders can reconstruct unfamiliar inputs well or learn an attack pattern from a contaminated reference corpus. Each gate therefore needs evaluation on both poisons and legitimate rare examples.

title: Data Augmentation Techniques
caption: **Data Augmentation Techniques**: Applying transformations like horizontal flips, rotations, and cropping creates variants of existing training examples. When the transformations preserve the task label, they can improve robustness to the represented variations and reduce overfitting. Their effect on generalization and poisoning resistance requires evaluation.
alt: Grid showing original image and augmented variants: horizontal flip, rotation, and cropping transformations applied to same source.
context:
[^fn-minimax-adversarial-formulation]: **Minimax**\index{Minimax!adversarial training}: Game-theoretic strategy from @vonneumann1928theorie that minimizes the maximum possible loss. In adversarial robustness, @madry2018towards formulate training as $\min_\ModelParameters\max_{\|\AdversarialPerturbation\| \leq \AdversarialPerturbationBudget} \LossFunction(\ParameterizedPredictor(\ModelInput+ \AdversarialPerturbation), \ExampleLabel)$: the model learns to minimize loss under a worst-case perturbation\index{Minimax!robust optimization formulation} within the chosen norm ball. The inner maximization is computationally expensive because it is usually approximated with iterative attacks such as PGD, so PGD-adversarial training is a budgeted robustness choice rather than a free objective change [@bai2021; @shafahi2019adversarial].

The image transformations displayed in @fig-data-augmentation demonstrate how data augmentation\index{Data Augmentation!techniques} expands training diversity: applying horizontal flips, rotations, and crops creates variants that preserve the label when the transform respects the class (a horizontally flipped digit need not) and can disrupt some localized poison patterns. Other transformations preserve an attack's trigger, so augmentation does not guarantee dilution. Random subsampling or bootstrap aggregating changes which poisoned records each model encounters; whether combining those models reduces the attack's effect requires evaluation against coordinated poisoning.

title: Training Compute of Notable Models
caption: **Training Compute of Notable Models**: Training compute of notable models from 2012 to 2025 on a logarithmic axis, all estimates from Epoch AI's Notable AI Models database [@sevilla2022; @epochai2026notable]. The solid least-squares fit corresponds to a doubling time of roughly `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.doubling_months_str` months; the dashed line doubles every two years, the cadence historically associated with transistor scaling, and the shaded gap between them widens every year. The axis counts operations rather than joules, so converting the trend into energy requires the realized efficiency of each run at a stated measurement boundary.
alt: Scatter plot of training compute in FLOPs against year on a log axis, rising from about 10 to the 18 for AlexNet in 2012 to about 10 to the 26 in 2025, with a solid red straight-line fit and a shallower gray dashed line that starts at the AlexNet point and doubles every two years. The region between the two lines is shaded and widens toward 2025.
context:
```

Growth in computational demand can outpace improvements in realized efficiency. @sevilla2022 estimate that the training compute of notable machine learning models doubled\index{AI Compute Growth!doubling time} roughly every six months after 2010, far faster than the two-year cadence historically associated with transistor scaling. The introduction traced this growth from AlexNet onward across seven to eight orders of magnitude (@fig-training-compute-trend); @fig-ai-compute-growth extends the same series through Grok-3 in 2025, which carries the span to nearly nine orders of magnitude, against a fitted doubling cadence of roughly `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.doubling_months_str` months. In `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.first_year_str`, AlexNet required about `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.first_flops_math` FLOPs of training compute, whereas GPT-4-class systems in `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.last_year_str` reached `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.last_flops_math`, an expansion of roughly `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.growth_million_str` million in `{python} ComputeGrowthTrend.span_years_str` years. Larger models, longer training runs, and rising serving volume each add to that total work through a different mechanism. Energy per operation can fall while total fleet energy rises; the outcome depends on how much useful work the fleet performs and how efficiently it performs that work.

title: Power and Energy Boundaries
caption: **Power and Energy Boundaries**: Substation grid feeds and facility cooling capacities impose instantaneous power caps on active accelerator concurrency. Integrating instantaneous power over wall-clock duration yields cumulative run energy; instantaneous power constraints and cumulative energy budgets represent distinct physical limits.
alt: Two panels. Panel a stacks equal server power slabs above a facility overhead block, up to a red grid-capacity line; a dashed slab for one more server crosses the line. Brackets mark one server, IT power, and facility power. Panel b plots power against wall-clock time as a fluctuating curve below the same cap, with the area under it shaded as total energy, a dashed average-power line, and a bracket marking job duration.
section: Power envelopes and the energy wall {#sec-sustainable-ai-energy-wall}
context:
The energy account divides work by realized work per joule, then applies facility overhead at the appropriate boundary. Physical infrastructure imposes a separate power constraint. The grid connection, electrical distribution, and cooling system limit the active fleet that can operate safely. A long run may consume substantial energy while remaining within its power envelope. Conversely, a short run may exceed available power even if its total energy is modest.

The two limits obey different arithmetic (@fig-energy-wall). The power limit is instantaneous. A facility cannot draw more than its grid feed ($\FacilityPower\le \GridFeedCapacity$), which caps the number of servers active at once ($\PoweredServerCount\le \InformationTechnologyPower/ \ServerPower$) regardless of how long a job runs. The energy account is cumulative, integrating average power over wall-clock time to give run energy ($\TotalEnergy = \AveragePower\times \JobDuration$). Exceeding electrical or thermal capacity can force power limiting, throttling, or protective shutdown. Cumulative energy instead enters the electricity and emissions accounts, which also depend on tariffs and the applicable grid emissions factors.

title: Model Scaling Laws
caption: **Model Scaling Laws**: In the ranges studied by @kaplan2020scaling, increasing model size, dataset size, and compute consistently reduced test loss. Each law is normalized to its loss at the smallest studied value, so on these log-log axes its slope is its exponent; the dashed staircase on the compute law marks the compute multiple that buys each successive fixed fractional reduction in loss. The figure reproduces source-paper notation, where $\Glyph{N}$ denotes parameter count and $\Glyph{C_{\text{min}}}$ denotes compute; elsewhere this book uses $\Parameters$ for parameter count and $\Operations$ for operation count. These scaling laws explain why larger models, more data, and increased compute became attractive design choices within that regime.
alt: Log-log plot of test loss relative to its starting value against the resource as a multiple of its smallest studied value. Three straight lines start at 1: dataset size in green with exponent minus 0.095 over a hundredfold range, parameters in blue with exponent minus 0.076 over a millionfold range, and compute in orange with exponent minus 0.050 over ten orders of magnitude, ending lowest. A dashed orange staircase of three tinted steps on the compute line is labeled each 10 percent lower loss costs 8.2 times compute.
context:
```

The scaling laws introduced in @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043 explain why that concentration keeps growing. Within the ranges studied by @kaplan2020scaling, test loss falls along smooth power laws\index{Scaling Laws!model} as compute, dataset tokens, and non-embedding parameters each expand over several orders of magnitude, with exponents of $-0.050$, $-0.095$, and $-0.076$ respectively (@fig-model-scaling).
